stem: A 58-year-old man with a history of long-standing hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden-onset weakness. Physical examination reveals dense paralysis of the left face, left arm, and left leg, accompanied by loss of vibration, proprioception, and pinprick sensation over the entire left side of the body. There are no visual field deficits, language abnormalities, or cranial nerve palsies other than a central lower facial droop. A non-contrast head CT reveals a small, focal lacunar infarct. Which of the following anatomical structures is most likely affected?

options.text: Anterior limb of the internal capsule
Posterior limb of the internal capsule
Ventral posteromedial (VPM) nucleus of the thalamus
Medial lemniscus in the caudal medulla

explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Posterior limb of the internal capsule.

The posterior limb of the internal capsule contains descending corticospinal motor tracts (conveying voluntary motor control to the contralateral body) and ascending third-order sensory fibers projecting from the thalamus (VPL/VPM) to the primary somatosensory cortex. A lacunar infarct in the posterior limb produces a dense contralateral combined sensorimotor stroke affecting the face, arm, and leg equally.

• Option A is incorrect: The anterior limb conveys frontopontine tracts and thalamocortical limbic projections involved in emotional and cognitive processing.
• Option B is incorrect: The genu carries corticobulbar fibers innervating cranial nerve motor nuclei; a lesion causes isolated contralateral lower facial and hypoglossal weakness without hemibody sensory loss.
• Option D is incorrect: The VPM nucleus relays facial sensation only, not the whole hemibody.
• Option E is incorrect: A caudal medullary medial lemniscus lesion produces contralateral loss of vibration and proprioception, sparing corticospinal motor pathways and pinprick sensation.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after the sudden onset of vertigo, severe nausea, and difficulty swallowing. Neurological examination reveals right-sided facial loss of pain and temperature sensation, left-sided body loss of pain and temperature sensation, right-sided Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis), hoarseness, loss of the gag reflex on the right, and severe right-sided limb ataxia. Occlusion of which of the following arteries is the most likely cause of this patient's presentation?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA).

This patient presents with Wallenberg syndrome (lateral medullary syndrome), classic for occlusion of the PICA or vertebral artery. The clinical findings map directly to lateral medullary structures:
• Nucleus ambiguus (CN IX, X): Dysphagia, hoarseness, decreased gag reflex, uvula deviation.
• Spinal trigeminal nucleus/tract: Ipsilateral facial loss of pain and temperature.
• Spinothalamic tract: Contralateral body loss of pain and temperature.
• Descending sympathetic fibers: Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).
• Inferior cerebellar peduncle: Ipsilateral limb ataxia.
• Vestibular nuclei: Vertigo, nystagmus, nausea, vomiting.

• Option A is incorrect: Medial medullary syndrome (ASA occlusion) manifests with contralateral hemiparesis, contralateral DCML sensory loss, and ipsilateral tongue deviation.
• Option B is incorrect: AICA occlusion causes lateral pontine syndrome, uniquely marked by ipsilateral facial paralysis (CN VII) and sensorineural hearing loss (CN VIII).

stem: A 71-year-old man presents with sudden-onset weakness in his right leg and urinary incontinence. On physical examination, he has 1/5 motor strength in his right lower extremity with a positive Babinski sign, while his right upper extremity exhibits 4+/5 strength. He also has marked sensory loss to pinprick and vibration over the right foot and leg, but normal sensation over the right face and arm. Which of the following cerebral arteries is most likely occluded?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Left anterior cerebral artery (ACA).

The anterior cerebral artery (ACA) supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, which corresponds to the lower extremity representation on the motor and sensory homunculi. Infarction of the ACA causes contralateral motor and sensory deficits affecting the leg and foot far more severely than the arm and face, often accompanied by frontal lobe signs such as urinary incontinence, abulia, and primitive reflexes.

• Option B is incorrect: MCA occlusion damages the lateral convexity of the hemisphere, resulting in contralateral face and arm weakness greater than leg weakness, along with aphasia or hemineglect.
• Option C is incorrect: PCA infarction causes contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.
• Options D and E are incorrect: Lenticulostriate and anterior choroidal infarcts damage the internal capsule, causing dense, proportionate weakness of the face, arm, and leg equally.

stem: A 23-year-old professional hockey player is struck on the side of the head by a puck. He suffers a brief period of concussion followed by complete lucidity. Three hours later, he complains of an excruciating headache and rapidly becomes lethargic. An unenhanced head CT reveals a biconvex, lentiform hyperdense collection that does not cross cranial suture lines. Fracturing of which of the following skull landmarks is most closely associated with this vascular injury?

options.text: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
Mastoid process of the temporal bone

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Pterion.

This patient has an epidural hematoma. The pterion is the junction of four skull bones: frontal, parietal, temporal, and greater wing of the sphenoid. It is the thinnest part of the calvarium. Deep to the pterion lies the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery (a branch of the maxillary artery). Fractures at this site lacerate the artery, resulting in arterial bleeding that strips the periosteal dura from the skull, creating a classic biconvex (lens-shaped) hematoma bounded by cranial suture lines.

• Option A is incorrect: Cribriform plate fracture tears olfactory fila (anosmia) and meninges (CSF rhinorrhea).
• Option C is incorrect: The foramen spinosum transmits the middle meningeal artery into the cranial vault, but calvarial impact fractures the pterion overlying the artery's calvarial branches.
• Option D is incorrect: The inion lies in the midline occipital bone overlying the torcular Herophili.

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents to the clinic with diplopia when walking down stairs and reading books. On examination, when she is asked to look downward and inward toward her nose with the left eye, she experiences vertical diplopia. She tilts her head toward her right shoulder to compensate. Which of the following cranial nerves is impaired, and where does it emerge from the brainstem?

options.text: Trochlear nerve (CN IV); dorsal midbrain inferior to the inferior colliculi
Oculomotor nerve (CN III); interpeduncular fossa of the ventral midbrain
Oculomotor nerve (CN III); dorsal midbrain superior to the superior colliculi

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Trochlear nerve (CN IV); dorsal midbrain inferior to the inferior colliculi.

The trochlear nerve (CN IV) innervates the superior oblique muscle, which depresses the adducted eye and intorts the globe. Lesions cause vertical diplopia that is most prominent when walking downstairs or reading (gazing downward and inward). Patients tilt their head away from the affected side (compensatory contralateral tilt) to extort the normal eye and align visual axes. Anatomically, CN IV is unique because it is the only cranial nerve that exits from the dorsal (posterior) surface of the brainstem, just caudal to the inferior colliculi.

• Option B is incorrect: CN III emerges ventrally from the interpeduncular fossa; lesions cause ptosis, a 'down-and-out' pupil, and mydriasis.
• Option C is incorrect: CN VI emerges ventrally at the pontomedullary junction and innervates the lateral rectus (abduction).
• Options D and E are incorrect: CN IV does not exit ventrally, and CN III does not exit dorsally.

stem: A 68-year-old man presents with acute-onset right-sided hemiballismus, characterized by involuntary, high-amplitude, violent, flinging movements of his right arm and leg. A head MRI reveals a discrete ischemic stroke in the deep subcortical brain. Degeneration or acute infarction of which of the following structures is most specifically responsible for this movement disorder?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Subthalamic nucleus of Luys.

Hemiballismus consists of rapid, involuntary, violent flinging movements of the contralateral limbs. It is caused by an acute lesion (usually a lacunar stroke from lenticulostriate or posterior cerebral perforators) in the contralateral subthalamic nucleus (STN). In the indirect pathway of the basal ganglia, the STN provides excitatory glutamatergic drive to the globus pallidus internus (GPi). Loss of STN excitation disinhibits the motor thalamus (VA/VL), leading to hyperkinetic motor cortical output.

• Option A is incorrect: Caudate atrophy occurs in Huntington disease, causing generalized chorea, psychiatric changes, and executive dysfunction.
• Option B is incorrect: Putaminal lesions are seen in Wilson disease and dystonia.
• Option D is incorrect: Increased (not decreased) GPi output produces the bradykinesia and rigidity of Parkinson disease.

stem: A 34-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis presents with horizontal diplopia during lateral gaze. On neurological examination, when she attempts to look to the left, her left eye abducts fully with horizontal nystagmus, but her right eye fails to adduct past the midline. However, when tested for near vision convergence, both eyes adduct symmetrically and constrict normally. This patient's deficit is localized to which of the following brainstem white matter tracts?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF).

This patient exhibits right internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). The medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) is a heavily myelinated brainstem tract that coordinates conjugate horizontal eye movements by transmitting signals from the contralateral abducens nucleus (CN VI in the pons) to the ipsilateral oculomotor nucleus (medial rectus subnucleus of CN III in the midbrain). Impaired right adduction on left conjugate gaze indicates a lesion of the right MLF. Convergence is spared because it is mediated by cortical inputs directly to CN III that bypass the MLF.

• Option A is incorrect: The central tegmental tract connects the red nucleus to the inferior olivary nucleus; damage causes palatal myoclonus.
• Option B is incorrect: The lateral lemniscus carries auditory information from the cochlear nuclei to the inferior colliculus.
• Option E is incorrect: The superior cerebellar peduncle carries dentatorubrothalamic fibers.

stem: A 54-year-old man presents with hoarseness, difficulty swallowing solid foods, and weakness shrugging his right shoulder. On physical examination, the uvula deviates to the left upon phonation, and the gag reflex is absent on the right. When asked to turn his head to the left against resistance, there is noticeable weakness of the right sternocleidomastoid muscle. Sensation to the posterior third of the tongue is absent. A tumor compressing which of the following skull base foramina would explain all of these findings?
explanation:
Correct Answer: D. Jugular foramen.

This patient has Vernet syndrome (jugular foramen syndrome), caused by compression of cranial nerves IX, X, and XI as they exit the skull base through the jugular foramen:
• CN IX (Glossopharyngeal): Loss of sensation on the posterior 1/3 of the tongue, loss of afferent limb of the gag reflex.
• CN X (Vagus): Uvula deviation to the contralateral (left) side, dysphagia, hoarseness, loss of efferent gag reflex.
• CN XI (Accessory): Weakness of the right sternocleidomastoid (causing difficulty turning the head to the left) and trapezius (shoulder droop).

• Option A is incorrect: The foramen ovale transmits CN V3, the lesser petrosal nerve, and accessory meningeal artery.
• Option B is incorrect: The foramen rotundum transmits CN V2.
• Option C is incorrect: The internal acoustic meatus transmits CN VII and CN VIII.
• Option E is incorrect: The hypoglossal canal transmits CN XII (tongue deviation).

stem: A 74-year-old woman is brought to the neurology clinic by her family because she can no longer communicate effectively. While her speech is effortless, melodious, and fluent, her sentences make no sense and consist of nonsensical neologisms and word substitutions (word salad). When given written and spoken commands, she cannot comprehend or follow them. She also cannot repeat simple phrases. A lesion in which of the following cortical areas supplied by the middle cerebral artery is responsible?

options.text: Brodmann areas 44 and 45 in the inferior frontal gyrus
Brodmann area 22 in the posterior superior temporal gyrus
Brodmann area 4 in the precentral gyrus
Brodmann areas 3, 1, and 2 in the postcentral gyrus
Brodmann area 39 in the angular gyrus

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Brodmann area 22 in the posterior superior temporal gyrus.

This patient has Wernicke (receptive/sensory/fluent) aphasia, characterized by impaired comprehension, intact speech fluency, and impaired repetition. Wernicke area corresponds to Brodmann area 22 in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere (supplied by the inferior division of the middle cerebral artery).

• Option A is incorrect: Broca area corresponds to Brodmann areas 44 and 45 in the inferior frontal gyrus; lesions produce non-fluent, halting, agrammatic speech with preserved comprehension.
• Option C is incorrect: Brodmann area 4 is the primary motor cortex in the precentral gyrus.
• Option E is incorrect: Brodmann area 39 is the angular gyrus; lesions in the dominant hemisphere produce Gerstmann syndrome (agraphia, acalculia, finger agnosia, left-right disorientation).

stem: A 66-year-old chronic alcoholic man presents with progressive ataxia and frequent falls. On physical examination, he demonstrates a wide-based, staggering, unsteady gait and marked titubation (bobbing of the trunk and head). However, when seated with his trunk supported, he performs rapid alternating movements, finger-to-nose testing, and heel-to-shin testing smoothly and without intention tremor or dysmetria. Neuropathology in this patient is most likely localized to which of the following regions?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cerebellar vermis.

The cerebellar vermis is the midline zone of the cerebellum that coordinates the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts, controlling axial balance, truncal stability, and gait. Chronic alcoholism and thiamine deficiency selectively cause atrophy of the anterior vermis, resulting in severe truncal ataxia, wide-based gait, and titubation, while sparing appendicular coordination of the limbs.

• Options B and D are incorrect: The lateral cerebellar hemispheres and dentate nuclei coordinate voluntary appendicular limb movements; lesions cause dysmetria, intention tremor, and dysdiadochokinesia of the ipsilateral limbs.
• Option C is incorrect: The flocculonodular lobe (vestibulocerebellum) controls eye movements and vestibular balance; lesions cause nystagmus, vertigo, and truncal instability.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with right visual field loss. Visual field testing reveals a right homonymous hemianopia with complete macular sparing. An MRI of the brain confirms an ischemic stroke in the occipital lobe. Which of the following cerebral arteries was most likely occluded, and which collateral vessel preserves macular vision?

options.text: Left PCA occluded; collateral supply from the left MCA
Left MCA occluded; collateral supply from the left ACA
Right PCA occluded; collateral supply from the right MCA
Left anterior choroidal artery occluded; collateral supply from the left PCA
Right ophthalmic artery occluded; collateral supply from the facial artery

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Left PCA occluded; collateral supply from the left MCA.

Infarction of the left primary visual cortex (Brodmann area 17) in the occipital lobe produces contralateral (right) homonymous hemianopia. The visual cortex is supplied by the posterior cerebral artery (PCA). Macular sparing occurs because the occipital pole (which represents the macula) possesses dual collateral blood supply from both the terminal branches of the PCA and the middle cerebral artery (MCA).

• Option B is incorrect: MCA occlusion damages optic radiations (Meyer loop or parietal radiations), causing quadrantanopias without macular sparing.
• Option C is incorrect: A right PCA infarction causes left homonymous hemianopia.
• Option D is incorrect: Anterior choroidal artery occlusion causes homonymous hemianopia without macular sparing.

stem: A 41-year-old woman is admitted to the intensive care unit with bacterial sphenoid sinusitis complicated by cavernous sinus thrombosis. On physical examination, her right eye is fixed in mid-position and cannot abduct laterally on command. When evaluating which structure is earliest affected, the physician recalls the neuroanatomy of the cavernous sinus. Which of the following cranial nerves courses freely through the interior venous lumen of the cavernous sinus alongside the internal carotid artery?
explanation:
Correct Answer: E. Abducens nerve (CN VI).

The cavernous sinus contains neurovascular structures arranged into two anatomical groups:
• Embedded within the lateral dural wall (from superior to inferior): CN III (Oculomotor), CN IV (Trochlear), CN V1 (Ophthalmic), and CN V2 (Maxillary).
• Free within the interior venous lumen of the sinus: Internal carotid artery and CN VI (Abducens nerve).
Because CN VI floats directly within the venous blood of the sinus immediately adjacent to the internal carotid artery, it is the most vulnerable nerve to early compression from thrombosis, carotid cavernous fistulas, or cavernous internal carotid aneurysms, leading to isolated lateral rectus palsy (failure of abduction).

• Options A, B, C, and D are incorrect: CN III, IV, V1, and V2 are embedded within the protective fibrous lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.

stem: A 22-year-old man survives a high-speed motorcycle crash resulting in multiple basilar skull fractures. Physical examination reveals clear, watery fluid dripping from his right nostril that tests positive for beta-2 transferrin. He also reports complete loss of his sense of smell. Shearing of delicate unmyelinated nerve fibers passing through which of the following skull base structures is the direct cause of this patient's anosmia?

options.text: Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone
Optic canal of the sphenoid bone

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone.

The olfactory nerve (CN I) consists of primary sensory axons that pass from the olfactory neuroepithelium through the perforations of the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone to synapse in the olfactory bulb. Fracture of the cribriform plate tears these delicate fila olfactoria and tears the underlying dura and arachnoid, resulting in permanent anosmia and CSF rhinorrhea (confirmed by beta-2 transferrin).

• Option B is incorrect: The optic canal transmits CN II and the ophthalmic artery.
• Option C is incorrect: The superior orbital fissure transmits CN III, IV, V1, and VI.
• Option D is incorrect: The foramen lacerum is occluded by fibrocartilage in vivo.
• Option E is incorrect: The stylomastoid foramen transmits the motor trunk of CN VII.

stem: A 60-year-old man with poorly controlled hypertension experiences an acute brainstem stroke. Physical examination demonstrates an ipsilateral flaccid paralysis of the tongue that deviates to the right upon protrusion, contralateral loss of vibration and position sense in the limbs, and contralateral spastic hemiparesis. Occlusion of which of the following arterial vessels produces this clinical triad of medial medullary syndrome?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Anterior spinal artery (ASA).

This patient presents with medial medullary syndrome (Dejerine syndrome), caused by occlusion of the anterior spinal artery (ASA) or vertebral artery paramedian branches. The syndrome damages three medial medullary structures:
1. Hypoglossal nucleus and CN XII fibers: Ipsilateral flaccid tongue paralysis with deviation toward the side of the lesion (right).
2. Pyramids (corticospinal tract): Contralateral spastic hemiparesis.
3. Medial lemniscus: Contralateral loss of vibration, conscious proprioception, and fine touch.
Pain and temperature sensation is spared because the spinothalamic tract is located laterally.

• Option A is incorrect: PICA occlusion causes lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome.
• Option C is incorrect: AICA occlusion causes lateral pontine syndrome.
• Option D is incorrect: Basilar artery paramedian branches supply the medial pons (causing abducens palsy and contralateral hemiparesis).

stem: A 35-year-old man undergoes resection of an acoustic neuroma (vestibular schwannoma) located at the cerebellopontine angle. Postoperatively, he exhibits complete paralysis of all muscles of facial expression on the right side, loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, and hyperacusis (extreme sensitivity to loud sounds). Which of the following cranial nerves was injured during the procedure, and what structure normally dampens loud sounds?

options.text: Vagus nerve (CN X); levator veli palatini

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Facial nerve (CN VII); stapedius.

The facial nerve (CN VII) emerges at the cerebellopontine angle adjacent to CN VIII. Injury causes peripheral lower motor neuron facial paralysis affecting both the upper and lower face. Branches of CN VII include:
• Nerve to the stapedius: The stapedius muscle dampens excessive vibrations of the stapes against the oval window in response to loud sounds; denervation causes hyperacusis.
• Chorda tympani: Transmits taste from the anterior 2/3 of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular and sublingual salivary glands.
• Greater petrosal nerve: Parasympathetic innervation to the lacrimal gland.

• Option A is incorrect: CN V3 innervates the tensor tympani, but its lesion does not cause facial paralysis or taste loss on the anterior 2/3 of the tongue.

stem: A 77-year-old man with memory loss undergoes brain MRI as part of a dementia workup. The radiologist notes severe, selective bilateral atrophy of the hippocampus and the primary white matter tract that projects from the subiculum of the hippocampus to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus. Disruption of this tract impairs the consolidation of new declarative memories. Which of the following structures is being described?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Fornix.

The fornix is a C-shaped bundle of white matter fibers that serves as the principal efferent projection tract of the hippocampal formation in the Papez circuit. It connects the hippocampus and subiculum to the mammillary bodies of the hypothalamus and the anterior thalamic nucleus. Bilateral transection or degeneration of the fornix impairs the Papez circuit, producing profound anterograde amnesia and inability to consolidate new declarative memories.

• Option A is incorrect: The anterior commissure connects the anterior temporal lobes and amygdalae.
• Option B is incorrect: The corpus callosum connects the bilateral neocortical hemispheres.
• Option D is incorrect: The stria terminalis is the primary efferent tract of the amygdala projecting to the hypothalamus and septal area.

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents to the clinic with unsteadiness and difficulty walking. Neurological testing demonstrates that she has an absent right patellar reflex and an absent right Achilles tendon reflex, with profound loss of vibratory sensation in her right lower extremity. Her motor strength and pinprick sensation are completely normal. Where are the primary cell bodies of the sensory neurons responsible for transmitting this vibratory input located?

options.text: Ventral horn of the spinal cord
Ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus

explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Dorsal root ganglion (DRG).

First-order sensory neurons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal (DCML) pathway (which convey vibration, fine touch, and conscious proprioception) are pseudounipolar neurons whose cell bodies reside in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG). Their peripheral processes innervate encapsulated mechanoreceptors (such as Pacinian corpuscles for vibration), while their central processes enter the spinal cord and ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal funiculus (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) without synapsing in the spinal cord.

• Option A is incorrect: The ventral horn contains somatic lower motor neuron cell bodies.
• Option B is incorrect: The substantia gelatinosa (Lamina II) contains second-order neurons for the pain and temperature pathway.
• Option D is incorrect: Nucleus gracilis contains second-order neurons of the DCML pathway in the medulla.
• Option E is incorrect: The VPL nucleus of the thalamus contains third-order sensory neurons.

stem: A 56-year-old woman suffers a subarachnoid hemorrhage. Catheter angiography demonstrates a ruptured berry aneurysm located at the junction of the internal carotid artery and the posterior communicating artery (PComA). Which of the following cranial nerve abnormalities is the most characteristic clinical sign of compression by an aneurysm at this specific anatomical location?

options.text: Ipsilateral mydriasis and ptosis with a 'down-and-out' eye
Contralateral loss of abduction with horizontal diplopia
Ipsilateral facial numbness in the V1 distribution
Ipsilateral facial paralysis including forehead weakness

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Ipsilateral mydriasis and ptosis with a 'down-and-out' eye.

The oculomotor nerve (CN III) emerges from the midbrain in the interpeduncular fossa and passes directly between the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and the superior cerebellar artery (SCA), running immediately adjacent to the posterior communicating artery (PComA). An aneurysm of the PComA compresses the superficial parasympathetic fibers of CN III first (causing a sluggish or fixed dilated 'blown' pupil / mydriasis), followed by somatic motor fibers (causing ptosis and a 'down-and-out' globe from unopposed action of the superior oblique and lateral rectus).

• Option B is incorrect: CN VI compression causes failure of abduction, associated with cavernous sinus or elevated ICP, not isolated PComA aneurysms.
• Option C is incorrect: V1 runs in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus.
• Option E is incorrect: Bitemporal hemianopia is caused by anterior communicating artery (AComA) aneurysms or pituitary macroadenomas compressing the optic chiasm.

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents to the clinic with bilateral lower extremity weakness and numbness. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals active demyelinating plaques in the corticospinal tracts and dorsal columns of the cervical spinal cord. In which of the following regions of the medulla oblongata do approximately 85% to 90% of the descending lateral corticospinal tract fibers decussate across the midline?

options.text: Rostral medulla at the level of the open fourth ventricle
Caudal medulla at the junction with the spinal cord

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Caudal medulla at the junction with the spinal cord.

The lateral corticospinal tract descends from the motor cortex through the corona radiata, posterior limb of the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle (crus cerebri), and basilar pons into the medullary pyramids. At the caudal medulla (immediately superior to the spinomedullary junction), approximately 85% to 90% of these fibers cross the midline at the pyramidal decussation to form the lateral corticospinal tract in the contralateral lateral funiculus of the spinal cord.

• Option A is incorrect: The rostral medulla features the open 4th ventricle and prominent inferior olives; decussation occurs caudally at the closed medulla.
• Option C is incorrect: The inferior olive relays climbing fibers to the contralateral cerebellum.
• Option E is incorrect: The crus cerebri is in the ventral midbrain, where corticospinal fibers are ipsilateral and have not yet decussated.

stem: A 63-year-old man who underwent resection of a meningioma presents with difficulty tasting food. Detailed cranial nerve examination reveals loss of general sensation and taste on the posterior one-third of the tongue, as well as an absent afferent gag reflex on the left side. Sensation and taste on the anterior two-thirds of his tongue are completely normal. Which of the following cranial nerves is responsible for both general somatic sensation and special visceral taste sensation on the posterior one-third of the tongue?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).

The tongue receives dual sensory innervation:
• Anterior 2/3 of tongue: General somatic sensation is mediated by the lingual nerve (branch of CN V3); special taste sensation is mediated by the chorda tympani (branch of CN VII).
• Posterior 1/3 of tongue: BOTH general somatic sensation AND special taste sensation are mediated by the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX).
• Root of tongue / epiglottis: General sensation and taste are mediated by the vagus nerve (CN X).
• Motor innervation: All intrinsic and extrinsic tongue muscles (except palatoglossus, CN X) are innervated by the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII).

• Options A and B are incorrect: CN V3 and CN VII innervate the anterior 2/3 of the tongue only.

stem: A 28-year-old primigravida presents for routine prenatal screening at 16 weeks of gestation. Maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein (MSAFP) is markedly elevated. A follow-up amniocentesis demonstrates elevated levels of both alpha-fetoprotein and acetylcholinesterase (AChE) in the amniotic fluid. High-resolution ultrasound reveals absence of the calvarium and cerebral hemispheres, with preservation of the brainstem and facial structures. Failure of which of the following embryological processes is responsible for this condition?

options.text: Closure of the caudal neuropore on Day 27–28
Closure of the rostral (cranial) neuropore on Day 25
Migration of cranial neural crest cells into the pharyngeal arches
Cleavage of the prosencephalon into two hemispheres
Radial migration of neuroblasts from the subventricular zone

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Closure of the rostral (cranial) neuropore on Day 25.

Anencephaly is an open neural tube defect caused by failure of the rostral (anterior/cranial) neuropore to close on approximately Day 25 of embryogenesis. Exposure of developing neural tissue to amniotic fluid leads to necrosis and failure of the forebrain and calvarium to develop. The open defect allows fetal CSF and tissue to transudate into amniotic fluid, causing elevated amniotic alpha-fetoprotein (AFP) and elevated acetylcholinesterase (AChE), the latter of which confirms an open neural tube defect.

• Option A is incorrect: Failure of the caudal neuropore to close on Day 27–28 causes spina bifida / myelomeningocele.
• Option C is incorrect: Defective cranial neural crest migration causes craniofacial dysmorphisms and DiGeorge syndrome.
• Option D is incorrect: Failure of prosencephalon cleavage causes holoprosencephaly.

stem: A healthy 1-month-old infant is brought to the pediatrician for a well-child checkup. Physical examination reveals a small tuft of dark coarse hair overlying the lower lumbar spine at the L5-S1 level. Neurological examination is completely normal, with brisk, symmetric lower extremity movements and intact anal sphincter tone. Prenatal screening showed a normal maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Spina bifida occulta.

Spina bifida occulta is the mildest form of neural tube defect, characterized by failure of the posterior bony vertebral arches to fuse (usually at L5-S1) while the overlying skin remains intact. The spinal cord and meninges are anatomically normal, and patients are typically asymptomatic with normal neurological examinations. Cutaneous markers such as a localized tuft of hair, skin dimple, hemangioma, or subcutaneous lipoma are common. Maternal serum AFP is normal because the defect is closed and skin-covered.

• Option B is incorrect: Meningocele involves herniation of the meninges and CSF through a bony vertebral defect, forming a skin-covered or open cystic sac.
• Option C is incorrect: Myelomeningocele involves herniation of both meninges and the spinal cord/nerve roots, resulting in motor, sensory, and sphincter deficits.
• Option D is incorrect: Myeloschisis is a severe, completely open defect where the neural plate failed to elevate and fold, leaving exposed neural placode on the back.

stem: A newborn delivered at 38 weeks of gestation is evaluated for a large, cystic lumbar mass that transilluminates. Examination demonstrates complete flaccid paraplegia of the lower limbs and an absent anal wink reflex. A sagittal brain MRI demonstrates downward displacement of both the cerebellar vermis and tonsils into the foramen magnum, associated with elongation of the brainstem and hydrocephalus secondary to aqueductal stenosis. Which of the following congenital malformations is present?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Chiari II (Arnold-Chiari) malformation.

Chiari II malformation is characterized by downward herniation of both the cerebellar vermis and tonsils through the foramen magnum into the upper cervical canal. This crowding obstructs CSF flow, kinking the brainstem and causing aqueductal stenosis and obstructive hydrocephalus. Chiari II malformation is almost universally associated with a lumbosacral myelomeningocele (herniation of spinal cord and meninges).

• Option A is incorrect: Chiari I malformation involves herniation of cerebellar tonsils only (>5 mm below foramen magnum); it typically presents in adulthood with headaches and neck pain, and is associated with syringomyelia, NOT myelomeningocele.
• Option C is incorrect: Dandy-Walker malformation is characterized by agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, cystic dilation of the 4th ventricle, and an enlarged posterior fossa.

stem: An infant presents with macrocephaly, delayed developmental milestones, and spastic diplegia. Brain MRI reveals marked agenesis of the cerebellar vermis, massive cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle filling the posterior fossa, and upward displacement of the tentorium cerebelli and torcular Herophili. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Dandy-Walker malformation.

Dandy-Walker malformation is a congenital posterior fossa anomaly characterized by the classic diagnostic triad:
1. Complete or partial agenesis of the cerebellar vermis.
2. Cystic dilation of the fourth ventricle.
3. Enlarged posterior cranial fossa with elevated tentorium cerebelli.
This malformation leads to non-communicating hydrocephalus, macrocephaly, motor delays, and cerebellar ataxia.

• Option A is incorrect: Chiari II has a small, crowded posterior fossa with downward tonsillar/vermian herniation and myelomeningocele.
• Option C is incorrect: Holoprosencephaly is failure of the forebrain to cleave.
• Option D is incorrect: Lissencephaly ('smooth brain') is a disorder of neuronal migration.

stem: A full-term infant is born with severe craniofacial dysmorphisms, including hypotelorism, a flat single-nostril proboscis, and a midline cleft lip and palate. Magnetic resonance imaging reveals a single, monoventricular brain without separation of the cerebral hemispheres into left and right sides. Mutations in which of the following embryological signaling pathways, or which chromosomal aneuploidy, is most strongly associated with this disorder?

options.text: Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway; Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway; Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome).

This infant has holoprosencephaly, caused by failure of the prosencephalon (forebrain) to cleave into two cerebral hemispheres along the midline during weeks 5 to 6 of development. It is strongly linked to mutations in the Sonic Hedgehog (SHH) pathway (which orchestrates ventral midline patterning of the brain and face) and Trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome). Phenotypes range from cyclopia and proboscis in severe forms to mild midline anomalies like a single central maxillary incisor or hypotelorism.

• Option B is incorrect: FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia and thanatophoric dysplasia.
• Options C and D are incorrect: Wnt and BMP regulate dorsal neural tube patterning (alar plate), not ventral prosencephalic cleavage.

stem: During human embryological development, the primary brain vesicles subdivide into five secondary vesicles. Which of the following secondary brain vesicles gives rise to the thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (pineal gland), and the optic cups/retina?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Diencephalon.

Embryological derivations of secondary brain vesicles:
• Prosencephalon (Forebrain) divides into:
  1. Telencephalon: Cerebral hemispheres, basal ganglia, hippocampus, lateral ventricles.
  2. Diencephalon: Thalamus, hypothalamus, epithalamus (pineal gland), optic vesicles/retina, neurohypophysis, 3rd ventricle.
• Mesencephalon (Midbrain): Midbrain, cerebral aqueduct of Sylvius.
• Rhombencephalon (Hindbrain) divides into:
  1. Metencephalon: Pons, cerebellum, upper 4th ventricle.
  2. Myelencephalon: Medulla oblongata, lower 4th ventricle.

stem: Neural crest cells represent a pluripotent population of migratory cells that originate at the margins of the neural folds. Which of the following groups of cells or tissues is entirely derived from neural crest cells?

options.text: Ventral horn motor neurons and astrocytes
Dorsal root ganglia, Schwann cells, and adrenal chromaffin cells
Pyramidal neurons of the cerebral cortex

explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Dorsal root ganglia, Schwann cells, and adrenal chromaffin cells.

Neural crest derivatives include ('MOTEL PASS'):
• Melanocytes
• Odontoblasts
• Tracheal cartilage
• Enterochromaffin cells
• Laryngeal cartilage
• Parafollicular (C) cells of thyroid
• Adrenal medulla (chromaffin cells)
• Schwann cells
• Spiral (aorticopulmonary) septum
• Sympathetic chain, dorsal root ganglia, cranial nerve sensory ganglia, and arachnoid/pia mater.

• Options A, B, and E are incorrect: Ventral horn motor neurons, cortical pyramidal neurons, oligodendrocytes, ependymal cells, and astrocytes are derived from the neuroectoderm of the neural tube.
• Option D is incorrect: Microglia are mesodermal in origin (monocyte/macrophage lineage).

stem: Public health agencies recommend periconceptional supplementation with 400 mcg of folic acid daily for all women of childbearing age to prevent neural tube defects. At the biochemical level, folate is converted to tetrahydrofolate (THF), which serves as an essential cofactor for which of the following metabolic pathways required for rapid neuroepithelial cell division during primary neurulation?

options.text: One-carbon transfer for purine and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis
Fatty acid beta-oxidation in the mitochondrial matrix
Oxidative phosphorylation via complex IV of the electron transport chain
Conversion of dopamine to norepinephrine via dopamine beta-hydroxylase

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. One-carbon transfer for purine and thymidylate (dTMP) synthesis.

Folic acid (vitamin B9) is reduced to tetrahydrofolate (THF), which acts as a carrier of one-carbon units necessary for the de novo synthesis of purines and thymidylate (dTMP via thymidylate synthase). Rapidly proliferating neuroepithelial cells during the 3rd and 4th weeks of embryogenesis depend on high rates of DNA replication for neural fold elevation, apposition, and fusion. Folate deficiency impairs DNA synthesis, arresting neurulation and resulting in anencephaly or spina bifida.

stem: A 26-year-old woman presents with suboccipital headaches exacerbated by coughing and bending forward. Neurological examination reveals bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in a 'cape-like' distribution across her neck and shoulders, while vibratory sensation and motor strength in her arms remain intact. A cervical spine MRI demonstrates a fluid-filled cavity (syrinx) within the central cord and herniation of the cerebellar tonsils 8 mm below the foramen magnum. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Chiari I malformation with syringomyelia.

Chiari I malformation is defined by downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils alone (>5 mm below the foramen magnum). It often remains asymptomatic until early adulthood, presenting with suboccipital cough-induced headaches and cerebellar ataxia. Over 50% of cases are associated with syringomyelia (a fluid-filled cavity within the central spinal canal, most commonly cervical). The syrinx selectively compresses the decussating fibers of the anterior white commissure, producing bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a 'cape-like' dermatomal distribution while sparing dorsal column touch/vibration.

• Option B is incorrect: Chiari II involves both tonsils and vermis herniation and is linked to lumbosacral myelomeningocele in infants.

stem: An infant with profound developmental delay and intractable infantile spasms undergoes neuroimaging. The MRI reveals a completely smooth cerebral surface lacking normal sulci and gyri (agyria), along with a markedly thickened, four-layered cerebral cortex. Disruption of which of the following cellular processes during gestational weeks 12 to 24 is responsible for this condition (lissencephaly)?

options.text: Radial migration of neuroblasts along radial glial scaffolds
Differentiation of the alar plate into the dorsal horn
Myelination of peripheral nerves by Schwann cells
Apoptosis of redundant motor neurons in the ventral horn

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Radial migration of neuroblasts along radial glial scaffolds.

Lissencephaly ('smooth brain') is a severe malformation of cortical development caused by arrest of neuronal radial migration between weeks 12 and 24 of gestation. Developing neuroblasts generated in the periventricular germinal zone normally migrate outward toward the pial surface along radial glial fibers to form the normal 6-layered neocortex ('inside-out' development). Genetic mutations in microtubule-associated proteins (e.g., LIS1, DCX/doublecortin) disrupt radial migration, producing a smooth cortex lacking gyri and a disorganized 4-layered cortex.

stem: In the developing spinal cord, the longitudinal groove known as the sulcus limitans divides the mantle zone into two functional regions: the dorsolateral alar plate and the ventrolateral basal plate. Which of the following adult spinal cord structures develops directly from the alar plate under the influence of Bone Morphogenetic Proteins (BMPs)?

options.text: Somatic motor neurons of the ventral horn
Autonomic motor neurons of the intermediolateral horn (T1-L2)
Sensory relay neurons and interneurons of the dorsal horn
Dorsal root ganglion sensory cell bodies

explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Sensory relay neurons and interneurons of the dorsal horn.

The sulcus limitans separates the developing mantle layer into:
• Alar plate (dorsal): Regulated by dorsal signaling molecules (BMPs and Wnt); gives rise to sensory neurons and interneurons of the dorsal horn.
• Basal plate (ventral): Regulated by ventral signaling from the notochord and floor plate (Sonic Hedgehog / SHH); gives rise to somatic motor neurons (ventral horn) and sympathetic visceral motor neurons (intermediolateral horn).

• Option D is incorrect: Dorsal root ganglion cell bodies arise from neural crest cells, not the alar plate of the neural tube.

stem: A newborn is delivered with microcephaly, sensorineural deafness, dense bilateral cataracts, and a harsh continuous machine-like murmur heard best at the left infraclavicular area (patent ductus arteriosus). The mother had an unimmunized pregnancy complicated by a low-grade fever and a fine pink maculopapular rash during the first trimester. Which of the following infectious agents is responsible for this congenital constellation?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Rubella virus.

Congenital rubella syndrome produces the classic clinical triad of:
1. Sensorineural deafness (most common)
2. Ocular defects (cataracts, retinopathy, microphthalmia)
3. Cardiac anomalies (patent ductus arteriosus [PDA], pulmonary artery stenosis)
Infected infants may also exhibit microcephaly, developmental delay, and purpuric 'blueberry muffin' skin lesions.

• Option A is incorrect: Congenital Toxoplasmosis triad is chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, and diffuse intracranial calcifications.
• Option B is incorrect: Congenital CMV manifests with periventricular calcifications, sensorineural hearing loss, and petechiae.

stem: Anatomists observe that in an 8-week-old human fetus, the spinal cord extends throughout the entire length of the vertebral canal, with coccygeal nerves exiting horizontally. However, in a normal adult, the spinal cord terminates at the L1-L2 vertebral level as the conus medullaris. Which of the following developmental mechanisms accounts for this apparent rostral 'ascent' of the spinal cord?

options.text: Apoptosis and resorption of the distal five sacral spinal cord segments
Differential elongation of the bony vertebral column relative to the spinal cord
Upward traction exerted by the enlarging cerebellum and brainstem
Failure of caudal neuropore closure leading to cord shortening
Involution of the dural sac below the thoracic level

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Differential elongation of the bony vertebral column relative to the spinal cord.

During embryogenesis, the spinal cord and vertebral column are initially of equal length. During later fetal development and childhood, the bony vertebral column and dura mater grow much more rapidly than the spinal cord. Consequently, the caudal tip of the spinal cord (conus medullaris) shifts relatively rostrally: ending at the L3 level at birth and at the L1-L2 vertebral disc space in adults. This differential growth pulls the lumbar and sacral nerve roots into an elongated sheaf of roots (the cauda equina) within the lumbar cistern.

stem: A 9-month-old infant of Ashkenazi Jewish descent is brought to the clinic for developmental regression. Over the past 3 months, he has lost the ability to sit up and roll over. On examination, he exhibits generalized hypotonia, hyperacusis (exaggerated startle response to sound), and a bright cherry-red spot in the macula of both eyes. The liver and spleen are not palpable. A deficiency of which of the following lysosomal enzymes, and accumulation of which substrate, explains this condition?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Hexosaminidase A; GM2 ganglioside.

Tay-Sachs disease is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by a deficiency of Hexosaminidase A, leading to toxic accumulation of GM2 ganglioside in neuronal lysosomes (demonstrating characteristic 'onion-skin' lamellar lysosomal inclusions on electron microscopy). Clinical hallmarks:
• Progressive neurodegeneration and loss of motor milestones
• Hyperacusis (exaggerated acoustic startle response)
• Macular cherry-red spot (caused by lipid accumulation in retinal ganglion cells surrounding the fovea)
• ABSENCE of hepatosplenomegaly (distinguishing it from Niemann-Pick disease).

• Option A is incorrect: Niemann-Pick disease is caused by sphingomyelinase deficiency and presents with a macular cherry-red spot PLUS hepatosplenomegaly and foam cells on histology.

stem: A 10-month-old child presents with progressive motor regression and failure to thrive. Physical examination reveals massive hepatosplenomegaly, severe hypotonia, and a cherry-red macular spot on fundoscopic examination. Bone marrow biopsy demonstrates lipid-laden foamy histiocytes. Which of the following lysosomal storage enzymes is deficient in this patient?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Sphingomyelinase (Niemann-Pick disease).

Niemann-Pick disease (Type A) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by deficiency of acid sphingomyelinase, resulting in accumulation of sphingomyelin. It presents in infancy with:
• Neurodegeneration and loss of motor skills
• Macular cherry-red spot
• Massive hepatosplenomegaly (due to reticuloendothelial accumulation)
• Foam cells (lipid-laden foamy macrophages) on bone marrow biopsy.
This is distinguished from Tay-Sachs disease by the presence of prominent hepatosplenomegaly.

• Option C is incorrect: Gaucher disease features hepatosplenomegaly and bone crises with crumpled tissue-paper macrophages, but NO cherry-red spot.

stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with progressive bone pain, recurrent fractures, and pancytopenia. Abdominal examination reveals marked splenomegaly. Bone marrow aspirate reveals numerous enlarged, lipid-laden macrophages with a cytoplasm that resembles 'wrinkled tissue paper' or 'crumpled silk.' Which of the following lysosomal storage diseases is characterized by this finding?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Gaucher disease.

Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disease, caused by an autosomal recessive deficiency of beta-glucocerebrosidase (acid beta-glucosidase), leading to accumulation of glucocerebroside. Clinical features:
• Hepatosplenomegaly (painless, massive)
• Pancytopenia (anemia, thrombocytopenia) due to splenic sequestration and marrow infiltration
• Bone crises, osteonecrosis of the femoral head, and Erlenmeyer flask bone deformities
• Histopathology: Gaucher cells, which are lipid-laden macrophages with striated cytoplasm resembling 'wrinkled tissue paper' or 'crumpled silk.'

• Option D is incorrect: Metachromatic leukodystrophy is caused by arylsulfatase A deficiency, resulting in central/peripheral demyelination without bone crises.
• Option E is incorrect: Krabbe disease features galactocerebrosidase deficiency and globoid cells.

stem: A 1-year-old child presents with progressive spasticity, irritability, optic atrophy, and loss of developmental milestones. Brain MRI demonstrates diffuse, symmetrical loss of myelin in the cerebral white matter. Brain biopsy reveals globoid, multinucleated cells clustered in perivascular spaces of the white matter. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is responsible for Krabbe disease?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Galactocerebrosidase (galactosylceramidase).

Krabbe disease (globoid cell leukodystrophy) is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disease caused by deficiency of galactocerebrosidase (galactosylceramidase), resulting in the accumulation of galactocerebroside and toxic psychosine in oligodendrocytes. Pathological hallmark:
• Destruction of myelin (severe dysmyelinating leukodystrophy)
• Accumulation of multinucleated, phagocytic 'globoid cells' surrounding blood vessels in white matter
• Clinical features: progressive peripheral neuropathy, spasticity, optic atrophy, developmental arrest, and death by age 2.

• Option B is incorrect: Arylsulfatase A deficiency causes metachromatic leukodystrophy (cerebroside sulfate accumulation).
• Option C is incorrect: Alpha-galactosidase A deficiency causes Fabry disease (angiokeratomas, neuropathic pain, renal/cardiac failure).

stem: A 4-year-old boy presents with progressive difficulty walking, frequent falls, and cognitive decline. Nerve conduction studies demonstrate markedly slowed motor conduction velocities consistent with demyelinating sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Sural nerve biopsy reveals brown-staining metachromatic granules within Schwann cells and macrophages when stained with cresyl violet or toluidine blue. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes causes this condition?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Arylsulfatase A.

Metachromatic leukodystrophy is an autosomal recessive lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of arylsulfatase A, resulting in the toxic accumulation of sulfatides (galactosyl sulfatide / cerebroside sulfate) in oligodendrocytes and Schwann cells. This causes diffuse central and peripheral demyelination, leading to progressive ataxia, spasticity, and dementia. Sulfatides shift the absorption spectrum of dyes such as cresyl violet, producing characteristic brown-gold 'metachromasia' on histological staining.

• Options C and D are incorrect: Mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler and Hunter syndromes) involve alpha-L-iduronidase and iduronate-2-sulfatase, accumulating heparan and dermatan sulfate.

stem: A newborn with micrognathia, low-set ears, and a cleft palate develops hypocalcemic tetany on day 2 of life. Echocardiogram demonstrates tetralogy of Fallot. Flow cytometry reveals an absolute absence of mature T lymphocytes. This patient's syndrome (DiGeorge syndrome, 22q11.2 deletion) results from defective migration of which of the following embryological cell types into the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Neural crest cells.

DiGeorge syndrome (22q11.2 deletion syndrome) results from defective migration of cranial neural crest cells into the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches and pharyngeal arches. This causes:
• Thymic aplasia: Absence of thymic shadow on chest X-ray, leading to severe T-cell immunodeficiency and recurrent viral/fungal infections.
• Parathyroid hypoplasia: Hypocalcemia causing neonatal tetany, seizures, or carpopedal spasms.
• Conotruncal cardiac defects: Tetralogy of Fallot, truncus arteriosus, interrupted aortic arch.
• Craniofacial dysmorphisms: Micrognathia, low-set malformed ears, cleft palate.

• Options B, C, and D are incorrect: The primary embryological defect is failure of neural crest cell migration into the pharyngeal apparatus.

stem: A 19-year-old woman with refractory epilepsy undergoes brain MRI. The scan demonstrates multiple small, smooth, rounded nodules of gray matter lining the lateral walls of both lateral ventricles, protruding into the ventricular lumen. These ectopic gray matter nodules are isointense to normal cerebral cortex on all pulse sequences. This developmental disorder (periventricular nodular heterotopia) is caused by failure of which of the following neuroembryological processes?

options.text: Failure of neuroblasts to initiate radial migration away from the ventricular zone
Failure of anterior neuropore closure during primary neurulation
Defective cleavage of the embryonic telencephalon along the midline
Excessive apoptosis of neuroblasts in the subplate zone
Failure of secondary neurulation in the caudal eminence

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Failure of neuroblasts to initiate radial migration away from the ventricular zone.

Periventricular nodular heterotopia (often X-linked dominant due to mutations in the filamin A / FLNA gene) is a disorder of neuronal migration. During cortical development, neuroblasts are born in the periventricular germinal zone and must migrate radially outward along radial glial fibers to reach the cortical plate. In periventricular heterotopia, subsets of neurons fail to initiate migration and remain arrested as ectopic nodules of normal-appearing gray matter along the ventricular lining, which act as epileptogenic foci.

• Option B is incorrect: Failure of neuropore closure causes anencephaly or spina bifida.
• Option C is incorrect: Defective telencephalic cleavage causes holoprosencephaly.
• Option E is incorrect: Defective secondary neurulation produces closed caudal spinal dysraphism.

stem: In a resting human neuron, the resting membrane potential settles at approximately -70 mV. While the electrogenic Na+/K+ ATPase pumps 3 Na+ ions out of the cell for every 2 K+ ions pumped in, which of the following membrane channels is the primary determinant of this resting negative electrical potential?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Non-gated (constitutively open) potassium leak channels.

The resting membrane potential of a neuron (typically -70 mV) is primarily determined by high resting membrane permeability to K+ ions via constitutively open, non-gated K+ leak channels (such as two-pore domain K2P channels). Because the resting membrane is approximately 25 to 100 times more permeable to K+ than to Na+, the membrane potential settles close to the equilibrium potential for potassium (EK ≈ -90 mV), as predicted by the Goldman-Hodgkin-Katz equation. The Na+/K+ ATPase maintains the chemical concentration gradients.

• Option A is incorrect: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open during the rapid depolarizing phase of the action potential.
• Option C is incorrect: Nicotinic channels open only in the presence of acetylcholine.

stem: A 32-year-old traveler consumes fugu (pufferfish) at an unlicensed coastal market. Within 45 minutes, he experiences intense perioral paresthesias, numbness of the tongue, nausea, and ascending flaccid paralysis of his limbs. Physical examination reveals intact mental status, absent deep tendon reflexes, and shallow respirations. Tetrodotoxin is confirmed as the causative agent. By which of the following molecular mechanisms does this toxin prevent action potential generation?

options.text: Selective blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels
Inhibition of delayed rectifier voltage-gated potassium channels
Blockade of presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels
Cleavage of the SNARE protein synaptobrevin

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Selective blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels.

Tetrodotoxin (found in pufferfish/fugu) and saxitoxin (found in 'red tide' dinoflagellates) bind with nanomolar affinity to site 1 on the extracellular pore of voltage-gated Na+ channels (Nav) in nerves and skeletal muscle. This physically blocks Na+ influx, completely arresting action potential upstroke and conduction. Patients experience perioral tingling, motor weakness, hyporeflexia, and death from respiratory paralysis, with completely preserved consciousness.

• Option B is incorrect: K+ channel blockers (e.g., 4-aminopyridine, tetraethylammonium) prolong action potential duration.
• Option C is incorrect: P/Q-type Ca2+ channels are blocked by Lambert-Eaton autoantibodies or omega-agatoxin.
• Option D is incorrect: Synaptobrevin is cleaved by tetanus toxin and botulinum toxin B, D, F, G.

stem: During the repolarization phase of a neuronal action potential, an axon cannot generate another action potential regardless of the strength or duration of the depolarizing electrical stimulus. Which of the following states of the voltage-gated sodium channel is responsible for this absolute refractory period?

options.text: Activation (m) gates are closed, inactivation (h) gates are open
Activation (m) gates are open, inactivation (h) gates are open

explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Inactivation (h) gates are closed.

Voltage-gated Na+ channels exist in three functional states controlled by two distinct gates:
1. Resting (closed): Activation (m) gate is closed; inactivation (h) gate is open. The channel is closed but excitable.
2. Activated (open): Both m and h gates are open. Occurs upon depolarization to threshold.
3. Inactivated: The slow inactivation (h) gate closes shortly after depolarization. Because the h gate is closed, the channel cannot be opened by any depolarizing stimulus. This state defines the absolute refractory period. The channel must repolarize toward resting potential to reset ('de-inactivate') the h gate before it can open again.

stem: A 45-year-old dentist prepares to perform an incision and drainage on a tense, acidic mandibular abscess. She injects 2% lidocaine locally around the inflamed tissue. However, despite adequate dosing, the patient continues to experience sharp pain during the incision. Which of the following physicochemical properties explains why local anesthetics have markedly reduced efficacy in infected, inflamed tissues?

options.text: Low extracellular pH shifts the anesthetic to its uncharged lipophilic form, speeding its entry
Low extracellular pH shifts the anesthetic to its charged (protonated) hydrophilic form, impairing membrane penetration
Inflammation activates tissue esterases that instantly degrade all amide local anesthetics
Acidosis irreversibly blocks the intracellular binding site of voltage-gated sodium channels
Vasoconstriction caused by acidosis rapidly washes the anesthetic out of the tissue

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Low extracellular pH shifts the anesthetic to its charged (protonated) hydrophilic form, impairing membrane penetration.

Local anesthetics are weak bases (pKa 8.0-9.0). To cross the neuronal lipid bilayer, they must exist in their uncharged, non-ionized lipophilic form (B). Once inside the axoplasm, the drug becomes protonated to its charged form (BH+), which binds to the inner pore of the voltage-gated Na+ channel to block conduction. In infected tissues, extracellular acidosis (pH < 6.0) shifts the equilibrium (Henderson-Hasselbalch equation) toward the ionized, protonated form (BH+). Because ionized molecules cannot readily diffuse across cell membranes, insufficient drug enters the axon, leading to failed anesthesia.

• Option A is incorrect: Acidic pH protonates the base, increasing the charged fraction, not the uncharged fraction.
• Option C is incorrect: Amide anesthetics are metabolized by hepatic CYP450 enzymes, not tissue esterases.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with chronic tuberculosis is prescribed an antimicrobial regimen including isoniazid. Four weeks into therapy, she develops recurrent generalized tonic-clonic seizures that are refractory to standard anticonvulsant therapy. Laboratory evaluation confirms marked deficiency of active pyridoxal phosphate (vitamin B6). The patient's neuronal hyperexcitability and seizures result from impaired synthesis of which of the following inhibitory neurotransmitters?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA).

GABA is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter of the brain. It is synthesized from glutamate via the enzyme glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), which strictly requires pyridoxal phosphate (PLP, the active form of vitamin B6) as a cofactor. Isoniazid inhibits pyridoxine phosphokinase and forms inactive complexes with pyridoxine, depleting B6. Reduced GAD activity decreases brain GABA levels, leading to loss of central inhibition, neuronal hyperexcitability, and refractory seizures (treated with IV pyridoxine).

• Option A is incorrect: Glycine is the primary inhibitory neurotransmitter in the spinal cord, synthesized from serine.
• Option C is incorrect: Glutamate is excitatory; its synthesis does not depend on GAD.

stem: A 24-year-old man presents to the emergency department with acute severe panic and agitation. He is administered IV lorazepam. Within minutes, his anxiety resolves and he becomes calm and drowsy. Lorazepam binds allosterically to the GABA-A receptor complex. Which of the following biophysical actions directly mediates the inhibitory effect of benzodiazepines?

options.text: Increases the duration of chloride channel opening
Increases the frequency of chloride channel opening
Directly gates the open state of the channel in the complete absence of GABA
Promotes potassium efflux via Gi-protein-coupled metabotropic receptors
Blocks presynaptic reuptake of GABA via GAT-1 transporters

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Increases the frequency of chloride channel opening.

The GABA-A receptor is an ionotropic, ligand-gated chloride channel composed of five subunits. 
• Benzodiazepines (e.g., lorazepam, diazepam) bind to an allosteric regulatory site and facilitate GABA binding, increasing the FREQUENCY of chloride channel opening in the presence of GABA ('Frenzodiazepines'). Influx of Cl- hyperpolarizes the membrane, inhibiting action potential generation.
• Barbiturates (e.g., phenobarbital), in contrast, increase the DURATION of chloride channel opening ('BarbiDURATes') and at high doses can directly open the channel even without GABA, explaining their higher risk of fatal respiratory depression.

• Option D is incorrect: Potassium efflux via Gi is mediated by GABA-B metabotropic receptors (e.g., baclofen).

stem: A neurobiologist studying hippocampal synaptic plasticity observes that low-frequency stimulation produces basal transmission, whereas high-frequency tetanic stimulation triggers long-term potentiation (LTP). LTP induction strictly requires the removal of an extracellular magnesium ion (Mg2+) that physically blocks which of the following postsynaptic glutamate receptors at resting membrane potentials?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. NMDA receptor.

The NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) receptor is a ligand-gated, calcium-permeable ionotropic glutamate receptor. At resting membrane potentials (-70 mV), extracellular Mg2+ physically blocks the channel pore. When adjacent AMPA receptors are activated by glutamate, the resulting Na+ influx depolarizes the postsynaptic membrane. This membrane depolarization expels the Mg2+ plug ('voltage-dependent unblock'). Glutamate and its co-agonist glycine can then open the unblocked NMDA channel, allowing high Ca2+ influx that activates CaMKII and PKC, leading to AMPA receptor insertion and long-term potentiation (LTP).

• Option A is incorrect: AMPA receptors are non-selective cation channels (Na+/K+) that are not blocked by Mg2+ at resting potentials.

stem: A 50-year-old woman with severe depression refractory to multiple medications is started on the non-selective monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) tranylcypromine. Two weeks later, she attends a wine and cheese party and consumes aged cheddar and chianti. Within 45 minutes, she develops a severe occipital throbbing headache, palpitations, and a blood pressure of 210/120 mmHg. Tyramine accumulation induced massive displacement and release of which of the following neurotransmitters?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Norepinephrine.

This patient is experiencing the 'cheese reaction' (hypertensive crisis) caused by combining a non-selective MAOI with tyramine-rich foods (aged cheeses, red wine, cured meats). Dietary tyramine is normally degraded by intestinal and hepatic monoamine oxidase A (MAO-A). When MAO-A is inhibited, tyramine enters the systemic circulation and is transported into sympathetic nerve terminals via the norepinephrine transporter (NET). Tyramine displaces stored norepinephrine from synaptic vesicles into the synaptic cleft, resulting in massive stimulation of alpha-1 and beta-1 adrenergic receptors, causing severe vasoconstriction and hypertensive crisis.

• Option A is incorrect: Combining MAOIs with serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, tramadol) causes Serotonin Syndrome, but tyramine specifically displaces stored catecholamines (norepinephrine).

stem: In the biosynthetic pathway of catecholamines in the central nervous system, what is the rate-limiting enzyme responsible for converting L-tyrosine into L-DOPA, and which essential cofactor does it require?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Tyrosine hydroxylase; Tetrahydrobiopterin (BH4).

Catecholamine synthesis pathway:
1. Tyrosine → L-DOPA via Tyrosine hydroxylase (RATE-LIMITING step; requires tetrahydrobiopterin / BH4 and molecular oxygen).
2. L-DOPA → Dopamine via DOPA decarboxylase (requires vitamin B6 / pyridoxal phosphate).
3. Dopamine → Norepinephrine via Dopamine beta-hydroxylase (requires vitamin C / ascorbic acid and copper).
4. Norepinephrine → Epinephrine via PNMT (requires SAM; stimulated by cortisol in adrenal medulla).

• Option A is incorrect: DOPA decarboxylase is downstream and is not rate-limiting.
• Option C is incorrect: Dopamine beta-hydroxylase converts dopamine to norepinephrine.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the clinic with severe mood disturbances, sleep dysregulation, and impulsive behavior. Neurological evaluation highlights the role of serotonergic pathways in modulating mood and affect. Where are the primary cell bodies of serotonin-producing projection neurons in the central nervous system concentrated, and what amino acid is the initial precursor?

options.text: Locus coeruleus in the dorsal rostral pons; Tyrosine
Raphe nuclei of the brainstem; Tryptophan
Tuberomammillary nucleus of the hypothalamus; Histidine

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Raphe nuclei of the brainstem; Tryptophan.

Serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine / 5-HT) is synthesized predominantly in the median and dorsal raphe nuclei located throughout the brainstem (midbrain, pons, and medulla). The biosynthetic precursor is the essential amino acid tryptophan:
1. Tryptophan → 5-hydroxytryptophan via Tryptophan hydroxylase (rate-limiting, requires BH4).
2. 5-hydroxytryptophan → Serotonin via Aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase (requires vitamin B6).

• Option A is incorrect: The locus coeruleus synthesizes norepinephrine from tyrosine.
• Option C is incorrect: The substantia nigra synthesizes dopamine.
• Option D is incorrect: The nucleus basalis of Meynert synthesizes acetylcholine.

stem: An elderly patient with memory impairment is diagnosed with Alzheimer disease and started on donepezil. Post-mortem studies of Alzheimer disease consistently demonstrate a marked loss of cholinergic projection neurons in the basal forebrain that normally project diffusely to the neocortex and hippocampus. Degeneration of which of the following specific nuclei is primarily responsible for this profound central acetylcholine deficiency?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Nucleus basalis of Meynert.

The nucleus basalis of Meynert (located in the substantia innominata of the basal forebrain) provides widespread cholinergic innervation to the cerebral cortex, amygdala, and hippocampus. Profound loss of these cholinergic neurons and reduced choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) activity are consistent hallmarks of Alzheimer disease, providing the pharmacological rationale for acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine).

• Option A is incorrect: The locus coeruleus is noradrenergic.
• Option C is incorrect: The VTA is dopaminergic (mesolimbic/mesocortical pathways).
• Option D is incorrect: The pedunculopontine nucleus regulates brainstem locomotion.

stem: A 7-year-old boy steps on a rusty nail while playing in an abandoned shed. Ten days later, he develops trismus (lockjaw), painful sustained facial contractions (risus sardonicus), and involuntary back arching spasms (opisthotonos) triggered by light and noise. Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) produced by Clostridium tetani is suspected. By which of the following mechanisms does this toxin produce spastic paralysis?

options.text: Cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP) in inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells), preventing glycine and GABA release
Cleaves SNAP-25 in somatic motor nerve terminals, preventing acetylcholine release
Directly antagonizes postsynaptic nicotinic receptors on skeletal muscle endplates
Blocks voltage-gated calcium channels on presynaptic autonomic nerves
Inactivates acetylcholinesterase at the neuromuscular junction

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cleaves synaptobrevin (VAMP) in inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells), preventing glycine and GABA release.

Tetanus toxin (tetanospasmin) enters motor nerve terminals and undergoes retrograde axonal transport to the spinal cord. It crosses synapses into inhibitory interneurons (Renshaw cells) in the spinal cord and brainstem. There, its zinc-metalloprotease light chain cleaves the SNARE protein synaptobrevin (VAMP-2), preventing vesicle fusion and exocytosis of the inhibitory neurotransmitters glycine and GABA. Loss of inhibitory drive disinhibits alpha motor neurons, causing uncontrolled muscle contraction, trismus, and tetanic spasms (spastic paralysis).

• Option B is incorrect: Botulinum toxin (serotypes A and E) cleaves SNAP-25 in peripheral motor nerve endings, blocking ACh release and producing FLACCID paralysis.

stem: During chemical synaptic transmission, the arrival of an action potential at the presynaptic nerve terminal triggers vesicle exocytosis and neurotransmitter release into the synaptic cleft. Which of the following critical intracellular events couples membrane depolarization to the fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic active zone?

options.text: Efflux of potassium ions through delayed rectifier channels
Influx of calcium ions through voltage-gated calcium channels
Influx of chloride ions through ionotropic GABA channels
Phosphorylation of the Na+/K+ ATPase by protein kinase A
Hydrolysis of cyclic GMP by phosphodiesterase 5

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Influx of calcium ions through voltage-gated calcium channels.

When a depolarizing action potential reaches the presynaptic bouton, it opens presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (P/Q-type and N-type). The resulting rapid influx of Ca2+ down its steep electrochemical gradient binds to synaptotagmin, the calcium sensor on synaptic vesicle membranes. Calcium-bound synaptotagmin interacts with SNARE core complexes (synaptobrevin, syntaxin, SNAP-25), driving vesicle fusion with the presynaptic plasma membrane and pore opening to release neurotransmitter.

• Options A, C, and D are incorrect: Intracellular Ca2+ influx is the universal, obligate signal coupling electrical depolarization to synaptic vesicle exocytosis.

stem: A neuropathologist examines a brain biopsy from the margin of a chronic cerebral infarct. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrates an intense proliferation of star-shaped glial cells that are strongly immunoreactive for Glial Fibrillary Acidic Protein (GFAP). Under normal physiological conditions, which of the following is a primary function of these astrocytes in the central nervous system?

options.text: Formation of myelin sheaths around multiple central axons
Buffering of extracellular potassium and uptake/recycling of synaptic glutamate
Immune surveillance and phagocytosis of cellular debris
Production of cerebrospinal fluid via modified choroid plexuses

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Buffering of extracellular potassium and uptake/recycling of synaptic glutamate.

Astrocytes are the most abundant glial cells in the CNS and express GFAP intermediate filaments. Major functions include:
1. Extracellular K+ spatial buffering to maintain neuronal excitability.
2. Uptake of synaptic glutamate via excitatory amino acid transporters (EAATs), converting it to glutamine via glutamine synthetase (the glutamate-glutamine cycle) to prevent excitotoxicity.
3. Induction and maintenance of the blood-brain barrier via astrocyte end-feet (podocytes).
4. Glycogen storage and lactate provision to neurons.
5. Formation of a 'glial scar' (astrogliosis/gliosis) following CNS injury.

• Option A is incorrect: Oligodendrocytes form CNS myelin.
• Option C is incorrect: Microglia perform phagocytosis and immune surveillance.
• Option D is incorrect: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and form choroid plexus epithelium.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with a history of HIV infection presents with progressive cognitive slowing and behavioral changes. Autopsy reveals diffuse microglial nodules and multinucleated giant cells within the subcortical white matter and basal ganglia (HIV-associated dementia). From which of the following embryological germ layers do microglial cells originate?
explanation:
Correct Answer: C. Mesoderm (mesenchymal monocyte/macrophage lineage).

Unlike all other central nervous system cells (neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependymal cells, which are derived from neuroectoderm), microglia originate from the embryonic mesoderm. Specifically, they arise from primitive macrophage precursors in the yolk sac that migrate into the developing neural tube during early embryogenesis. Microglia serve as resident CNS macrophages. In HIV-associated dementia, HIV enters the brain via infected monocytes/macrophages and infects microglia, forming characteristic multinucleated giant cells.

• Options A and B are incorrect: Neuroectoderm gives rise to neurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and ependyma; neural crest gives rise to Schwann cells and PNS ganglia.

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with sudden, brief, shock-like sensations radiating down her spine into her legs upon flexing her neck forward (Lhermitte sign). An MRI reveals multiple hyperintense periventricular and spinal cord lesions on T2/FLAIR sequences. Her condition is characterized by autoimmune destruction of central myelin. Which of the following glial cells produces myelin sheaths for multiple axons in the central nervous system, and what is its histological appearance?

options.text: Oligodendrocyte; round nucleus with clear halo ('fried egg' appearance)
Astrocyte; star-shaped cell with GFAP filaments

explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Oligodendrocyte; round nucleus with clear halo ('fried egg' appearance).

Oligodendrocytes are neuroectoderm-derived glial cells that produce and maintain myelin sheaths in the central nervous system. A single oligodendrocyte can extend processes to myelinate segments of up to 30 to 50 separate axons. On routine histological sections, oligodendrocytes display a rounded, dark nucleus surrounded by a clear cytoplasmic halo (often described as a 'fried egg' appearance). They are the target of autoimmune demyelination in multiple sclerosis.

• Option A is incorrect: Schwann cells myelinate a single internode of a single axon in the peripheral nervous system and are derived from neural crest cells.

stem: Under resting conditions, the brain consumes approximately 20% of the body's total glucose and oxygen despite representing only 2% of total body mass. During periods of prolonged fasting or starvation lasting longer than 48 to 72 hours, which of the following circulating substrates crosses the blood-brain barrier via monocarboxylate transporters to provide the majority of the brain's energy needs?
explanation:
Correct Answer: B. Ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate).

Under normal well-fed conditions, the brain is an obligate consumer of D-glucose (transported across the BBB by GLUT1 and into neurons by GLUT3). However, during prolonged fasting or starvation (>48-72 hours), hepatic glycogen stores are depleted. The liver oxidizes fatty acids to generate ketone bodies (beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate). These water-soluble ketone bodies cross the blood-brain barrier via monocarboxylate transporters (MCT1) and are converted in neurons into acetyl-CoA, providing up to 60-70% of the brain's ATP and sparing muscle protein from gluconeogenesis.

• Option A is incorrect: Long-chain free fatty acids cannot cross the blood-brain barrier in significant quantities to meet metabolic demand.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with painful muscle spasms and stiffness. Laboratory evaluation confirms the presence of high-titer autoantibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase (anti-GAD antibodies), establishing a diagnosis of Stiff-Person syndrome. Physiologically, GAD catalyzes the decarboxylation of which of the following excitatory amino acids to produce the central nervous system's primary inhibitory neurotransmitter?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Glutamate.

Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) catalyzes the conversion of the excitatory neurotransmitter L-glutamate into gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), the major inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS.
