On Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI), the central non-enhancing core of the lesion shows intensely bright hyperintensity with corresponding dark hypointensity on the ADC map (marked restricted diffusion). Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Bacterial brain abscess.

A bacterial brain abscess appears on contrast MRI as a smooth, uniformly thin, ring-enhancing capsule surrounded by prominent vasogenic edema. The definitive imaging feature that distinguishes an abscess from a necrotic tumor (glioblastoma or metastasis) is Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI):
• Abscess core contains viscous pus composed of dense, packed neutrophils, necrotic debris, and cellular macromolecules, which severely restricts the Brownian motion of water molecules.
• This produces marked central restricted diffusion (bright on DWI, dark on ADC map).
• In contrast, the necrotic core of a glioblastoma is serous fluid that does NOT restrict diffusion (dark on DWI, bright on ADC).

stem: A 48-year-old woman presents with bilateral lower extremity weakness and visual disturbances. MRI of the brain and spine reveals multiple demyelinating lesions. On sagittal T2/FLAIR sequences of the brain, several linear, finger-like hyperintense plaques are observed extending perpendicularly outward from the ependymal surface of the lateral ventricles into the corpus callosum ('Dawson fingers'). Which of the following histological processes is responsible for these characteristic MRI findings?

options.text: Perivenular lymphocytic inflammation and demyelination surrounding deep medullary veins
Arterial microinfarctions within the territory of lenticulostriate perforators
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis of long circumferential pontine arteries
Metastatic tumor seeding through the Virchow-Robin spaces

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Perivenular lymphocytic inflammation and demyelination surrounding deep medullary veins.

'Dawson fingers' are a classic radiographic hallmark of multiple sclerosis on sagittal FLAIR or T2 MRI sequences. They appear as ovoid or linear demyelinating plaques oriented perpendicularly to the ventricular margins, extending into the corpus callosum and centrum semiovale. Neuropathologically, MS is a perivenular inflammatory disease: autoreactive T-cell infiltration and complement-mediated myelin destruction occur along the path of deep medullary venules that drain perpendicularly into the subependymal veins of the lateral ventricles.

stem: A 72-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to the emergency department with sudden severe right hemiparesis and stupor. A non-contrast head CT reveals a 4.5 cm hyperdense (65 HU) collection centered in the left putamen and posterior limb of the internal capsule, with surrounding hypodense edema and mass effect compressing the left lateral ventricle. Rupture of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms involving which of the following arterial branches is the most common cause of this hypertensive intraparenchymal hemorrhage?

options.text: Lenticulostriate arteries (branches of the middle cerebral artery)
Cortical branches of the anterior cerebral artery

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Lenticulostriate arteries (branches of the middle cerebral artery).

Chronic hypertension causes hyaline arteriolosclerosis and lipohyalinosis of small, deep penetrating arterioles, leading to the formation of Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysms. Rupture of these microaneurysms causes spontaneous intraparenchymal (intracerebral) hemorrhage. The most common anatomical site is the basal ganglia / putamen (~50-60% of cases), supplied by the lenticulostriate branches of the middle cerebral artery (MCA). Other common sites include the thalamus, pons, and cerebellar hemispheres.

• Option D is incorrect: Berry aneurysms of the anterior communicating artery rupture into the subarachnoid space (causing subarachnoid hemorrhage), not the deep basal ganglia.

stem: A 21-year-old unrestrained driver is involved in a high-speed rollover motor vehicle collision. In the trauma bay, his Glasgow Coma Scale score is 4 (E1V1M2), and he is intubated. Initial non-contrast head CT reveals no skull fractures, no epidural or subdural hematomas, and only a tiny punctate petechial hyperdensity at the gray-white matter interface of the frontal lobe. An urgent MRI using Gradient Echo (GRE) and Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging (SWI) reveals numerous punctate hypointense blooming lesions distributed throughout the gray-white junction and the splenium of the corpus callosum. Which of the following traumatic injuries is present?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Diffuse axonal injury (DAI).

Diffuse axonal injury (DAI) is caused by high-velocity rotational acceleration-deceleration forces that generate shear stress at interfaces between tissues of differing density (most prominently the gray-white matter junction, corpus callosum, and dorsal brainstem). Axons stretch and shear, disrupting the axoskeleton and axonal transport, causing axonal retraction balls (beta-APP immunoreactive). Patients present in immediate coma that is strikingly disproportionate to early CT findings (which may appear normal or show subtle punctate hemorrhages). GRE and SWI sequences on MRI are diagnostic, revealing punctate hypointense microbleeds ('blooming artifact') from sheared microvessels.

stem: An 8-year-old boy presents with progressive morning headaches, vomiting, and gait ataxia. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the brain reveals a well-circumscribed cystic lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere containing an intensely enhancing mural nodule. The surrounding brain parenchyma shows minimal vasogenic edema. Surgical resection is performed. Histopathology reveals bipolar cells with long, thin 'hair-like' cytoplasmic processes and corkscrew-shaped eosinophilic Rosenthal fibers. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Pilocytic astrocytoma.

Pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade 1) is the most common primary brain tumor in children. It most frequently arises in the cerebellum. Radiographic appearance:
• Well-circumscribed, cystic lesion with an intensely enhancing mural nodule on contrast MRI.
Histological hallmarks:
• Bipolar astrocytic cells with long, thin processes ('hair-like' / pilocytic).
• Rosenthal fibers: Corkscrew-shaped, brightly eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions composed of alpha-B-crystallin and heat shock proteins.
• Excellent prognosis following surgical resection.

• Option B is incorrect: Medulloblastoma is a solid, poorly differentiated embryonal tumor (small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes) in the cerebellar vermis.

stem: A 6-year-old boy presents with unsteady gait, frequent falls, and morning vomiting. Brain MRI demonstrates a solid, contrast-enhancing mass originating from the cerebellar vermis in the midline, compressing the fourth ventricle and causing obstructive hydrocephalus. Histopathological evaluation reveals sheets of densely packed small round blue cells with hyperchromatic nuclei, high mitotic index, and Homer Wright rosettes (tumor cells surrounding a central neuropil). Which of the following is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Medulloblastoma.

Medulloblastoma is the most common malignant brain tumor in childhood (WHO grade 4). It is a primitive neuroectodermal embryonal tumor that characteristically arises in the midline cerebellar vermis (in the roof of the 4th ventricle). It can obstruct the 4th ventricle causing non-communicating hydrocephalus and has a propensity to 'drop metastasize' via CSF pathways to the cauda equina in the spinal cord. Histology reveals small, poorly differentiated cells with high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratio ('small round blue cell tumor') forming Homer Wright pseudorosettes.

stem: A 12-year-old girl is evaluated for short stature and delayed puberty. Visual field testing reveals bitemporal hemianopia. Contrast CT of the head reveals a cystic, lobulated suprasellar mass with prominent ring-like peripheral calcifications. When aspirating the cyst during surgery, the neurosurgeon notes thick, viscous fluid with glistening cholesterol crystals resembling 'motor oil.' From which of the following embryological structures does this craniopharyngioma derive?

options.text: Rathke pouch (surface ectoderm outpouching of the stomodeum)
Neural crest cells of the optic cup

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Rathke pouch (surface ectoderm outpouching of the stomodeum).

Craniopharyngioma is a benign, epithelial suprasellar tumor derived from remnants of Rathke pouch (an embryonic diverticulum of stomodeal surface ectoderm that gives rise to the anterior pituitary / adenohypophysis). It displays a bimodal age distribution (peaks at 5-14 years and 50-75 years). Classic triad:
1. Bitemporal hemianopia (suprasellar mass compressing the optic chiasm from above).
2. Endocrine deficiencies: Growth hormone deficiency causing short stature; hypopituitarism; diabetes insipidus.
3. Imaging: Suprasellar cystic mass with prominent peripheral calcification.
Pathology: Cyst fluid rich in cholesterol crystals resembling dark 'motor oil'; wet keratin and squamous epithelium.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with chronic headaches. Contrast-enhanced MRI reveals a 3 cm, well-circumscribed, extra-axial mass arising from the right middle cranial fossa. The radiologist notes that the tumor demonstrates uniform T1 hypointensity, T2 hyperintensity, and intense, uniform enhancement. Intravenous Gadolinium-based contrast agents are used routinely in clinical neuroimaging. Which of the following principles explains how gadolinium creates contrast enhancement on T1-weighted MRI sequences?

options.text: Paramagnetic gadolinium shortens the T1 relaxation time of surrounding water protons, producing bright hyperintensity wherever the blood-brain barrier is disrupted
Gadolinium directly blocks X-ray photon penetration via high atomic density
Gadolinium induces radiofrequency emissions by decaying via beta-plus emission
Gadolinium binds permanently to neuronal cell membranes, increasing sodium permeability
Gadolinium cools local brain tissue, slowing proton spin precession

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Paramagnetic gadolinium shortens the T1 relaxation time of surrounding water protons, producing bright hyperintensity wherever the blood-brain barrier is disrupted.

Gadolinium (Gd3+) is a rare earth metal with seven unpaired electrons, making it strongly paramagnetic. When chelated (to prevent toxicity) and injected intravenously, it remains within intravascular spaces unless the blood-brain barrier is compromised. Gadolinium does not emit signal itself; instead, its fluctuating magnetic field dramatically accelerates the spin-lattice (T1) relaxation rate of adjacent hydrogen nuclei (water protons). Shortening T1 relaxation causes tissues to recover longitudinal magnetization much faster, resulting in high signal intensity (BRIGHT enhancement) on T1-weighted images in areas of vascular breakdown (tumors, infections, inflammation).

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents to the clinic with memory loss and difficulty managing finances. A brain MRI is ordered to differentiate Alzheimer disease from vascular dementia. The scan demonstrates diffuse cerebral cortical atrophy, predominantly affecting the entorhinal cortex and temporal lobes. Which of the following specific temporal lobe structures exhibits the earliest and most severe atrophy in early-stage Alzheimer disease?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Hippocampus.

In Alzheimer disease, neurodegeneration and neurofibrillary tangle pathology begin in the transentorhinal cortex and spread directly to the hippocampus (CA1 subfield and subiculum) before involving diffuse association neocortex. High-resolution volumetric MRI demonstrates progressive, disproportionate atrophy of the hippocampus and parahippocampal gyrus, accompanied by compensatory enlargement of the temporal horns of the lateral ventricles, correlating closely with the severity of early episodic anterograde memory impairment.

• Option B is incorrect: Substantia nigra atrophy occurs in Parkinson disease.
• Option C is incorrect: Caudate atrophy occurs in Huntington disease.

stem: A 52-year-old man presents with progressive loss of sensation in both legs. Neurological examination reveals severe impairment of vibration sense (tested with a 128-Hz tuning fork) and conscious proprioception in his feet and ankles, while pain and temperature sensation remain completely intact. Which of the following anatomical pathways conveys vibratory sense, two-point discrimination, and conscious proprioception from the lower extremities to the brain?

options.text: Fasciculus gracilis of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway
Fasciculus cuneatus of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Fasciculus gracilis of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.

The Dorsal Column-Medial Lemniscal (DCML) pathway conveys discriminative touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception. The dorsal funiculus is divided into two white matter tracts:
• Fasciculus Gracilis: Located medially; carries fibers from the lower body (lower extremities and trunk below spinal level T6; 'gracilis = grass/ground').
• Fasciculus Cuneatus: Located laterally; carries fibers from the upper body (upper extremities and neck above spinal level T6; 'cuneatus = clouds/arms').
Both tracts ascend ipsilaterally in the spinal cord without decussating until reaching the medulla.

• Option C is incorrect: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature.

stem: In the dorsal column-medial lemniscal (DCML) pathway, primary afferent axons ascend uncrossed in the posterior funiculus of the spinal cord to the lower brainstem. Where do these first-order sensory axons synapse with the cell bodies of second-order neurons, and where do the second-order axons decussate across the midline?

options.text: Synapse in Nucleus Gracilis and Nucleus Cuneatus in the caudal medulla; decussate as internal arcuate fibers in the caudal medulla
Synapse in the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal cord; decussate via the anterior white commissure
Synapse in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus; decussate in the midbrain
Synapse in the inferior olivary nucleus; decussate in the pons
Synapse in the red nucleus; decussate in the ventral tegmental decussation

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Synapse in Nucleus Gracilis and Nucleus Cuneatus in the caudal medulla; decussate as internal arcuate fibers in the caudal medulla.

The DCML pathway consists of a three-neuron chain:
1. First-order neuron: Cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion (DRG); large myelinated axons enter the cord and ascend ipsilaterally in the fasciculus gracilis or cuneatus.
2. Second-order neuron: Synapse in the Nucleus Gracilis (lower limb) or Nucleus Cuneatus (upper limb) in the closed caudal medulla. Axons exit these nuclei as internal arcuate fibers, DECUSSATE across the midline (sensory decussation) in the caudal medulla, and ascend as the Medial Lemniscus through the brainstem.
3. Third-order neuron: Synapse in the Ventral Posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus, projecting via the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus).

stem: A 44-year-old man presents with unsteady gait, particularly when walking in the dark. On physical examination, when he stands with his feet together and eyes open, he is steady and maintains his balance. However, when he is instructed to close his eyes, he immediately begins to sway violently and would fall without support. This positive Romberg sign indicates pathology in which of the following sensory systems?

options.text: Conscious proprioception mediated by the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Conscious proprioception mediated by the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.

Maintaining balance requires at least two of three sensory modalities: (1) Vision, (2) Vestibular function, and (3) Proprioception (joint position sense via DCML). 
• In the Romberg test, the patient stands with feet together. Opening the eyes allows visual compensation for defective proprioception.
• Closing the eyes removes visual input. If proprioception is impaired (sensory ataxia), the patient sways and loses balance (positive Romberg test).
• In contrast, a patient with cerebellar ataxia sways and falls with eyes open AND closed because the motor coordinating center itself is damaged.

stem: A sensory physiologist records action potentials from cutaneous mechanoreceptors in human fingertips. A vibrating mechanical probe vibrating at high frequency (200-300 Hz) is placed against the skin. The receptor responds with rapid, transient action potentials at the onset and offset of the stimulus, adapting within milliseconds. Histological examination reveals a large, ovoid encapsulated structure composed of concentric lamellae of flattened Schwann cells surrounding a central unmyelinated axon terminal ('onion-skin' appearance). Which mechanoreceptor is being tested?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Pacinian corpuscle.

Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting (phasic) mechanoreceptors located deep in the dermis, subcutaneous tissue, ligaments, and periosteum. Histologically, they consist of a single myelinated axon terminating in a large, encapsulated structure of concentric lamellae (resembling a sliced onion). They are tuned to detect deep pressure and high-frequency vibration (optimal at 200-300 Hz). The outer fluid-filled lamellae act as a mechanical filter: sustained pressure deforms the capsule transiently, but the fluid rapidly redistributes, ending receptor potential firing unless the stimulus changes frequency.

stem: A blind individual reads Braille text by gliding their fingertips across raised dots. Which of the following cutaneous mechanoreceptors, located in the basal layer of the epidermis, is slowly adapting (type 1) and provides the high spatial resolution necessary for distinguishing static shapes, sharp edges, and fine surface textures?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Merkel disc (Merkel cell-neurite complex).

Merkel discs (slowly adapting type 1 mechanoreceptors) are unencapsulated nerve endings associated with specialized neuroendocrine Merkel cells in the stratum basale of the epidermis. They have small, distinct receptive fields with sharp borders. Because they adapt slowly, they fire continuously during sustained mechanical contact. They provide the highest tactile spatial acuity of all mechanoreceptors, enabling humans to resolve points separated by <1 mm, detect fine edges, and read Braille.

• Option C is incorrect: Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting, detecting dynamic light touch and low-frequency flutter.

stem: Which of the following encapsulated mechanoreceptors is situated within the dermal papillae of hairless (glabrous) skin (such as the fingertips, palms, and soles), adapting rapidly to detect dynamic light flutter, low-frequency vibration (30-50 Hz), and minute slips across the skin to facilitate grip control?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Meissner corpuscle.

Meissner corpuscles are rapidly adapting (phasic) encapsulated mechanoreceptors located in the dermal papillae of glabrous (hairless) skin, oriented perpendicular to the skin surface. They have small receptive fields and are exquisitely sensitive to dynamic light touch, motion, low-frequency flutter (30-50 Hz), and slip between the fingers and a held object. Rapid feedback from Meissner corpuscles triggers immediate reflex adjustments of grip force to prevent dropping objects.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with a history of untreated syphilis contracted 25 years ago. He complains of sudden, lancinating, lightning-like pains shooting down his legs and extreme difficulty walking in the dark. Physical examination reveals a wide-based, stomping gait, loss of vibratory and position sense in both lower extremities, a positive Romberg test, absent knee and ankle reflexes, and bilateral pupils that constrict to accommodation but do not react to light (Argyll Robertson pupils). Which of the following pathological processes characterizes this patient's tabes dorsalis?

options.text: Progressive demyelination and degeneration of dorsal roots and dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus)
Infarction of the anterior spinal artery territory
Expansion of a syrinx within the anterior white commissure
Degeneration of upper and lower motor neurons without sensory involvement
Selective autoimmune demyelination of the spinothalamic tracts

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Progressive demyelination and degeneration of dorsal roots and dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus).

Tabes dorsalis is a late manifestation of tertiary neurosyphilis (Treponema pallidum infection). Pathogenesis:
• Progressive spirochetal destruction, chronic inflammation, and demyelination of dorsal nerve roots and the dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) of the spinal cord.
Clinical presentation:
• Impaired vibration and conscious proprioception -> sensory ataxia (high-stepping, stomping gait, positive Romberg sign).
• Loss of deep tendon reflexes (hyporeflexia/areflexia).
• Severe, paroxysmal, lancinating (lightning) pains in the limbs.
• Argyll Robertson pupils ('Prostitute's pupil': Accommodates to near vision but does not React to light).
• Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy due to loss of joint position sense.

stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of Crohn disease and ileal resection presents with progressive tingling in her feet, unsteadiness when walking, and cognitive slowing. Physical examination reveals spastic paraparesis in both lower extremities, brisk 3+ patellar reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar responses (positive Babinski sign), and profound loss of vibration and joint position sense in both feet and shins. Pain and temperature sensation are normal. Laboratory testing reveals megaloblastic anemia with elevated serum methylmalonic acid and homocysteine levels. Degeneration of which of the following spinal cord white matter tracts occurs in subacute combined degeneration (SCD)?

options.text: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Anterolateral spinothalamic tracts and anterior horn motor neurons
Ventral corticospinal tracts and rubrospinal tracts
Spinothalamic tracts and anterior corticospinal tracts

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts.

Subacute combined degeneration (SCD) is caused by Vitamin B12 (cobalamin) deficiency (marked by elevated methylmalonic acid and homocysteine, unlike folate deficiency which elevates homocysteine only). Impaired myelin maintenance results in bilateral, symmetrical vacuolar demyelination of:
1. Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus): Loss of vibration and conscious proprioception, sensory ataxia, positive Romberg test.
2. Lateral corticospinal tracts: Upper motor neuron signs (spastic paraparesis, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski signs).
3. Spinocerebellar tracts: Limb ataxia.
Pain and temperature sensations are typically spared.

stem: A 70-year-old man undergoes sensory testing. The neurologist uses an aesthesiometer (two-point discriminator) to touch the skin simultaneously at two points. On the patient's fingertips, he can reliably distinguish two distinct points separated by only 2 to 3 mm. However, on his upper back, he cannot perceive two points until they are separated by more than 40 mm. Which of the following neuroanatomical principles explains this dramatic difference in tactile spatial resolution?

options.text: Fingertips have a much higher density of mechanoreceptors with small receptive fields, and disproportionately large cortical representation on the primary somatosensory homunculus
The back has only unmyelinated C fibers that transmit discriminative touch
Mechanoreceptors on the back bypass the thalamus and project directly to the insula
Fingertip sensory fibers do not decussate in the medulla
The fasciculus gracilis carries fibers from the fingertips with faster conduction velocities

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Fingertips have a much higher density of mechanoreceptors with small receptive fields, and disproportionately large cortical representation on the primary somatosensory homunculus.

Two-point discrimination threshold is determined by two factors:
1. Peripheral receptor density and receptive field size: The fingertips and lips possess an exceptionally high density of Merkel discs and Meissner corpuscles, each with tiny receptive fields (<2-3 mm) and minimal overlap. The back has sparse mechanoreceptors with large receptive fields (>40 mm).
2. Central cortical magnification: In the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus), the somatotopic homunculus is non-linear: body regions with high receptor density (fingers, hands, lips, tongue) occupy disproportionately vast areas of cortical processing tissue.

stem: A 61-year-old man presents with sudden loss of sensation over the entire left side of his body, including his face, arm, trunk, and leg. Testing demonstrates complete loss of discriminative touch, vibration, joint position sense, and pinprick sensation on the left, with no motor weakness. A head MRI reveals a small lacunar stroke in the thalamus. In which of the following thalamic nuclei do third-order sensory neurons of the DCML and spinothalamic pathways (from the body) synapse?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Ventral posterolateral (VPL) nucleus.

The Ventral Posterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus receives ascending second-order sensory fibers from the body:
• Medial lemniscus (DCML: vibration, proprioception, fine touch).
• Spinothalamic tract (ALS: pain and temperature).
VPL third-order neurons project via the posterior limb of the internal capsule to the primary somatosensory cortex.

• Option B is incorrect: The Ventral Posteromedial (VPM) nucleus receives trigeminal sensory inputs from the FACE ('VPM = Make-up on face; VPL = Legs/body').
• Option C is incorrect: LGN relays vision (Light).
• Option D is incorrect: MGN relays hearing (Music).

stem: In the brainstem, second-order axons of the DCML pathway ascend as the medial lemniscus. How are body parts somatotopically organized within the medial lemniscus as it traverses the medulla oblongata compared to the midbrain?

options.text: In the medulla, lower extremity fibers are situated ventrally; as the tract ascends to the pons and midbrain, lower extremity fibers rotate to a lateral position
Upper extremity fibers are situated medially throughout the entire brainstem
Facial sensory fibers run within the medial lemniscus
Lower extremity fibers are situated dorsally in the medulla and medially in the midbrain
There is no somatotopic arrangement within brainstem white matter tracts

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. In the medulla, lower extremity fibers are situated ventrally; as the tract ascends to the pons and midbrain, lower extremity fibers rotate to a lateral position.

Somatotopy of the Medial Lemniscus:
• In the rostral medulla: The medial lemniscus is vertically oriented along the midline. Fibers representing the lower body (from nucleus gracilis) lie ventrally (adjacent to the pyramids), while upper body fibers (from nucleus cuneatus) lie dorsally ('standing upright on the pyramids').
• In the pons and midbrain: The medial lemniscus rotates into a horizontal ribbon. Lower body fibers shift laterally, while upper body fibers shift medially ('reclining on the tegmentum').
This ensures that as fibers enter the thalamus, lower extremity fibers enter lateral VPL and upper extremity fibers enter medial VPL.

stem: Which of the following slowly adapting (type 2) encapsulated mechanoreceptors, located deep within the dermis and joint capsules, responds maximally to sustained lateral skin stretch and joint rotation, playing a key role in perceiving finger position and hand conformation?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Ruffini endings (corpuscles).

Ruffini endings (slowly adapting type 2 mechanoreceptors) are spindle-shaped, encapsulated structures located deep within the reticular dermis, subcutaneous tissue, and fibrous joint capsules. They consist of branched nerve terminals intertwined with bundles of collagen fibers. When skin is stretched laterally or a joint rotates, the collagen fibers tighten and squeeze the nerve endings. Because they adapt slowly, they fire continuously to signal directional skin stretch, finger conformation, and joint kinematics.

stem: A 38-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis presents with a newly developed 'numb, clumsy hand.' Neurological examination reveals normal motor strength and normal light touch perception. However, when an object (such as a key or a coin) is placed into her right hand with her eyes closed, she cannot recognize or name the object by touch alone (astereognosis). She also cannot identify numbers traced on her right palm (agraphesthesia). This deficit (tactile agnosia) localizes to which of the following cortical structures?

options.text: Contralateral primary somatosensory and somatosensory association cortex (parietal lobe)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Contralateral primary somatosensory and somatosensory association cortex (parietal lobe).

Astereognosis (inability to identify an object by touch alone) and agraphesthesia (inability to identify numbers traced on the skin) are complex cortical sensory modalities (discriminative cortical sensation). While basic tactile sensation requires an intact peripheral nerve, DCML tract, and VPL thalamus, the higher-order synthesis of texture, shape, size, and weight requires the primary somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus, Brodmann areas 3, 1, 2) and the posterior parietal association cortex (Brodmann areas 5 and 7) of the contralateral hemisphere.

stem: Primary somatosensory afferent fibers conveying touch and vibration from peripheral receptors are classified according to the Erlanger-Gasser nerve fiber classification system. Which of the following nerve fiber types mediates fine discriminative touch, vibration, and conscious proprioception?

options.text: A-alpha and A-beta fibers (large diameter, heavily myelinated, fast conduction velocity)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. A-alpha and A-beta fibers (large diameter, heavily myelinated, fast conduction velocity).

Nerve fiber classification:
• A-alpha fibers (Group I): Largest diameter (13-20 um), heavily myelinated, fastest conduction (80-120 m/s); convey proprioception from muscle spindles (Ia) and Golgi tendon organs (Ib).
• A-beta fibers (Group II): Large diameter (6-12 um), heavily myelinated (35-75 m/s); convey fine discriminative touch, vibration, and pressure from cutaneous mechanoreceptors (Meissner, Pacinian, Merkel, Ruffini).
• A-delta fibers (Group III): Small diameter (1-5 um), thinly myelinated (5-30 m/s); convey fast, sharp pain and cold temperature.
• C fibers (Group IV): Smallest diameter (0.2-1.5 um), unmyelinated, slowest conduction (0.5-2 m/s); convey slow, burning/dull pain, warm temperature, and itch.

stem: A 50-year-old man undergoes neurological testing. A tuning fork vibrating at 128 Hz is placed over his right medial malleolus. Sensation is perceived normally. In the dorsal column of the spinal cord, where is the fasciculus gracilis located relative to the fasciculus cuneatus?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Medial to the fasciculus cuneatus.

In the dorsal funiculus of the spinal cord:
• Fasciculus gracilis occupies the medial portion, immediately adjacent to the posterior median septum. It carries ascending fibers from lower sacral, lumbar, and lower thoracic levels (T7 and below).
• Fasciculus cuneatus is added laterally as upper thoracic and cervical roots enter the cord (T6 and above). Therefore, cuneatus lies lateral to gracilis.
At cervical spinal cord levels, the dorsal column contains both tracts (gracilis medially, cuneatus laterally).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with numbness in her left arm. Testing shows impaired vibration and proprioception in her left fingers and wrist, with normal sensation in her legs. A focal demyelinating plaque in the cervical spinal cord is suspected. Which of the following tracts in the left cervical posterior funiculus is damaged?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Left fasciculus cuneatus.

Sensory fibers from the upper extremity (C2-T6) enter the spinal cord and ascend ipsilaterally in the fasciculus cuneatus (the lateral subdivision of the dorsal column). Because the fibers have not yet reached the caudal medulla, they have not decussated; therefore, a lesion in the left fasciculus cuneatus produces IPSILATERAL loss of vibration, fine touch, and conscious proprioception in the left upper extremity.

• Option B is incorrect: Left fasciculus gracilis carries fibers from the left lower extremity.

stem: Which of the following sensory structures acts as a specialized proprioceptor embedded in parallel with skeletal muscle extrafusal fibers, detecting changes in muscle length (stretch) to mediate the monosynaptic deep tendon reflex?

options.text: Muscle spindle (intrafusal muscle fibers innervated by Group Ia sensory afferents)
Golgi tendon organ (innervated by Group Ib sensory afferents)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Muscle spindle (intrafusal muscle fibers innervated by Group Ia sensory afferents).

Muscle spindles are specialized stretch receptors encapsulated in parallel with skeletal muscle extrafusal fibers. They consist of intrafusal fibers (nuclear bag and chain fibers) innervated by Group Ia sensory afferents (detecting rate of stretch) and Group II afferents (detecting static length). Tapping a tendon stretches the muscle spindle, activating Ia afferents that enter the spinal cord and monosynaptically excite alpha motor neurons to cause reflexive contraction (the myotatic / deep tendon reflex). Gamma motor neurons adjust the sensitivity of the spindle.

• Option B is incorrect: Golgi tendon organs are arranged in SERIES at the musculotendinous junction, innervated by Group Ib afferents, and sense muscle TENSION (mediating the inverse myotatic reflex).

stem: A neurophysiologist investigates the inverse myotatic reflex (autogenic inhibition). When a muscle generates extreme contractile force, this proprioceptive receptor activates Group Ib afferents that synapse on inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, relaxing the contracting muscle to prevent tendon avulsion. Which receptor is responsible?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Golgi tendon organ (GTO).

Golgi tendon organs (GTOs) are encapsulated sensory receptors arranged in SERIES with extrafusal muscle fibers at the musculotendinous junction. They are innervated by fast Group Ib sensory axons. GTOs are exquisitely sensitive to changes in muscle TENSION (contractile force). When excessive contraction threatens to tear the tendon, GTO firing activates Ib inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, which inhibit alpha motor neurons to the homonymous muscle, causing it to relax (the inverse myotatic reflex / autogenic inhibition).

stem: A 75-year-old man presents with chronic sensory loss in his feet. Examination reveals loss of vibratory perception up to his mid-shins, with preserved pinprick sensation. Which of the following tuning forks is the standard clinical instrument used to evaluate vibratory threshold in the dorsal column pathway?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. 128-Hz tuning fork.

A 128-Hz tuning fork is the standard instrument for assessing vibratory sense in a neurological examination. Vibratory sense is mediated by Pacinian corpuscles and transmitted via large myelinated A-beta fibers in the DCML pathway. Vibratory sensation is typically the earliest sensory modality lost in peripheral neuropathies (e.g., diabetic neuropathy) and subacute combined degeneration.

• Option B is incorrect: A 512-Hz tuning fork is used for auditory acuity testing (Rinne and Weber tests).

stem: A 58-year-old woman with a subacute brainstem stroke exhibits loss of vibration, fine touch, and proprioception over the entire right side of her body (arms and legs), with completely normal facial sensation and normal pain and temperature sensation throughout. A discrete ischemic lesion in which of the following brainstem structures on the left side explains this isolated deficit?

options.text: Medial lemniscus in the left pons
Spinal trigeminal tract in the left medulla
Spinothalamic tract in the right medulla
Left corticospinal tract in the crus cerebri

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Medial lemniscus in the left pons.

The medial lemniscus contains second-order axons from the contralateral nucleus gracilis and cuneatus that have already decussated in the caudal medulla. As it ascends through the pons and midbrain, it carries discriminative touch, vibration, and proprioception from the contralateral hemibody (right side). Because trigeminal sensory fibers (from the face) ascend separately in the trigeminothalamic tract and spinothalamic fibers (pain/temp) ascend laterally, an isolated lesion of the left medial lemniscus in the pons causes contralateral (right-sided) loss of touch/vibration/proprioception while sparing facial sensation and pain/temperature.

stem: A 24-year-old man is brought to the trauma bay after being stabbed in the right thoracic back. Neurological examination reveals right-sided spastic paralysis of his leg with hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign, right-sided loss of vibratory sense and joint position sense below the level of the umbilicus, and left-sided loss of pain and temperature sensation starting at the level of the groin (L1). What is the name of this spinal cord hemisection syndrome?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Brown-Séquard syndrome.

Brown-Séquard syndrome results from hemisection of the spinal cord (e.g., from penetrating trauma). The neurological findings reflect the decussation patterns of spinal tracts:
1. Ipsilateral UMN weakness below the lesion (due to transection of the uncrossed descending lateral corticospinal tract).
2. Ipsilateral loss of vibration, fine touch, and proprioception below the lesion (due to transection of the uncrossed ascending dorsal columns).
3. Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation starting 1 to 2 segments below the lesion (due to transection of the ascending spinothalamic tract, whose fibers cross the anterior white commissure 1-2 segments above their entry level).
4. Complete ipsilateral sensory loss and flaccid LMN paralysis at the level of the lesion (destruction of local dorsal and ventral horn cells).

stem: A 68-year-old man undergoes surgical repair of a large thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm. Postoperatively, he is noted to have complete flaccid paralysis of both lower extremities with absent deep tendon reflexes, urinary retention, and bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation below the T10 dermatome. Remarkably, his vibratory sensation and conscious proprioception in both feet and legs are completely normal. Ischemia of which of the following arterial vessels is responsible for this anterior spinal artery syndrome?

options.text: Artery of Adamkiewicz (great anterior radiculomedullary artery)
Vertebral arteries at the foramen magnum

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Artery of Adamkiewicz (great anterior radiculomedullary artery).

Anterior spinal artery syndrome (Beck syndrome) results from infarction of the anterior two-thirds of the spinal cord. In the lower thoracic and lumbosacral cord, the single anterior spinal artery depends heavily on radicular feeding arteries, most notably the Artery of Adamkiewicz (great anterior radiculomedullary artery), which typically arises from a left posterior intercostal or lumbar artery between T9 and T12. Clamping or resection during thoracic/abdominal aortic aneurysm surgery can precipitate ischemia of the anterior 2/3 of the cord. Hallmarks:
• Bilateral corticospinal tract infarction: Spastic paraplegia.
• Bilateral spinothalamic tract infarction: Loss of pain and temperature below the lesion.
• Bilateral anterior horn destruction: LMN signs at the level, urinary retention.
• Sparing of dorsal columns: Vibration and proprioception remain completely intact because the posterior 1/3 of the cord is perfused by the paired posterior spinal arteries.

stem: A 72-year-old man with severe cervical spondylosis is involved in a rear-end motor vehicle collision, suffering a hyperextension injury to his neck. Physical examination demonstrates marked weakness and flaccidity in his arms and hands (1/5 strength), while his legs exhibit only mild weakness (4/5 strength). He also has patchy sensory loss over his shoulders and arms. Brain and spine MRI demonstrates acute contusion centered in the middle of the cervical spinal cord. Which of the following syndromes is present?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Central cord syndrome.

Central cord syndrome is the most common incomplete spinal cord injury syndrome. It characteristically occurs in elderly patients with pre-existing cervical spondylosis and canal stenosis who suffer a hyperextension injury to the neck. The center of the cervical spinal cord is contused. Hallmarks:
• Disproportionately greater motor impairment in the UPPER extremities than in the lower extremities. In the lateral corticospinal tract, fibers are organized somatotopically from medial to lateral: Cervical fibers are located medially (closest to the central canal), while lumbar/sacral fibers are situated laterally. A central lesion damages the medial cervical hand/arm fibers first.
• Patchy sensory loss in the upper extremities due to disruption of decussating spinothalamic fibers.

stem: A 56-year-old man presents with progressive muscle weakness and fasciculations. Physical examination reveals atrophy and fasciculations of the tongue, wasting of the intrinsic muscles of the hands, brisk 3+ biceps and patellar reflexes, spasticity in the legs, and bilateral extensor plantar responses (positive Babinski signs). Sensation to pinprick, vibration, and temperature is completely normal, and bowel and bladder sphincter control is preserved. Denervation and loss of both upper and lower motor neurons characterizes which of the following fatal neurodegenerative diseases?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS / Lou Gehrig disease) is a progressive neurodegenerative disease characterized by the combined degeneration of both Upper Motor Neurons (UMNs: Betz cells in the motor cortex, corticospinal tracts) and Lower Motor Neurons (LMNs: cranial nerve motor nuclei in the brainstem and anterior horn alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord).
• LMN signs: Muscle atrophy, fasciculations, flaccid weakness.
• UMN signs: Spasticity, hyperreflexia, positive Babinski sign, pseudobulbar affect.
• Pure motor disorder: Sensory, autonomic, and sphincter functions are characteristically spared.
• Associated with mutations in SOD1 (superoxide dismutase 1), C9orf72 hexanucleotide repeat expansions, and cytoplasmic TDP-43 inclusions. Pharmacotherapy includes riluzole (glutamate release inhibitor) and edaravone.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with chronic back pain suddenly develops severe low back pain, numbness in her perineum and buttocks ('saddle anesthesia'), bilateral asymmetric leg weakness, and overflow urinary incontinence. Physical examination reveals absent Achilles tendon reflexes bilaterally and poor anal sphincter tone. Emergency lumbar spine MRI reveals a massive herniated L4-L5 intervertebral disc compressing multiple lumbosacral nerve roots. Compression of which of the following anatomical structures defines cauda equina syndrome?

options.text: Lumbosacral nerve roots in the lumbar cistern below the termination of the conus medullaris (L2)
Sacral spinal cord segments S1 to S5 within the conus medullaris
Thoracic spinal cord white matter at the T10 level
Denticulate ligaments of the cervical dura

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Lumbosacral nerve roots in the lumbar cistern below the termination of the conus medullaris (L2).

Cauda equina syndrome is a neurosurgical emergency caused by compression of the cauda equina (the collection of intradural lumbosacral nerve roots L2 through S5 descending through the lumbar cistern below the termination of the conus medullaris at L1-L2). Causes include massive midline disc herniation, spinal canal stenosis, trauma, or epidural tumors. Clinical hallmarks:
• Severe radicular pain shooting into the legs.
• Asymmetric flaccid paraparesis of the lower extremities with hyporeflexia/areflexia (pure LMN lesion, since nerve roots are peripheral nerves).
• 'Saddle anesthesia' (sensory loss in dermatomes S3-S5: perineum, perianal, buttocks, inner thighs).
• Bowel and bladder dysfunction: Urinary retention with overflow incontinence and decreased anal sphincter tone.
Immediate surgical decompression is required to prevent permanent paraplegia and incontinence.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with sudden urinary and fecal incontinence. Neurological examination reveals bilateral, symmetrical perianal numbness (S3-S5), preserved patellar and Achilles reflexes with extensor plantar responses (positive Babinski signs), and mild, symmetrical leg weakness. In distinguishing this from cauda equina syndrome, the physician recognizes conus medullaris syndrome. At which of the following vertebral levels is the conus medullaris normally situated in an adult?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. L1-L2 vertebral disc space.

The conus medullaris is the tapered caudal termination of the spinal cord, located at the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults. 
• Conus medullaris syndrome results from injury to the sacral cord segments and conus (at L1-L2). It is characterized by sudden, early, severe bilateral bladder and bowel incontinence, bilateral symmetrical saddle numbness (perianal), and mixed UMN (hyperreflexia, Babinski) and LMN signs.
• Cauda equina syndrome, by contrast, is compression of nerve roots below L2, resulting in asymmetric radicular pain, flaccid LMN weakness, hyporeflexia, and later-onset incontinence.

stem: An anesthesiologist performs a diagnostic lumbar puncture on an adult patient. The needle is inserted in the midline at the L3-L4 intervertebral space, guided by the supracristal plane (Tuffier line connecting the superior borders of the iliac crests). As the needle advances, it encounters a sudden release of resistance ('pop') as it traverses which of the following ligaments immediately before entering the epidural space?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Ligamentum flavum.

Layers traversed during a lumbar puncture (from superficial to deep):
1. Skin
2. Subcutaneous tissue
3. Supraspinous ligament (connects tips of spinous processes)
4. Interspinous ligament (connects adjacent spinous processes)
5. Ligamentum flavum (dense, yellow elastic ligament connecting laminae; gives a characteristic tactile 'pop' as the needle pierces it)
6. Epidural space (contains internal vertebral venous plexus and fat)
7. Dura mater ('second pop')
8. Arachnoid mater
9. Subarachnoid space (contains CSF and cauda equina nerve roots).

stem: A 30-year-old woman presents with band-like numbness around her abdomen at the level of her umbilicus. Sensory mapping confirms loss of pinprick and light touch sensation across a circular dermatome that corresponds precisely to the umbilicus. Which of the following spinal nerves innervates this landmark dermatome?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. T10 spinal nerve.

Key landmark dermatomes:
• C2: Occiput / back of head
• C3: High neck
• C4: Low neck / supraclavicular
• C6: Thumb ('six-shooter')
• C7: Middle finger
• C8: Pinky finger (little finger)
• T4: Nipples ('T4 at the teat-pore')
• T7: Xiphoid process
• T10: Umbilicus ('belly-but-TEN')
• L1: Inguinal ligament / groin
• L4: Patella / knee
• L5: Big toe / dorsum of foot
• S1: Little toe / lateral foot / Achilles
• S2-S4: Perineum / saddle area ('sits on S2-S4').

stem: A 42-year-old man presents with sharp, shooting pain radiating down his right leg to the lateral border of his foot and little toe. Neurological examination reveals an absent right Achilles tendon (ankle-jerk) reflex and weakness when asked to walk on his tiptoes (plantarflexion of the foot). Sensation to pinprick is diminished over the lateral foot and sole. Herniation of the intervertebral disc compressing which of the following nerve roots is responsible?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. S1 nerve root (L5-S1 disc herniation).

Lumbosacral radiculopathies:
• S1 radiculopathy (typically L5-S1 disc herniation): Pain and sensory loss along the posterior leg, lateral malleolus, and little toe. Motor weakness in plantarflexion (gastrocnemius/soleus, inability to walk on toes). Absent Achilles tendon reflex (S1-S2: 'ankle jerk').
• L5 radiculopathy (L4-L5 disc): Pain and sensory loss on the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot / big toe. Weakness in foot dorsiflexion and big toe extension (extensor hallucis longus, difficulty heel-walking). Reflexes are typically normal.
• L4 radiculopathy (L3-L4 disc): Pain and sensory loss across the anterior knee and medial lower leg. Weakness in knee extension (quadriceps). Diminished patellar reflex (L3-L4).

stem: A 50-year-old carpenter presents with shooting pain from his neck down his right arm into his thumb and index finger. Neurological examination reveals weakness during forearm flexion and supination, and his right brachioradialis reflex is completely absent. Sensory testing demonstrates loss of sensation over the lateral forearm, thumb, and index finger. Compression of which of the following cervical spinal nerve roots is responsible?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. C6 nerve root.

Cervical radiculopathies:
• C6 radiculopathy (C5-C6 disc herniation): Radiating pain and sensory loss over the lateral forearm, thumb, and index finger. Motor weakness of biceps and brachioradialis (forearm flexion and wrist extension). Diminished brachioradialis and biceps reflexes.
• C5 radiculopathy: Deltoid weakness (arm abduction), sensory loss over lateral shoulder. Diminished biceps reflex.
• C7 radiculopathy: Triceps weakness (elbow extension), sensory loss over middle finger. Diminished triceps reflex.
• C8 radiculopathy: Weakness of intrinsic hand muscles, sensory loss over little finger (pinky). Normal reflexes.

stem: A 3-month-old infant is brought to the clinic because of generalized weakness and poor motor development. On physical examination, the infant is hypotonic, lies in a 'frog-leg' posture, and has tongue fasciculations and symmetric flaccid paralysis with absent deep tendon reflexes. Sensation is intact and mental status is normal. Genetic testing reveals a homozygous deletion of the SMN1 (survival motor neuron) gene on chromosome 5q. Degeneration of which of the following spinal cord structures occurs in Spinal Muscular Atrophy (Werdnig-Hoffmann disease)?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Anterior (ventral) horn alpha motor neurons.

Spinal Muscular Atrophy (SMA Type 1 / Werdnig-Hoffmann disease) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by homozygous deletion or loss-of-function mutations in the SMN1 gene on chromosome 5q. SMN protein is required for the assembly of spliceosomal snRNPs. Deficiency causes selective degeneration and apoptosis of lower motor neurons in the anterior (ventral) horns of the spinal cord and brainstem motor nuclei. Hallmarks:
• 'Floppy baby' syndrome with severe generalized hypotonia and symmetric flaccid paralysis.
• Tongue fasciculations and weak cry/suck.
• Areflexia.
• Normal sensation and normal intellect.

stem: A 6-year-old unimmunized child living in a region with endemic poliovirus develops fever, headache, vomiting, and stiff neck, followed 4 days later by acute, asymmetric flaccid paralysis of his right lower extremity. Deep tendon reflexes in the right leg are absent, but sensation is entirely normal. Destruction of which of the following cell types by the poliovirus enterovirus causes this pure motor flaccid paralysis?

options.text: Somatic motor neurons of the anterior (ventral) horns
Pseudounipolar neurons of the dorsal root ganglia
Ependymal cells lining the central canal
Preganglionic sympathetic neurons of the intermediolateral horn

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Somatic motor neurons of the anterior (ventral) horns.

Poliomyelitis is caused by poliovirus (an enterovirus, positive-sense single-stranded RNA virus). After replication in the oropharyngeal and gastrointestinal mucosa and Peyer patches, the virus disseminates hematogenously to the central nervous system. Poliovirus has selective tropism for alpha motor neurons located in the anterior (ventral) horns of the spinal cord and motor nuclei of the brainstem. Lysis of anterior horn cells produces asymmetric flaccid paralysis, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, and areflexia, with completely spared sensory function.

stem: An adult human spinal cord contains 31 pairs of spinal nerves. How do the spinal nerves exit the vertebral column relative to their corresponding pedicles in the cervical region compared to the thoracic and lumbar regions?

options.text: Cervical nerves C1-C7 exit ABOVE their corresponding vertebrae; C8 exits between C7 and T1; thoracic and lumbar nerves exit BELOW their corresponding vertebrae
All spinal nerves exit below their corresponding numbered vertebrae
All spinal nerves exit above their corresponding numbered vertebrae
Cervical nerves exit below their vertebrae; thoracic and lumbar nerves exit above
Spinal nerves exit through the anterior longitudinal ligament

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cervical nerves C1-C7 exit ABOVE their corresponding vertebrae; C8 exits between C7 and T1; thoracic and lumbar nerves exit BELOW their corresponding vertebrae.

Anatomy of spinal nerve exit:
• There are 7 cervical vertebrae but 8 cervical spinal nerves.
• Nerves C1 through C7 exit the vertebral canal ABOVE their numerically corresponding vertebrae (e.g., C1 nerve exits above C1 vertebra; C7 nerve exits above C7 vertebra).
• Nerve C8 exits BELOW the C7 vertebra (between C7 and T1 vertebrae).
• From T1 downward, every spinal nerve exits BELOW its numerically corresponding vertebra (e.g., T1 nerve exits below T1 vertebra; L4 nerve exits below L4 vertebra).

stem: A 16-year-old boy presents with progressive clumsiness, frequent falls, and difficulty walking. Neurological examination reveals bilateral limb ataxia, loss of vibratory and position sense in both feet, absent deep tendon reflexes, bilateral extensor plantar responses (Babinski sign), and marked pes cavus (high arched feet) with hammer toes. Echocardiogram reveals hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Genetic testing demonstrates an expanded GAA trinucleotide repeat on chromosome 9q in the frataxin gene. Which of the following conditions is present?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Friedreich ataxia.

Friedreich ataxia is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by an expanded GAA trinucleotide repeat in the FXN gene (chromosome 9q), encoding frataxin (an iron-binding mitochondrial protein). Frataxin deficiency leads to iron accumulation, reactive oxygen species, and mitochondrial dysfunction. Degeneration involves:
• Spinocerebellar tracts: Progressive gait and limb ataxia.
• Dorsal columns: Loss of vibration and proprioception, areflexia.
• Lateral corticospinal tracts: Spastic weakness, positive Babinski signs.
• Peripheral sensory nerves.
Associated non-neurological features include hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (leading cause of death in ~50% of patients), diabetes mellitus, and skeletal deformities (pes cavus, kyphoscoliosis).

stem: A 22-year-old man undergoes a routine physical examination. The physician lightly strokes the inner aspect of the patient's upper thigh with a tongue depressor, observing immediate reflexive elevation of the ipsilateral testicle. Which of the following spinal cord segments mediates this normal cremasteric reflex?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. L1-L2 spinal segments.

The cremasteric reflex tests spinal cord segments L1 and L2:
• Afferent limb: Ilioinguinal nerve (L1) or femoral branch of the genitofemoral nerve detects tactile stimulation of the upper medial thigh.
• Central integration: L1-L2 spinal cord segments.
• Efferent limb: Genital branch of the genitofemoral nerve (L1-L2) stimulates contraction of the cremaster muscle, pulling the ipsilateral testis superiorly.

• Option B is incorrect: S2-S4 mediates the anal wink reflex (pudendal nerve) and bulbocavernosus reflex.

stem: During a neurological exam, the physician gently strokes the perianal skin with a cotton swab, observing a reflexive contraction of the external anal sphincter muscle (anal wink reflex). Which of the following nerve roots and peripheral nerves mediates this reflex?

options.text: S3-S4 nerve roots via the pudendal nerve
L1-L2 nerve roots via the genitofemoral nerve
L4-L5 nerve roots via the femoral nerve
S1-S2 nerve roots via the tibial nerve
T10-T12 nerve roots via the iliohypogastric nerve

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. S3-S4 nerve roots via the pudendal nerve.

The anal wink (anal sphincter) reflex evaluates the integrity of the lowest sacral spinal cord segments (S3, S4, and S5):
• Light scratching of the perianal skin stimulates afferent sensory fibers of the pudendal nerve (S2-S4).
• Efferent motor fibers travel back via the inferior rectal branch of the pudendal nerve (S3-S4) to cause reflexive contraction of the external anal sphincter.
Loss of the anal wink reflex indicates a lesion of the sacral spinal cord (conus medullaris) or lumbosacral nerve roots (cauda equina).

stem: A 25-year-old man who sustained a complete spinal cord transection at the T2 level 6 months ago presents to the emergency department with a pounding headache, facial flushing, profuse sweating above the chest, and severe hypertension (220/115 mmHg) accompanied by bradycardia (48 beats/min). The episode was triggered by an obstructed urinary catheter with bladder distension. Which of the following life-threatening conditions is occurring?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Autonomic dysreflexia (hyperreflexia).

Autonomic dysreflexia occurs in patients with chronic spinal cord injuries AT OR ABOVE the T6 level. Mechanism:
1. Noxious stimulus below the lesion (most commonly bladder distension or fecal impaction) triggers visceral afferents entering the spinal cord.
2. This evokes massive sympathetic preganglionic output from the splanchnic sympathetic chain (T6-L2).
3. Intense peripheral vasoconstriction causes severe hypertension.
4. Carotid and aortic baroreceptors detect hypertension and stimulate the brainstem vagus nerve (CN X), causing reflex bradycardia.
5. Descending inhibitory signals from the brainstem cannot cross the cord transection (at T2) to turn off sympathetic outflow below the lesion.
Net result: Profuse vasodilation/flushing/sweating ABOVE the lesion, severe vasoconstriction/goosebumps/pale skin BELOW the lesion, and malignant hypertension.

stem: Immediately following an acute traumatic transection of the cervical spinal cord, a patient enters the phase of 'spinal shock.' Which of the following neurological examination findings is characteristically present during acute spinal shock, prior to the eventual emergence of spastic paraplegia?

options.text: Transient flaccid paralysis, complete loss of all sensation, and complete absence of deep tendon and autonomic reflexes below the lesion
Immediate severe hyperreflexia with clonus and clasp-knife spasticity
Isolated loss of pain sensation with intact motor tone

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Transient flaccid paralysis, complete loss of all sensation, and complete absence of deep tendon and autonomic reflexes below the lesion.

Spinal shock refers to the immediate, transient state of complete loss of spinal cord function distal to an acute spinal cord injury. Despite damage to descending upper motor neuron pathways (which eventually produces spasticity and hyperreflexia weeks later), the acute sudden withdrawal of tonic descending facilitatory input causes spinal neurons to become completely hyperpolarized and unresponsive. Hallmarks of spinal shock:
• Flaccid paralysis of all muscles below the lesion.
• Complete areflexia (absent deep tendon reflexes, absent bulbocavernosus and anal wink reflexes).
• Loss of autonomic vasomotor tone (hypotension/bradycardia = neurogenic shock).
As spinal neurons develop denervation supersensitivity over weeks, reflexes return and transition to chronic spasticity.

stem: In the spinal cord, preganglionic sympathetic autonomic neurons originate in the intermediolateral cell column (IML). Across which of the following spinal cord segments is the intermediolateral cell column anatomically present?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. T1 to L2 spinal segments.

The intermediolateral (IML) cell column forms the lateral horn of gray matter in the spinal cord and contains the cell bodies of preganglionic sympathetic neurons. It is present exclusively from spinal segments T1 through L2 (the thoracolumbar outflow of the sympathetic nervous system). Their myelinated axons exit through ventral roots as white rami communicantes to enter the sympathetic paravertebral chain.

• Option C is incorrect: S2 to S4 contains the sacral parasympathetic nucleus (craniosacral outflow), which innervates pelvic viscera via pelvic splanchnic nerves.

stem: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive bilateral spastic weakness in his legs and arms. Neurological examination reveals that when his arm is passively flexed, there is initial high resistance that suddenly gives way, allowing the joint to collapse into full flexion ('clasp-knife spasticity'). Clasp-knife rigidity is a hallmark of upper motor neuron lesions and is mediated by which of the following proprioceptors?

options.text: Golgi tendon organs activating Ib inhibitory interneurons in response to high tension
Muscle spindles activating Ia excitatory afferents
Pacinian corpuscles in the joint capsule

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Golgi tendon organs activating Ib inhibitory interneurons in response to high tension.

Clasp-knife spasticity is a classic sign of an Upper Motor Neuron (UMN) corticospinal tract lesion. When a spastic muscle is passively stretched, exaggerated muscle spindle sensitivity (hyperactive stretch reflex) initially causes marked resistance to movement. However, as passive stretch continues, contractile tension within the tendon reaches a high threshold that vigorously activates Golgi tendon organs (GTOs). Group Ib afferents from GTOs stimulate inhibitory interneurons in the spinal cord, which suddenly inhibit alpha motor neurons, causing the muscle to instantly relax ('give way') like the closing blade of a pocketknife.

stem: A 22-year-old chef accidentally touches a scorching hot skillet. She experiences an immediate, sharp, well-localized sensation of intense pain, followed a few seconds later by a prolonged, poorly localized, throbbing and burning ache. Which of the following nerve fiber types mediates the initial, rapid 'first pain,' and which fiber mediates the subsequent, slow 'second pain'?

options.text: A-delta fibers mediate first pain; C fibers mediate second pain
A-alpha fibers mediate first pain; A-beta fibers mediate second pain
C fibers mediate first pain; A-delta fibers mediate second pain
A-beta fibers mediate first pain; C fibers mediate second pain
B fibers mediate first pain; A-gamma fibers mediate second pain

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. A-delta fibers mediate first pain; C fibers mediate second pain.

Cutaneous nociceptive pain is conveyed by two distinct populations of primary sensory afferents:
1. A-delta fibers: Medium-diameter, thinly myelinated fibers with moderate conduction velocity (5-30 m/s). They terminate in Rexed laminae I and V of the dorsal horn and mediate fast, sharp, pricking, well-localized 'first pain' (thermal and high-threshold mechanical nociception).
2. C fibers: Small-diameter, unmyelinated fibers with slow conduction velocity (0.5-2 m/s). They terminate in Rexed lamina II (substantia gelatinosa) and release glutamate, Substance P, and CGRP. They mediate slow, burning, dull, aching, poorly localized 'second pain' (polymodal nociceptors).

• Option B is incorrect: A-alpha and A-beta fibers convey proprioception and discriminative touch, not pain.

stem: Primary sensory afferent fibers conveying pain and temperature enter the spinal cord via the lateral division of the dorsal root. Before synapsing with second-order projection neurons in the dorsal horn gray matter, these axons ascend or descend 1 to 2 spinal segments within which of the following white matter tracts?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Dorsolateral tract of Lissauer.

Upon entering the dorsolateral aspect of the spinal cord, central processes of primary nociceptive neurons (A-delta and C fibers) divide into ascending and descending collateral branches that run within the tract of Lissauer (dorsolateral fasciculus). They travel 1 to 2 spinal segments rostrally or caudally before penetrating the dorsal horn to synapse on second-order neurons in Rexed laminae I (marginal zone), II (substantia gelatinosa), and V (nucleus proprius).

• Option D is incorrect: The anterior white commissure is where second-order spinothalamic axons decussate across the midline.

stem: In the anterolateral spinothalamic system, second-order projection neurons have their cell bodies in the dorsal horn. Where do their axons decussate across the midline to reach the contralateral anterolateral funiculus?

options.text: Anterior white commissure, crossing obliquely 1 to 2 spinal cord levels above the level of entry
Posterior gray commissure at the exact segment of entry
Sensory decussation of the caudal medulla
Pyramidal decussation of the closed medulla

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Anterior white commissure, crossing obliquely 1 to 2 spinal cord levels above the level of entry.

Second-order axons of the anterolateral system (spinothalamic tract) originate from cell bodies in the dorsal horn (Rexed laminae I and V). They course ventromedially and decussate across the midline in the Anterior White Commissure, traveling obliquely upward over 1 to 2 spinal cord segments. After crossing, they ascend in the contralateral anterolateral funiculus to the brainstem and thalamus. Because of this 1-2 segment oblique crossing, a unilateral spinal cord lesion (e.g., Brown-Séquard syndrome) results in loss of pain and temperature on the contralateral side starting 1 to 2 dermatomes BELOW the anatomical level of the lesion.

stem: A 54-year-old woman with chronic diabetic peripheral neuropathy rubs her sore feet with her hands, noticing that vigorous rubbing provides temporary relief from her burning pain. According to the Gate Control Theory of Pain proposed by Melzack and Wall, which of the following mechanisms explains why mechanical touch relieves nociceptive pain?

options.text: Activation of large, myelinated A-beta fibers stimulates inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa, which inhibit pain transmission from A-delta and C fibers
Tactile rubbing activates descending pathways from the locus coeruleus that deplete acetylcholine in the ventral horn
Mechanical stimulation irreversibly destroys substance P receptors on primary nociceptors
Rubbing causes immediate endocytosis of all postsynaptic AMPA and NMDA receptors
Tactile input hyperpolarizes Schwann cells, preventing saltatory conduction

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Activation of large, myelinated A-beta fibers stimulates inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa, which inhibit pain transmission from A-delta and C fibers.

According to the Gate Control Theory of Pain (Melzack & Wall):
• Transmission of pain from primary A-delta and C fibers to second-order spinothalamic neurons in the dorsal horn is modulated by a 'neural gate' in Rexed lamina II (substantia gelatinosa).
• Non-painful tactile mechanical stimulation activates large-diameter, myelinated A-beta fibers.
• Collateral branches of these A-beta fibers excite inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa.
• These interneurons release GABA and enkephalin, presynaptically inhibiting neurotransmitter release from C fibers and postsynaptically hyperpolarizing second-order transmission cells, effectively 'closing the gate' to pain signaling.
This explains why rubbing a bumped elbow, massage therapy, and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) provide analgesia.

stem: The central nervous system possesses an intrinsic descending analgesia system that suppresses pain transmission at the level of the spinal dorsal horn. Stimulation of neurons in the periaqueductal gray (PAG) of the midbrain activates serotonergic neurons in which of the following brainstem nuclei to project descending inhibitory axons to the substantia gelatinosa?

options.text: Nucleus raphe magnus in the rostral ventromedial medulla

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Nucleus raphe magnus in the rostral ventromedial medulla.

The descending pain modulation circuit:
1. Neurons in the Periaqueductal Gray (PAG) of the midbrain receive inputs from the cortex, amygdala, and hypothalamus.
2. Excitatory projections from the PAG project to the Rostral Ventromedial Medulla (RVM), specifically targeting the Nucleus Raphe Magnus (serotonergic, 5-HT) and the Locus Coeruleus (noradrenergic, NE) in the pons.
3. Descending axons from the Nucleus Raphe Magnus travel down the dorsolateral funiculus to the spinal cord dorsal horn.
4. Serotonin and norepinephrine release activates local enkephalin-containing inhibitory interneurons in Rexed lamina II (substantia gelatinosa).
5. Enkephalins bind presynaptic and postsynaptic mu-opioid receptors, blocking substance P and glutamate release and hyperpolarizing second-order projection neurons.

stem: A 58-year-old man presents with acute retrosternal chest tightness radiating down the medial aspect of his left arm into his little finger. Electrocardiogram confirms acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction. The patient's left arm pain is an example of referred visceral pain. According to the convergence-projection theory, which of the following neuroanatomical mechanisms explains why myocardial ischemia is perceived as somatic pain in the T1-T4 dermatomes?

options.text: Visceral sensory afferents from the heart and somatic sensory afferents from the left arm converge onto the same second-order spinothalamic neurons in the T1-T4 dorsal horn
Myocardial ischemia releases inflammatory cytokines that travel hematogenously to the brachial plexus
The phrenic nerve carries parasympathetic motor fibers directly to the pectoralis major
Cervical sympathetic ganglia send motor efferents that cause spasm of the ulnar artery
Cardiac pain signals decussate in the corpus callosum instead of the spinal cord

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Visceral sensory afferents from the heart and somatic sensory afferents from the left arm converge onto the same second-order spinothalamic neurons in the T1-T4 dorsal horn.

According to the Convergence-Projection Theory of referred pain:
• Visceral organs have sparse sensory innervation and do not have separate dedicated pathways to the primary somatosensory cortex.
• Visceral nociceptive afferents from the heart travel along sympathetic nerves and enter the upper thoracic spinal cord (segments T1 to T4).
• In the dorsal horn, these visceral afferents converge and synapse onto the SAME second-order spinothalamic projection neurons that receive somatic nociceptive inputs from the T1-T4 dermatomes (which correspond to the precordial chest, axilla, and medial aspect of the left arm).
• When the cerebral cortex receives signals from these second-order neurons, it projects the sensation to the more frequently stimulated somatic dermatome (the left arm and chest).

stem: A 45-year-old woman presents with severe right upper quadrant abdominal pain and fever. Ultrasound confirms acute cholecystitis with gallstones. In addition to right upper quadrant tenderness, she reports sharp pain localized to the tip of her right shoulder and inferior angle of her right scapula (Boas sign). Inflammation of the gallbladder irritating the under-surface of the diaphragm causes referred shoulder pain via which of the following nerves?

options.text: Right lateral cutaneous nerve of the thigh (L2-L3)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Right phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5).

Referred shoulder pain from subdiaphragmatic irritation (Kehr sign for splenic rupture, or gallbladder inflammation in acute cholecystitis) is mediated by the phrenic nerve. The diaphragm receives sensory innervation from the phrenic nerve (roots C3, C4, C5; 'C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive'). Sensory afferents enter the cervical spinal cord at C3-C5, converging onto second-order neurons that also receive somatic sensation from the supraclavicular nerves (C3-C4 dermatome over the shoulder tip). Irritation of the diaphragmatic peritoneum is therefore perceived as pain over the ipsilateral shoulder.

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic with severe sunburn across her shoulders. When her partner lightly drapes a soft cotton shirt over her sunburned skin, she recoils in agony, perceiving the light touch as excruciatingly painful. What clinical term describes the perception of a normally innocuous, non-painful stimulus as painful?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Allodynia.

Key pain terminology:
• Allodynia: Pain resulting from a stimulus that does not normally provoke pain (e.g., light touch of clothing or a gentle breeze on sunburned skin, or touching the face in trigeminal neuralgia). It reflects sensitization of central dorsal horn neurons (central sensitization) and phenotypic switching of low-threshold A-beta mechanoreceptors.
• Hyperalgesia: An exaggerated or increased pain response to a stimulus that is normally painful (e.g., a mild pinprick on inflamed skin feeling like a knife stab).
• Paresthesia: An abnormal spontaneous sensation (tingling, 'pins and needles') that is not unpleasant or painful.
• Anesthesia dolorosa: Pain perceived in an area that is completely numb and anesthetic.

stem: Following tissue injury, an 'inflammatory soup' of chemical mediators is released into the interstitial fluid surrounding peripheral nociceptive nerve terminals, sensitizing them and lowering their activation thresholds (primary peripheral sensitization). Which of the following inflammatory mediators directly binds and sensitizes the TRPV1 (transient receptor potential vanilloid 1) non-selective cation channel on unmyelinated C fibers?

options.text: Protons (extracellular H+ ions), Bradykinin, and Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Protons (extracellular H+ ions), Bradykinin, and Prostaglandin E2 (PGE2).

Tissue trauma, infection, and ischemia cause damaged cells, mast cells, platelets, and macrophages to release an 'inflammatory soup':
• Bradykinin: Binds B2 Gq receptors, activating PKC to phosphorylate and lower the activation threshold of TRPV1.
• Prostaglandins (PGE2, PGI2): Bind EP/IP Gs receptors, activating PKA to phosphorylate Na+ channels (Nav1.8) and TRPV1.
• Protons (H+, tissue acidosis): Directly gate and open the TRPV1 pore at physiological temperatures.
• Histamine, Serotonin, ATP, Nerve Growth Factor (NGF), and Substance P.
Together, these mediators dramatically lower the threshold of heat- and mechanosensitive nociceptors, producing primary hyperalgesia at the site of injury.

stem: A 58-year-old man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with burning, shooting pain in both feet that is worse at night. Physical examination reveals a symmetrical 'stocking-glove' distribution of pinprick hyperalgesia and loss of 10-g monofilament tactile sensation. The physician prescribes a topical capsaicin cream (derived from chili peppers). What is the mechanism of action by which capsaicin relieves neuropathic pain?

options.text: Initial activation of the TRPV1 receptor leads to sustained calcium influx, causing functional desensitization and depletion of substance P from nociceptive nerve terminals
Irreversible blockade of voltage-gated potassium channels
Selective competitive antagonism of mu-opioid receptors
Direct inhibition of cycloxygenase-2 (COX-2) in endothelial cells
Allosteric enhancement of GABA-A chloride channels

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Initial activation of the TRPV1 receptor leads to sustained calcium influx, causing functional desensitization and depletion of substance P from nociceptive nerve terminals.

Capsaicin is a potent, selective agonist of the TRPV1 (Transient Receptor Potential Vanilloid 1) receptor, an ionotropic non-selective cation channel normally activated by noxious heat (>43°C) and protons on C and A-delta nociceptors.
• Initial application: Causes opening of TRPV1, influx of Na+ and Ca2+, and intense burning pain, erythema, and itching.
• Repeated application: Chronic, excessive Ca2+ influx leads to osmotic swelling, mitochondrial dysfunction, reversible retraction of epidermal nerve terminals, and prolonged DESENSITIZATION of nociceptors, accompanied by depletion of Substance P. This provides sustained analgesia in diabetic neuropathy and post-herpetic neuralgia.

stem: A 60-year-old man with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy is evaluated in the clinic. As discussed in CBIL Case 1, diabetic polyneuropathy results from chronic hyperglycemia. Which of the following biochemical pathways is responsible for intracellular sorbitol accumulation, osmotic stress, and depletion of NADPH in peripheral nerves?

options.text: Polyol pathway (Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, consuming NADPH)
Hexosamine pathway converting fructose-6-phosphate to UDP-GlcNAc
Protein kinase C pathway activated by diacylglycerol
Advanced glycation end-product (AGE) formation via non-enzymatic fructosamine

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Polyol pathway (Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol, consuming NADPH).

In diabetic neuropathy (CBIL Case 1):
• Schwann cells and peripheral axons take up glucose via insulin-independent GLUT transporters. In chronic hyperglycemia, intracellular glucose saturates hexokinase and is shunted into the Polyol pathway.
• Aldose reductase reduces glucose to Sorbitol, consuming NADPH.
• Sorbitol dehydrogenase slowly oxidizes sorbitol to fructose, using NAD+.
Pathological consequences:
1. Sorbitol is polar and cannot cross cell membranes; its accumulation generates intracellular hyperosmotic stress, drawing water in and causing Schwann cell swelling.
2. Depletion of NADPH deprives Glutathione Reductase of the reducing equivalents needed to regenerate reduced glutathione (GSH), causing severe oxidative stress and free radical damage.
3. Advanced Glycation End-products (AGEs) cross-link extracellular matrix proteins, leading to microvascular endoneurial ischemia.

stem: A 55-year-old man with diabetic polyneuropathy is evaluated for severe nocturnal neuropathic foot pain. As outlined in CBIL Case 1, which of the following oral medications is considered first-line pharmacotherapy for painful diabetic neuropathy by binding to the alpha-2-delta auxiliary subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels, thereby reducing excitatory neurotransmitter release?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Pregabalin (or Gabapentin).
