Lasmiditan is a 'ditan' that selectively activates which of the following serotonin receptor subtypes, successfully aborting migraine without causing vasoconstriction of coronary or cerebral arteries?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. 5-HT1F receptor.

Lasmiditan is a high-affinity, selective 5-HT1F receptor agonist (a 'ditan'). Unlike triptans (which bind 5-HT1B and 5-HT1D receptors and produce vascular smooth muscle vasoconstriction), 5-HT1F receptors are located exclusively on central and peripheral trigeminal neurons and do NOT produce vasoconstriction. Activating 5-HT1F inhibits trigeminal calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) release and blocks central pain transmission. Lasmiditan is FDA-approved for acute migraine abortive therapy in patients with cardiovascular disease, coronary artery disease, or uncontrolled hypertension.

stem: A 48-year-old man presents with sharp, excruciating, unilateral headache attacks localized to the temple that occur 15 to 20 times per day, lasting 10 to 20 minutes each. The attacks are accompanied by ipsilateral conjunctival injection and rhinorrhea. He is treated with a 48-hour trial of oral indomethacin, which produces complete and rapid abolition of all headache attacks. Which of the following Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgias is defined by this absolute therapeutic response to indomethacin?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Paroxysmal hemicrania.

Paroxysmal hemicrania is a Trigeminal Autonomic Cephalalgia (TAC) with key differences from cluster headache:
• Shorter duration: Attacks last 2 to 30 minutes (cluster attacks last 15-180 minutes).
• Higher frequency: Occur >5 to 20 times per day (cluster attacks occur 1-8 times/day).
• Female predominance (cluster has male predominance).
• Hallmark diagnostic criterion: Complete, prompt, absolute response to therapeutic doses of Indomethacin (an NSAID), which is diagnostic ('indomethacin-responsive headache').

stem: A 21-year-old college student presents with throbbing headaches, nausea, and vomiting. He mentions that his mother and maternal uncle suffer from similar episodes that are accompanied by temporary unilateral hemiparesis and ataxia. Genetic sequencing reveals a missense mutation in the CACNA1A gene encoding the pore-forming alpha-1A subunit of neuronal Cav2.1 (P/Q-type) voltage-gated calcium channels. Which of the following is the diagnosis?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Familial Hemiplegic Migraine type 1 (FHM1).

Familial Hemiplegic Migraine (FHM) is an autosomal dominant subtype of migraine with aura characterized by reversible motor weakness (hemiparesis) during the aura phase:
• FHM1 (~50% of cases): Caused by gain-of-function mutations in CACNA1A (chromosome 19p), encoding the alpha-1A pore subunit of P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels (Cav2.1). Increased calcium influx causes excessive cortical glutamate release, lowering the threshold for cortical spreading depression.
• FHM2: Mutations in ATP1A2 (alpha-2 subunit of Na+/K+ ATPase).
• FHM3: Mutations in SCN1A (voltage-gated Na+ channel Nav1.1).

stem: A 35-year-old woman presents to the clinic with chronic daily headaches. In evaluating secondary headache disorders, the physician reviews the 'SNOOP' mnemonic for dangerous headache red flags. Which of the following clinical features represents a 'red flag' requiring emergent neuroimaging and lumbar puncture?

options.text: Sudden onset 'thunderclap' headache, systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss), focal neurological deficits, or new headache in an immunocompromised patient
Bilateral band-like pressure after 8 hours of computer work
Unilateral throbbing headache that resolves after 2 hours of sleep in a dark room
Headache that worsens with menstruation and improves with NSAIDs
Pericranial muscle tightness that resolves with neck massage

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Sudden onset 'thunderclap' headache, systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss), focal neurological deficits, or new headache in an immunocompromised patient.

The 'SNOOP' mnemonic identifies red-flag headache symptoms requiring urgent neuroimaging (CT/MRI) and further workup:
• S: Systemic symptoms (fever, weight loss, night sweats, malignancy) or Systemic disease (HIV, cancer, immunocompromised)
• N: Neurological signs or symptoms (confusion, papilledema, focal deficits, seizures)
• O: Onset is sudden (thunderclap headache peaking in <1 minute, suggestive of SAH)
• O: Older age at onset (new headache onset after age 50, suggestive of temporal arteritis or tumor)
• P: Pattern change or Positional headache (worse lying down / standing up, or triggered by Valsalva, coughing, or exercise).

stem: A 29-year-old woman presents with headaches that occur exclusively when standing up or sitting upright, resolving completely within 15 minutes of lying flat (orthostatic headache). She had an uncomplicated epidural catheter placed 3 days ago for labor analgesia. Physical examination is normal when supine. Which of the following conditions is the most likely cause of this postural headache?

options.text: Low-pressure headache secondary to post-dural puncture CSF leak

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Low-pressure headache secondary to post-dural puncture CSF leak.

Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH / low-pressure headache) occurs when an accidental dural puncture during spinal or epidural anesthesia leads to persistent leakage of CSF into the epidural space. Hallmarks:
• Orthostatic / postural headache: Excruciating bilateral throbbing headache within 15 minutes of standing or sitting upright, promptly relieved by lying supine.
• Pathophysiology: Loss of CSF volume lowers intracranial pressure. In the upright position, the brain sags caudally within the skull, exerting painful traction on pain-sensitive meninges, anchoring veins, and cranial nerves (CN V, IX, X).
• Treatment: Conservative (bed rest, hydration, caffeine); if refractory, an epidural blood patch (autologous blood injected into epidural space to clot and seal the dural hole) is curative.

stem: A 23-year-old woman with a history of migraine with aura presents to her gynecologist requesting oral contraceptive pills. Why are combined estrogen-progestin oral contraceptive pills strictly contraindicated in women who experience migraine WITH aura?

options.text: Markedly increased synergistic risk of ischemic stroke
Oral contraceptives cause acute subarachnoid hemorrhage

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Markedly increased synergistic risk of ischemic stroke.

Migraine with aura is an independent risk factor for ischemic stroke (relative risk ~2.0 to 2.5). Combined estrogen-containing oral contraceptive pills (COCs) induce hepatic synthesis of clotting factors and increase the risk of venous and arterial thromboembolism. In women with migraine WITH aura, adding estrogen-containing contraceptives creates a multiplicative, synergistic increase in the risk of ischemic stroke (risk increases by 6- to 9-fold, and up to 30-fold if the patient also smokes). Therefore, combined hormonal contraceptives are contraindicated in women with migraine with aura (progestin-only pills, levonorgestrel IUD, or copper IUD are safe alternatives).

stem: A 40-year-old woman with chronic migraine (>15 headache days per month for >6 months) has failed trials of propranolol, topiramate, and amitriptyline. The neurologist recommends intramuscular injections of onabotulinumtoxinA (Botox) administered across 31 pericranial head and neck sites according to the PREEMPT protocol. What is the mechanism of action by which botulinum toxin prevents chronic migraine?

options.text: Cleaves SNAP-25 in peripheral sensory nerve endings, inhibiting the release of CGRP, substance P, and glutamate from trigeminovascular afferents
Directly blocks post-junctional nicotinic receptors on smooth muscle
Inhibits the enzyme cyclooxygenase-1 in circulating platelets
Stimulates GABA-A receptor chloride opening in the locus coeruleus
Increases intracranial pressure to stabilize CSF dynamics

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cleaves SNAP-25 in peripheral sensory nerve endings, inhibiting the release of CGRP, substance P, and glutamate from trigeminovascular afferents.

OnabotulinumtoxinA is FDA-approved specifically for the prevention of CHRONIC migraine (≥15 headache days/month, with at least 8 being migrainous, for ≥3 months). Mechanism in migraine:
• Botulinum toxin heavy chain binds to SV2 receptors on unmyelinated C-fiber and thinly myelinated A-delta trigeminal and cervical sensory nerve terminals in pericranial muscles.
• The light chain enters the cytosol and cleaves SNAP-25, preventing vesicle fusion.
• This blocks the peripheral exocytosis of inflammatory and nociceptive neurotransmitters (CGRP, Substance P, and glutamate), preventing peripheral sensitization and dampening the afferent signals that trigger central sensitization in the brainstem.

stem: A 50-year-old man presents with chronic daily tension-type headaches that occur 20 days per month. He has been taking excessive doses of ibuprofen with minimal effect. The physician decides to start prophylactic pharmacotherapy. Which of the following medications is the first-line evidence-based prophylactic drug of choice for chronic tension-type headache?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Amitriptyline.

Amitriptyline (a tricyclic antidepressant) is the established first-line evidence-based preventive medication for chronic tension-type headache (as well as an effective migraine preventive). Mechanisms:
• Inhibits the reuptake of Serotonin (SERT) and Norepinephrine (NET), augmenting endogenous descending inhibitory pain pathways in the spinal dorsal horn and trigeminal spinal nucleus.
• Antagonizes 5-HT2 and NMDA receptors, reducing central sensitization.
Adverse anticholinergic effects: Dry mouth, drowsiness, constipation, urinary retention, weight gain, and QT prolongation.

stem: Endocannabinoids such as anandamide (N-arachidonoylethanolamine) and 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) serve as retrograde synaptic messengers in the central nervous system. How are these endogenous ligands synthesized and released at central synapses?

options.text: Synthesized on demand from membrane phospholipid precursors in the postsynaptic neuron upon depolarization, then diffuse retrogradely to act on presynaptic CB1 receptors
Stored in dense-core vesicles in the presynaptic terminal and exocytosed in response to voltage-gated calcium influx
Produced constitutively in astrocytic end-feet and transported across the blood-brain barrier via glucose transporter 1 (GLUT-1)
Synthesized in the rough endoplasmic reticulum as prepropeptides and cleaved in the Golgi apparatus before anterograde axonal transport
Released continuously by oligodendrocytes into the node of Ranvier to maintain axonal conduction velocity

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Synthesized on demand from membrane phospholipid precursors in the postsynaptic neuron upon depolarization, then diffuse retrogradely to act on presynaptic CB1 receptors.

Endocannabinoids (anandamide and 2-AG) are unconventional neurotransmitters because they are lipid molecules synthesized 'on demand' rather than stored in synaptic vesicles:
1. Postsynaptic depolarization causes intracellular calcium influx (or Gq-coupled receptor activation), activating phospholipase D (for anandamide) or phospholipase C / diacylglycerol lipase (for 2-AG).
2. These lipophilic mediators traverse the postsynaptic membrane into the synaptic cleft and travel retrogradely to bind presynaptic cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptors.
3. Activation of presynaptic CB1 receptors inhibits presynaptic neurotransmitter release (depolarization-induced suppression of inhibition [DSI] if GABA is blocked, or depolarization-induced suppression of excitation [DSE] if glutamate is blocked).

• Option B is incorrect: Endocannabinoids are not stored in vesicles; their hydrophobic nature prevents vesicular compartmentalization.

stem: Cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptors are among the most abundant G-protein coupled receptors in the human brain. What is the downstream signal transduction mechanism activated upon agonist binding to the CB1 receptor?

options.text: Coupling to Gi/o proteins, leading to inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, closure of voltage-gated N- and P/Q-type calcium channels, and opening of inward-rectifying potassium channels
Coupling to Gs proteins, leading to adenylyl cyclase activation, elevated cyclic AMP, and protein kinase A phosphorylation
Coupling to Gq proteins, activating phospholipase C to generate inositol trisphosphate (IP3) and diacylglycerol (DAG)
Intrinsic tyrosine kinase autophosphorylation activating the MAP kinase cascade
Direct opening of ligand-gated chloride channels causing fast postsynaptic hyperpolarization

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Coupling to Gi/o proteins, leading to inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, closure of voltage-gated N- and P/Q-type calcium channels, and opening of inward-rectifying potassium channels.

CB1 receptors are presynaptic Gi/o-protein coupled receptors. Their downstream cascade includes:
• Inhibition of adenylyl cyclase -> decreases intracellular cyclic AMP (cAMP) and reduces PKA activity.
• Inhibition of presynaptic voltage-gated N-type and P/Q-type calcium channels -> reduces presynaptic calcium influx required for SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion.
• Activation of G-protein-coupled inwardly rectifying potassium channels (GIRK) -> hyperpolarizes the presynaptic terminal.
Together, these actions potently suppress the exocytosis of classical neurotransmitters (glutamate, GABA, acetylcholine, and norepinephrine) from the presynaptic terminal.

stem: A neuropharmacologist is mapping the anatomical distribution of cannabinoid receptors in the human body. Which of the following correctly pairs the cannabinoid receptor subtype with its predominant tissue distribution and primary physiological role?

options.text: CB1: Central nervous system (basal ganglia, hippocampus, cerebellum); CB2: Immune cells (spleen, tonsils, microglia)
CB1: Peripheral mast cells and eosinophils; CB2: Cerebral cortex and thalamic relay nuclei
CB1: Cardiac pacemakers and atria; CB2: Renal glomeruli and proximal tubules
CB1: Medullary respiratory rhythm centers; CB2: Spinal dorsal horn primary nociceptors
CB1: Skeletal muscle neuromuscular junctions; CB2: Hepatic biliary canaliculi

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. CB1: Central nervous system (basal ganglia, hippocampus, cerebellum); CB2: Immune cells (spleen, tonsils, microglia).

Distribution of cannabinoid receptors:
• CB1 receptors: Predominantly expressed in the CNS, with highest densities in the basal ganglia (substantia nigra, globus pallidus), cerebellum (mediating motor coordination and balance), hippocampus (mediating short-term memory deficits), and cerebral cortex. Notably, CB1 density is remarkably sparse in the brainstem cardiorespiratory centers, explaining why cannabis overdose does not cause fatal respiratory depression.
• CB2 receptors: Primarily localized peripherally on immune system tissues (spleen, tonsils, macrophages, B cells, T cells) and CNS microglia. CB2 activation mediates immunosuppressive and anti-inflammatory effects by modulating cytokine release without producing psychotropic effects.

stem: A 28-year-old man who smokes cannabis daily presents with a 6-month history of recurrent, debilitating episodes of severe nausea, cyclical vomiting, and colicky abdominal pain. Extensive GI workups, including upper endoscopy and abdominal CT, are completely normal. During history taking, he states that the only thing that relieves his nausea is taking scalding hot showers multiple times each day. Which of the following conditions is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Cyclic vomiting syndrome secondary to migraine
Gastroparesis secondary to diabetic autonomic neuropathy

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome.

Cannabinoid Hyperemesis Syndrome (CHS) is a clinical disorder characterized by:
1. Chronic, heavy, daily cannabis use (usually >1 year).
2. Cyclic, severe nausea, intractable vomiting, and colicky periumbilical abdominal pain.
3. Pathognomonic compulsive hot bathing or showering: Patients spend hours in hot water because heat activates cutaneous transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) receptors, which restores hypothalamic thermoregulation and causes splanchnic vasodilation, temporarily counteracting cannabis-induced hypothermia and GI dysmotility.
4. Resolution of symptoms upon complete cannabis cessation.

• First-line acute symptomatic relief includes haloperidol and topical capsaicin cream (TRPV1 agonist). Conventional antiemetics (ondansetron, promethazine) are notoriously ineffective.

stem: A patient with cannabinoid hyperemesis syndrome presents to the emergency department in distress. What is the mechanism of action by which application of topical capsaicin cream to the periumbilical region provides rapid symptomatic relief of nausea and abdominal pain?

options.text: Stimulates peripheral cutaneous TRPV1 receptors, mimicking the thermal sensory input of hot showers and downregulating hypothalamic and splanchnic nociceptive signaling
Competitively antagonizes CB1 receptors in the chemoreceptor trigger zone
Inhibits postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors in the area postrema
Blocks serotonin 5-HT3 receptors on vagal afferents in the gastrointestinal mucosa
Promotes gastric emptying by agonizing motilin receptors in the duodenum

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Stimulates peripheral cutaneous TRPV1 receptors, mimicking the thermal sensory input of hot showers and downregulating hypothalamic and splanchnic nociceptive signaling.

Chronic high-dose THC exposure desensitizes both CB1 and TRPV1 receptors in the enteric nervous system and hypothalamus. Heat and capsaicin:
• Both activate TRPV1 receptors (the heat- and capsaicin-sensitive ion channel), which redirects cerebral/cutaneous blood flow, corrects cannabis-mediated splanchnic hypoperfusion, and overrides aberrant visceral pain signals to the brainstem vomiting centers.
• Capsaicin cream applied to the abdomen or back is therefore standard-of-care adjuvant pharmacotherapy in acute CHS presentations in the emergency department.

stem: A 54-year-old man undergoing adjuvant chemotherapy for metastatic colon adenocarcinoma suffers from intractable chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) despite trials of ondansetron and dexamethasone. He is prescribed dronabinol. What is the active pharmaceutical chemical in dronabinol?

options.text: Inhibitor of fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Synthetic delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC).

Dronabinol (Marinol) is an orally administered synthetic delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol (THC). Indications FDA-approved for dronabinol:
1. Chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting (CINV) in patients who have failed to respond adequately to conventional antiemetics.
2. Anorexia and weight loss (cachexia) associated with AIDS.

• Cannabidiol (Option B) is Epidiolex, approved for pediatric epilepsy, not dronabinol.

stem: A 4-year-old child with a refractory genetic epileptic encephalopathy characterized by multiple daily polymorphic seizures (atonic drop attacks and tonic seizures) is diagnosed with Lennox-Gastaut syndrome. Which of the following cannabis-derived compounds is FDA-approved specifically for refractory pediatric seizure disorders such as Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cannabidiol (CBD).

Epidiolex is an FDA-approved, highly purified plant-derived oral solution of Cannabidiol (CBD). It is approved for the treatment of seizures associated with:
1. Lennox-Gastaut syndrome (LGS)
2. Dravet syndrome (severe myoclonic epilepsy of infancy)
3. Tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC)
Unlike THC, CBD has negligible affinity for CB1 receptors, is non-intoxicating (does not cause euphoria), and exerts anticonvulsant activity via antagonism of GPR55, desensitization of TRPV1 channels, and modulation of intracellular calcium.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis suffers from painful, spastic lower extremity spasms that are refractory to baclofen and tizanidine. In several countries, an oromucosal spray containing a 1:1 ratio of delta-9-THC and cannabidiol (nabiximols / Sativex) is approved for this condition. What is the clinical benefit of combining cannabidiol (CBD) with THC in medical cannabis formulations?

options.text: CBD acts as a negative allosteric modulator of CB1, mitigating the intoxicating psychoactive adverse effects, tachycardia, and anxiety caused by THC while synergistically improving muscle spasticity
CBD completely blocks THC absorption across mucosal membranes
CBD irreversibly binds to and inactivates hepatic cytochrome P450 3A4 to eliminate all drug metabolism
CBD converts delta-9-THC into delta-8-THC in the bloodstream
CBD stimulates peripheral histamine release to induce sedation

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. CBD acts as a negative allosteric modulator of CB1, mitigating the intoxicating psychoactive adverse effects, tachycardia, and anxiety caused by THC while synergistically improving muscle spasticity.

CBD modulates the pharmacodynamic profile of THC:
• CBD functions as a negative allosteric modulator (NAM) at the CB1 receptor, dampening the maximum efficacy of THC at CB1. This reduces THC-induced tachycardia, panic, paranoia, and cognitive impairment.
• Concurrently, CBD and THC act synergistically on non-CB1 targets (glycine receptors, 5-HT1A, TRPV1) to provide enhanced analgesia and reduction in spasticity (the 'entourage effect').

stem: A 21-year-old college student presents to the student health clinic 45 minutes after smoking marijuana. Physical examination reveals bilateral conjunctival injection, dry oral mucosa, heart rate of 115/min, and blood pressure of 105/65 mmHg. Which physiological mechanism explains the pathognomonic conjunctival injection and tachycardia seen in acute cannabis intoxication?

options.text: Vasodilation of episcleral blood vessels via CB1 activation, and reflex tachycardia secondary to decreased peripheral vascular resistance combined with direct sympathetic activation
Potent constriction of anterior ciliary arteries with compensatory hypertension
Direct stimulation of muscarinic M3 receptors on ciliary body smooth muscle
Immune complex deposition in the episcleral capillary beds
Release of histamine from conjunctival mast cells via IgE cross-linking

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Vasodilation of episcleral blood vessels via CB1 activation, and reflex tachycardia secondary to decreased peripheral vascular resistance combined with direct sympathetic activation.

Acute cannabis intoxication features classic cardiovascular and ocular findings:
1. Conjunctival injection: Cannabinoids cause active vasodilation of conjunctival/episcleral vessels (and lowers intraocular pressure), producing bright red, bloodshot eyes.
2. Tachycardia: Acute THC ingestion causes prominent sinus tachycardia (dose-dependent increase by 20-50 bpm) through sympathetic stimulation, inhibition of parasympathetic vagal tone, and reflex baroreceptor compensation for mild peripheral vasodilation/orthostatic hypotension.
3. Xerostomia (dry mouth): Submandibular and parotid glands express CB1/CB2 receptors; cannabinoid activation inhibits salivary secretion.

stem: A 24-year-old man who has been smoking cannabis multiple times daily for 3 years abruptly discontinues use when applying for a new job. Three days later, he presents complaining of severe irritability, restlessness, insomnia, vivid disturbing dreams, night sweats, nausea, and loss of appetite. He has lost 2 kg over the past week. What is the expected time course for DSM-5 Cannabis Withdrawal Syndrome?

options.text: Symptoms onset within 24 to 72 hours, peak between days 2 and 6, and typically resolve within 1 to 2 weeks
Symptoms onset within 30 minutes, peak at 4 hours, and completely resolve within 12 hours
Symptoms do not appear until 4 weeks after cessation and persist indefinitely
Cannabis produces only psychological craving without any physical or physiological withdrawal syndrome
Withdrawal always culminates in life-threatening grand mal seizures and autonomic instability similar to delirium tremens

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Symptoms onset within 24 to 72 hours, peak between days 2 and 6, and typically resolve within 1 to 2 weeks.

DSM-5 Cannabis Withdrawal Syndrome occurs in heavy, prolonged users after abrupt cessation:
• Symptoms include: irritability, anger, aggression, anxiety, sleep difficulty (insomnia, strange/vivid dreams), decreased appetite/weight loss, depressed mood, and physical symptoms (sweats, chills, headache, abdominal pain).
• Time course: Because THC is highly lipophilic and stored in adipose tissue, it is slowly eliminated. Withdrawal begins within 24-48 hours, peaks at day 2-6, and gradually resolves within 1-2 weeks.
• Unlike alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, cannabis withdrawal is not fatal and does not cause seizures or delirium tremens.

stem: Synthetic cannabinoids (often sold illicitly under street names such as 'K2' or 'Spice') carry a significantly higher risk of severe toxicity, agitation, psychosis, tachyarrhythmias, and death compared to natural cannabis. What pharmacological property accounts for the dramatically increased toxicity of synthetic cannabinoids?

options.text: Synthetic cannabinoids act as high-potency, full agonists at the CB1 receptor with high intrinsic activity, whereas delta-9-THC is only a partial agonist
Synthetic cannabinoids selectively antagonize dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum
Synthetic cannabinoids contain high concentrations of pure cannabidiol
Synthetic cannabinoids are irreversibly cleared by pulmonary surfactant rather than hepatic metabolism
Synthetic cannabinoids block voltage-gated chloride channels in peripheral nerves

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Synthetic cannabinoids act as high-potency, full agonists at the CB1 receptor with high intrinsic activity, whereas delta-9-THC is only a partial agonist.

Pharmacological difference:
• Natural THC is a low-efficacy partial agonist at the CB1 receptor. Even at saturating doses, it achieves only partial receptor activation.
• Illicit synthetic cannabinoids (e.g., JWH-018, AM-2201) are full agonists at CB1 with binding affinities up to 100-800 times greater than THC. They produce maximal receptor activation without any modulatory CBD. This leads to profound toxic delirium, hallucinations, extreme tachycardia, acute kidney injury, seizures, and fatal cardiac arrhythmias.

stem: Why does a massive overdose of pure cannabis or delta-9-THC virtually never result in fatal respiratory depression, in stark contrast to overdoses involving opioids or barbiturates?

options.text: CB1 receptors are virtually absent in the brainstem medullary respiratory centers (pre-Bötzinger complex)
THC is rapidly hydrolyzed by serum cholinesterase within 5 seconds of entering the bloodstream
Cannabinoids directly stimulate medullary phrenic motor neurons to prevent hypoventilation
Cannabinoids stimulate central chemoreceptors in the carotid body to double the respiratory drive
CB1 receptors are coupled exclusively to excitatory Gs proteins in the central nervous system

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. CB1 receptors are virtually absent in the brainstem medullary respiratory centers (pre-Bötzinger complex).

Fatal opioid and sedative overdoses occur because mu-opioid and GABA-A receptors are heavily expressed in brainstem respiratory control centers (pre-Bötzinger complex and solitary tract nucleus), blunting responsiveness to arterial carbon dioxide.
In contrast, CB1 receptors have an extremely low density in brainstem cardiorespiratory centers. As a result, massive doses of cannabis cause sedation and intoxication without shutting down the brainstem respiratory rhythm generator, giving THC an extraordinarily wide therapeutic index.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the clinic because of worsening social withdrawal, paranoid delusions, and auditory hallucinations. A detailed family history reveals that her maternal uncle has schizophrenia. Epidemiological studies demonstrate that heavy, early-onset adolescent cannabis use is associated with a significantly increased risk of developing schizophrenia. Which polymorphism is associated with increased vulnerability to cannabis-induced psychosis in adolescents?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) Val158Met polymorphism.

Gene-environment interactions in cannabis-induced psychosis:
• Adolescents carrying the Val/Val genotype of the catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT) gene (which metabolizes dopamine) have a significantly higher risk of developing psychotic disorders and schizophrenia if they use cannabis during adolescent neurodevelopment.
• THC enhances mesolimbic dopamine transmission while disrupting prefrontal dopamine clearance, accelerating psychosis in genetically vulnerable individuals.

stem: Which of the following enzymes is responsible for the rapid degradation and intracellular inactivation of the endocannabinoid anandamide (AEA) following its cellular reuptake?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH).

Endocannabinoid degradation enzymes:
• Anandamide (AEA) is primarily hydrolyzed into arachidonic acid and ethanolamine by Fatty Acid Amide Hydrolase (FAAH), a membrane-bound serine hydrolase located in postsynaptic intracellular membranes.
• 2-Arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) is primarily broken down into arachidonic acid and glycerol by Monoacylglycerol Lipase (MAGL), located presynaptically.
• Pharmacological inhibitors of FAAH (or genetic FAAH mutations) increase endogenous anandamide levels, producing analgesia and anxiolysis without cannabis intoxication.

stem: A 32-year-old patient who uses cannabis regularly undergoes a routine urine drug screening. Although his last cannabis use was 3 weeks ago, his urine immunoassay remains positive for 11-nor-9-carboxy-delta-9-THC (THC-COOH). What pharmacokinetic property of cannabinoids explains this prolonged detection window?

options.text: High lipophilicity with extensive sequestration in adipose tissue, followed by slow, prolonged redistribution into the circulation and elimination
Covalent irreversible binding to albumin in plasma preventing glomerular filtration
Continuous endogenous de novo synthesis of THC by bone marrow adipocytes
Enterohepatic recirculation driven by bacterial beta-glucuronidase that multiplies drug mass
Storage in insoluble renal tubular calculi that slowly erode over months

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. High lipophilicity with extensive sequestration in adipose tissue, followed by slow, prolonged redistribution into the circulation and elimination.

Pharmacokinetics of THC:
• THC is extraordinarily lipophilic with a large volume of distribution (~10 L/kg). Following inhalation or ingestion, it rapidly distributes into highly vascular tissues (brain, liver) and then partitions into body fat stores (adipose tissue).
• In chronic heavy users, THC slowly leaches back out of fat deposits into the bloodstream over days to weeks, where it is metabolized by hepatic CYP2C9 and CYP3A4 to 11-hydroxy-THC (active) and carboxy-THC (inactive THC-COOH), which undergoes glucuronidation and renal excretion. As a result, urine drug tests can remain positive for up to 30 days or longer in chronic users.

stem: Which of the following describes the mechanism by which cannabis consumption stimulates acute hyperphagia, colloquially known as 'the munchies'?

options.text: Activation of CB1 receptors in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus and olfactory bulb, enhancing appetite and odor detection while stimulating pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons to release beta-endorphin
Direct inhibition of lateral hypothalamic orexin synthesis
Profound suppression of circulating ghrelin levels in gastric fundic glands
Upregulation of leptin receptor signaling in the ventromedial hypothalamus
Direct antagonism of neuropeptide Y (NPY) receptors in the gut

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Activation of CB1 receptors in the hypothalamic arcuate nucleus and olfactory bulb, enhancing appetite and odor detection while stimulating pro-opiomelanocortin (POMC) neurons to release beta-endorphin.

Cannabinoids stimulate appetite through multiple convergent central mechanisms:
1. Hypothalamus: CB1 activation in the arcuate and paraventricular nuclei paradoxically stimulates POMC neurons to release appetite-stimulating beta-endorphins and increases Neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) signaling.
2. Olfactory bulb: CB1 activation on cortical feedback projections enhances odor sensitivity and food aroma detection.
3. Nucleus accumbens: Enhances dopamine release, amplifying the hedonic reward value ('palatability') of food.

stem: A 10-year-old child with Dravet syndrome is treated with cannabidiol (Epidiolex) alongside clobazam for refractory seizures. At a follow-up visit, the parents report that the child has become severely somnolent, lethargic, and unsteady on his feet. Which pharmacokinetic drug interaction between cannabidiol and clobazam explains this clinical presentation?

options.text: Cannabidiol inhibits CYP2C19, leading to markedly elevated serum concentrations of N-desmethylclobazam, the active sedating metabolite of clobazam
Clobazam displaces cannabidiol from plasma proteins, increasing free active CBD by 500%
Cannabidiol induces CYP3A4, accelerating the conversion of clobazam into inactive glucuronide conjugates
Clobazam blocks intestinal absorption of cannabidiol via P-glycoprotein competition
Cannabidiol directly antagonizes GABA-A receptors, producing paradoxical sedation

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Cannabidiol inhibits CYP2C19, leading to markedly elevated serum concentrations of N-desmethylclobazam, the active sedating metabolite of clobazam.

High-yield drug interaction:
• Clobazam (a 1,5-benzodiazepine) is metabolized by CYP3A4 to N-desmethylclobazam (norclobazam), an active metabolite with a long half-life that mediates significant sedation.
• Norclobazam is further metabolized and cleared by CYP2C19.
• Cannabidiol is a potent inhibitor of CYP2C19. When co-administered, CBD causes a 3- to 5-fold increase in plasma concentrations of active N-desmethylclobazam, resulting in profound sedation, somnolence, drooling, and ataxia. Management requires reducing the dose of clobazam.

stem: An anti-obesity medication developed in the 2000s, rimonabant, was designed to suppress appetite by functioning as an inverse agonist/antagonist at the CB1 receptor. Although effective for weight loss, it was withdrawn worldwide due to serious neuropsychiatric adverse effects. Which adverse effects led to its withdrawal?

options.text: Severe depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation
Fulminant hepatic necrosis and liver failure

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Severe depression, anxiety, and suicidal ideation.

Rimonabant was a potent selective CB1 inverse agonist. By blocking endogenous endocannabinoid tone in the mesolimbic reward system and amygdala:
• It effectively reduced appetite and body weight.
• However, blocking tonic CB1 signaling in emotional processing circuits led to severe dysphoria, major depressive episodes, unprovoked panic attacks, and completed suicides. This led to its abrupt withdrawal from the global market and demonstrated the vital role of basal endocannabinoid tone in maintaining normal mood and emotional homeostasis.

stem: In the human hippocampus, cannabinoid CB1 receptors are heavily expressed on cholecystokinin (CCK)-positive GABAergic interneurons. How does exogenous delta-9-THC intake impair short-term memory encoding and working memory in humans?

options.text: Disrupts physiological theta and gamma oscillations and suppresses long-term potentiation (LTP) in CA1 pyramidal neurons
Causes immediate apoptosis of CA3 pyramidal hippocampal neurons
Irreversibly degrades acetylcholinesterase in the medial septum
Selectively blocks NMDA glutamate channels in the dentate gyrus directly
Stimulates microglial engulfment of dendritic spines in the entorhinal cortex within minutes

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Disrupts physiological theta and gamma oscillations and suppresses long-term potentiation (LTP) in CA1 pyramidal neurons.

Mechanisms of cannabis-induced memory impairment:
• High density of CB1 receptors in hippocampal CA1, CA3, and dentate gyrus. CB1 activation suppresses both GABA and glutamate release from hippocampal terminals.
• In the absence of coordinated physiological synaptic control, hippocampal theta and gamma oscillatory rhythms (necessary for synaptic synchronization and working memory) are desynchronized.
• Furthermore, tonic CB1 activation inhibits the induction of Long-Term Potentiation (LTP), impairing the consolidation of new short-term memories into long-term storage.

stem: A 42-year-old patient with chemotherapy-associated nausea asks about the differences between smoking/inhaling cannabis versus consuming oral cannabinoid edibles. What primary pharmacokinetic difference distinguishes oral ingestion of THC from pulmonary inhalation?

options.text: Oral THC undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism converting it into 11-hydroxy-THC, a more potent active metabolite with delayed onset and longer duration of action
Inhaled THC has a bioavailability of 100% and zero distribution to adipose tissue
Oral THC is completely destroyed by gastric hydrochloric acid and exhibits zero systemic absorption
Inhaled THC is metabolized exclusively in the pulmonary alveoli by carbonic anhydrase
Oral THC reaches peak plasma concentrations within 2 minutes of ingestion

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Oral THC undergoes extensive first-pass hepatic metabolism converting it into 11-hydroxy-THC, a more potent active metabolite with delayed onset and longer duration of action.

Comparison of cannabis routes:
• Inhalation (smoking/vaping): Rapid pulmonary alveolar absorption into arterial blood, bypassing hepatic first-pass metabolism. Onset within seconds to minutes; peak blood levels in 10-30 minutes; duration 2-4 hours.
• Oral ingestion (edibles): Slow, erratic GI absorption with heavy first-pass hepatic metabolism by CYP2C9 and CYP3A4. A major portion of delta-9-THC is converted into 11-hydroxy-delta-9-THC, a metabolite that readily crosses the blood-brain barrier and is more potent and psychoactive than delta-9-THC itself. Onset is delayed (30-90 minutes), peak is delayed (2-4 hours), and duration is significantly prolonged (6-12 hours), often leading to accidental overconsumption.

stem: Opioid receptors (mu, delta, and kappa) are class A G-protein coupled receptors. At the cellular level within the substantia gelatinosa of the spinal dorsal horn, what dual ionic mechanisms mediate opioid-induced inhibition of neurotransmission?

options.text: Closure of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (inhibiting glutamate and substance P exocytosis) and opening of postsynaptic G-protein-coupled inward-rectifying potassium channels (hyperpolarizing projection neurons)
Opening of presynaptic sodium channels and closure of postsynaptic chloride channels
Direct blockade of postsynaptic AMPA receptors and stimulation of presynaptic calcium influx
Closure of postsynaptic potassium channels leading to prolonged subthreshold depolarization
Opening of presynaptic calcium channels to activate calcineurin phosphatase

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Closure of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels (inhibiting glutamate and substance P exocytosis) and opening of postsynaptic G-protein-coupled inward-rectifying potassium channels (hyperpolarizing projection neurons).

Opioid receptors couple to inhibitory Gi/o proteins to block pain transmission via two simultaneous actions:
1. Presynaptic action: In primary nociceptive afferents (A-delta and C fibers), activated G-beta/gamma subunits bind to and inhibit voltage-gated Ca2+ channels (N-type and P/Q-type). This prevents calcium entry upon action potential arrival, blocking exocytosis of Substance P, CGRP, and glutamate.
2. Postsynaptic action: In second-order spinothalamic neurons, G-beta/gamma subunits open G-protein inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK) channels, allowing K+ to exit the cell. This produces hyperpolarization (IPSPs), making the second-order neuron resistant to firing.

stem: In the endogenous descending pain-modulating pathway, electrical or pharmacological stimulation of the periaqueductal gray (PAG) produces profound analgesia. How does activation of the periaqueductal gray recruit descending pathways to inhibit nociception at the spinal cord dorsal horn?

options.text: PAG neurons project to the rostral ventromedial medulla (nucleus raphe magnus) and locus coeruleus, which send serotonergic and noradrenergic fibers to activate enkephalin-releasing inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa
PAG axons project directly to peripheral pain receptors in the dermis to degrade bradykinin
PAG neurons release GABA directly into the corticospinal tract to inhibit lower motor neurons
PAG stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
PAG neurons activate thalamic VPL neurons to overwhelm the somatosensory cortex with tactile input

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. PAG neurons project to the rostral ventromedial medulla (nucleus raphe magnus) and locus coeruleus, which send serotonergic and noradrenergic fibers to activate enkephalin-releasing inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa.

Descending pain modulation circuit:
1. Midbrain periaqueductal gray (PAG) expresses high levels of mu-opioid receptors. Opioid binding disinhibits PAG projection neurons (by hyperpolarizing tonic GABAergic interneurons).
2. Excitatory projections travel from PAG down to the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM, specifically the Nucleus Raphe Magnus) and the Locus Coeruleus (pons).
3. Nucleus raphe magnus sends serotonergic (5-HT) fibers and locus coeruleus sends noradrenergic (NE) fibers down the dorsolateral funiculus into the spinal dorsal horn.
4. Serotonin and norepinephrine bind to alpha-2 and 5-HT receptors on local inhibitory interneurons in the substantia gelatinosa, triggering the release of endogenous opioids (enkephalin and dynorphin), which inhibit primary nociceptive afferents.

stem: A 58-year-old man with end-stage renal disease (ESRD) on hemodialysis suffers severe postoperative pain after femoral neck fracture repair. The intern orders high-dose intravenous morphine. Over the next 24 hours, the patient develops profound respiratory depression, altered mental status, and myoclonic jerks. Accumulation of which morphine metabolites explains this clinical presentation in renal failure?

options.text: Morphine-6-glucuronide (potent mu-agonist causing respiratory depression) and Morphine-3-glucuronide (neurotoxic metabolite causing myoclonus and hyperalgesia)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Morphine-6-glucuronide (potent mu-agonist causing respiratory depression) and Morphine-3-glucuronide (neurotoxic metabolite causing myoclonus and hyperalgesia).

Morphine hepatic metabolism produces two active glucuronide conjugates cleared by the kidneys:
1. Morphine-6-glucuronide (M6G): Highly active at mu-opioid receptors, with analgesic and respiratory depressant potency ~4 to 6 times greater than morphine itself. In renal failure, M6G accumulates, causing profound, prolonged coma and respiratory depression.
2. Morphine-3-glucuronide (M3G): Accounts for ~50-60% of morphine metabolites. It has no mu-opioid activity but is neurotoxic; accumulation produces central nervous system hyperexcitability, allodynia, myoclonus, and seizures.
• Morphine and codeine should be avoided in renal insufficiency; fentanyl or methadone (which lack active renally cleared metabolites) are safer alternatives.

stem: A 48-year-old woman with a history of major depressive disorder treated with sertraline (an SSRI) undergoes an orthopedic procedure. Postoperatively, she is administered intravenous meperidine for pain and shivering. Two hours later, she develops a temperature of 39.8°C (103.6°F), severe agitation, diaphoresis, hyperreflexia, and sustained ocular clonus. What pharmacological interaction caused this life-threatening condition?

options.text: Meperidine inhibits neuronal serotonin reuptake (SERT), interacting synergistically with sertraline to trigger Serotonin Syndrome
Meperidine accelerates hepatic conversion of sertraline into toxic metabolites
Sertraline competitively blocks mu-opioid receptors, causing acute opioid withdrawal
Meperidine and sertraline trigger malignant hyperthermia via ryanodine receptor gene mutation
Meperidine induces acute adrenal insufficiency by blocking 11-beta-hydroxylase

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Meperidine inhibits neuronal serotonin reuptake (SERT), interacting synergistically with sertraline to trigger Serotonin Syndrome.

Meperidine (Demerol) has unique pharmacological properties distinguishing it from other opioids:
• In addition to mu-opioid agonism, meperidine is a serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SRI).
• Co-administration with SSRIs, SNRIs, or MAO inhibitors leads to excessive intrasynaptic serotonin, causing Serotonin Syndrome (Hunter criteria: neuromuscular hyperactivity [hyperreflexia, clonus], autonomic hyperactivity [hyperthermia, tachycardia, diaphoresis], and altered mental status).
• Furthermore, meperidine's metabolite normeperidine lowers the seizure threshold. Meperidine also has atropine-like anticholinergic properties (mydriasis, tachycardia).

stem: A 34-year-old woman enrolled in a methadone maintenance program for severe opioid use disorder presents for an annual checkup. A routine electrocardiogram reveals a corrected QT (QTc) interval of 520 ms (normal <450 ms). What is the mechanism by which methadone causes QT prolongation and increases the risk of Torsades de Pointes?

options.text: Blocks human ether-a-go-go-related gene (hERG) voltage-gated potassium channels (IKr) in cardiac ventricular myocytes
Directly activates cardiac L-type calcium channels to prolong phase 2 plateau
Inhibits cardiac Ryanodine receptors causing intracellular calcium overload
Competitively antagonizes muscarinic M2 receptors on the SA node
Blocks fast voltage-gated sodium channels (phase 0) without altering repolarization

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Blocks human ether-a-go-go-related gene (hERG) voltage-gated potassium channels (IKr) in cardiac ventricular myocytes.

Methadone cardiac toxicity:
• Methadone is a full mu-opioid agonist and NMDA receptor antagonist with a very long elimination half-life (15-60 hours).
• However, it blocks the hERG-encoded rapid delayed rectifier potassium channel (IKr) in ventricular myocytes, delaying cardiac repolarization.
• This leads to concentration-dependent QTc prolongation, predisposing patients to the polymorphic ventricular tachycardia known as Torsades de Pointes, especially at doses >100 mg/day or when combined with other QT-prolonging drugs (e.g., fluconazole, ciprofloxacin, citalopram).

stem: A 29-year-old man with opioid dependence actively taking 80 mg of oxycodone daily presents to an addiction clinic. The physician administers a dose of sublingual buprenorphine. Within 45 minutes, the patient becomes violently agitated, sweating, shivering, and vomiting, with severe piloerection, abdominal cramps, and dilated pupils. What pharmacological property of buprenorphine precipitated this acute withdrawal state?

options.text: Buprenorphine has very high binding affinity for mu-opioid receptors but low intrinsic activity (partial agonist), displacing full agonists from the receptor
Buprenorphine is a pure competitive antagonist at mu, delta, and kappa receptors
Buprenorphine rapidly blocks GABA-A receptors in the locus coeruleus
Buprenorphine is metabolized into naloxone in the oral mucosa
Buprenorphine induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes within 30 minutes

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Buprenorphine has very high binding affinity for mu-opioid receptors but low intrinsic activity (partial agonist), displacing full agonists from the receptor.

Buprenorphine is a partial mu-opioid agonist with extraordinarily high receptor affinity:
• When administered to a patient who has full agonists (e.g., oxycodone, heroin, methadone) occupying their mu receptors, buprenorphine's high affinity allows it to displace the full agonist from the receptor.
• However, because buprenorphine has low intrinsic efficacy, net receptor signaling drops precipitously from 100% to ~30-40%.
• This abrupt drop in downstream signal transduction precipitates severe Precipitated Opioid Withdrawal. To avoid this, buprenorphine induction must occur only after the patient is already in mild-to-moderate spontaneous withdrawal (Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale [COWS] score ≥8-12).

stem: Suboxone is a widely prescribed sublingual film containing a 4:1 fixed-dose combination of buprenorphine and naloxone for maintenance treatment of opioid use disorder. What is the pharmacological rationale for adding naloxone to this formulation?

options.text: Naloxone has negligible sublingual/oral bioavailability due to extensive first-pass metabolism, but if crushed and injected intravenously, it blocks opioid receptors and precipitates immediate withdrawal to deter IV abuse
Naloxone synergistically enhances the analgesic and euphoric potency of sublingual buprenorphine
Naloxone prevents buprenorphine-induced QT prolongation in cardiac myocytes
Naloxone increases the sublingual absorption of buprenorphine across the oral mucosa
Naloxone accelerates the clearance of buprenorphine by inducing CYP3A4

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Naloxone has negligible sublingual/oral bioavailability due to extensive first-pass metabolism, but if crushed and injected intravenously, it blocks opioid receptors and precipitates immediate withdrawal to deter IV abuse.

Suboxone design:
• When taken sublingually as prescribed, buprenorphine is absorbed across the oral mucosa (~30-50% bioavailability). In contrast, naloxone has poor sublingual absorption (<10%) and undergoes >95% first-pass hepatic glucuronidation, rendering it pharmacologically inactive when taken by mouth.
• However, if an individual attempts to dissolve the film and inject it intravenously, naloxone enters the systemic circulation directly without first-pass clearance, where it potently blocks mu-opioid receptors and precipitates immediate, severe withdrawal. This acts as an abuse-deterrent.

stem: A 52-year-old woman with advanced ovarian cancer receives escalating doses of oral oxycodone for malignant pelvic pain. Over several months, she requires increasing doses to achieve pain relief. However, which of the following physiological effects of opioids NEVER exhibits tolerance despite chronic, high-dose therapy?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Miosis (pupillary constriction) and Constipation.

High-yield opioid tolerance concept:
• Patients rapidly develop tolerance to analgesia, euphoria, sedation, respiratory depression, and nausea through receptor desensitization (GRK phosphorylation and beta-arrestin recruitment) and receptor downregulation.
• However, tolerance does NOT develop to:
  1. Miosis (pinpoint pupils via parasympathetic Edinger-Westphal nucleus outflow).
  2. Constipation (inhibition of peristalsis and secretomotor transmission via myenteric and submucosal plexus opioid receptors in the GI tract).
• Therefore, chronic opioid users always require prophylactic bowel regimens (stimulant laxatives and stool softeners) to prevent obstipation.

stem: A 64-year-old man on chronic high-dose methadone for chronic back pain suffers from severe, refractory opioid-induced constipation (OIC) that has failed treatment with senna, docusate, and polyethylene glycol. The physician prescribes methylnaltrexone. Why does methylnaltrexone relieve constipation without reversing pain relief or precipitating opioid withdrawal?

options.text: Methylnaltrexone contains a quaternary amine group with permanent positive charge, preventing it from crossing the blood-brain barrier
Methylnaltrexone selectively antagonizes kappa-opioid receptors in the colon
Methylnaltrexone is degraded into glucose in the stomach and never absorbed
Methylnaltrexone stimulates smooth muscle motilin receptors exclusively
Methylnaltrexone activates central mu-opioid receptors while blocking peripheral muscarinic receptors

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Methylnaltrexone contains a quaternary amine group with permanent positive charge, preventing it from crossing the blood-brain barrier.

Methylnaltrexone (and naloxegol) are peripheral mu-opioid receptor antagonists (PAMORAs):
• Methylnaltrexone has a methylated quaternary ammonium group, giving it a fixed positive ionic charge and high polarity. It cannot cross the lipid bilayer of the blood-brain barrier.
• Consequently, it blocks mu-opioid receptors on the enteric nervous system (restoring intestinal motility and fluid secretion) without entering the CNS, completely preserving central opioid analgesia without precipitating central withdrawal.

stem: A 23-year-old man is found unresponsive in an alleyway with shallow respirations of 4/min, heart rate of 52/min, blood pressure of 90/58 mmHg, and pinpoint pupils (1 mm bilaterally). Intravenous naloxone (0.4 mg) is administered, and within 90 seconds his respirations increase to 16/min and he awakens. Given naloxone's pharmacokinetic profile, why must this patient be closely monitored in the emergency department for several hours?

options.text: Naloxone has a short elimination half-life (~30 to 90 minutes) and may be eliminated while longer-acting opioids remain active, leading to recurrent respiratory arrest ('renarcotization')
Naloxone irreversibly inhibits hepatic CYP3A4, causing delayed accumulation of endogenous epinephrine
Naloxone triggers delayed anaphylactic shock in >50% of patients after 3 hours
Naloxone transforms into morphine-6-glucuronide via serum transaminases
Naloxone induces permanent miosis that impairs neurological pupillary checks

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Naloxone has a short elimination half-life (~30 to 90 minutes) and may be eliminated while longer-acting opioids remain active, leading to recurrent respiratory arrest ('renarcotization').

Naloxone kinetics and emergency management:
• Naloxone is a competitive opioid antagonist with a rapid onset (1-2 minutes IV) but a short half-life of only ~30-90 minutes.
• Most abused opioids (methadone, extended-release oxycodone, or fentanyl analogs) have elimination half-lives or active depot kinetics lasting many hours or days.
• Once naloxone levels decline, uneliminated opioid molecules will reoccupy the vacated mu receptors, precipitating a lethal recurrence of respiratory depression ('renarcotization'). Patients must be observed for at least 2 to 4 hours (longer for methadone/ER formulations) and may require a continuous naloxone infusion.

stem: A 30-year-old pregnant woman in labor is administered intravenous butorphanol for labor analgesia. What are the receptor properties of butorphanol, and what unique psychiatric adverse effect is associated with kappa-opioid receptor agonism?

options.text: Kappa-receptor agonist and mu-receptor partial agonist/antagonist; kappa agonism produces dysphoria, hallucinations, and sedation
Pure mu-receptor full agonist; kappa antagonism produces extreme euphoria
Delta-receptor agonist and NMDA blocker; kappa agonism causes hyperthermia
GABA-A positive allosteric modulator and mu antagonist; kappa agonism causes insomnia
Selective CB1 receptor agonist; kappa agonism causes profound appetite stimulation

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Kappa-receptor agonist and mu-receptor partial agonist/antagonist; kappa agonism produces dysphoria, hallucinations, and sedation.

Mixed agonist-antagonists (Butorphanol, Pentazocine, Nalbuphine):
• Kappa-opioid receptor: Agonist. Produces spinal analgesia, sedation, and decreases postoperative shivering, but kappa activation inhibits dopamine release in the nucleus accumbens, producing dysphoria, depersonalization, psychotomimetic reactions, and vivid nightmares.
• Mu-opioid receptor: Antagonist or weak partial agonist. Causes less respiratory depression than full agonists (has a respiratory ceiling effect) but can precipitate acute withdrawal if administered to a patient dependent on full mu agonists.

stem: Which of the following cellular mechanisms mediates the lethal effect of acute opioid overdose leading to hypoxemic brain injury and death?

options.text: Direct suppression of the respiratory rhythm generator in the medullary pre-Bötzinger complex and blunting of brainstem chemoreceptor sensitivity to arterial hypercapnia (PaCO2)
Massive coronary artery vasospasm causing transmural myocardial infarction
Irreversible bronchoconstriction due to selective leukotriene D4 release
Complete paralysis of the diaphragm due to blockade of nicotinic receptors at the motor end plate
Rupture of pulmonary alveoli secondary to severe hypocapnia

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Direct suppression of the respiratory rhythm generator in the medullary pre-Bötzinger complex and blunting of brainstem chemoreceptor sensitivity to arterial hypercapnia (PaCO2).

Mechanisms of opioid-induced respiratory depression:
• Mu-opioid receptors are densely concentrated in the pre-Bötzinger complex (the pacemaker of respiratory rhythm in the ventrolateral medulla) and the nucleus tractus solitarius.
• Opioid activation hyperpolarizes these pacemaker neurons, decreasing respiratory frequency and tidal volume.
• Crucially, opioids shift the carbon dioxide response curve to the right, blunting the respiratory drive in response to elevated arterial PaCO2. Ventilation drops, severe respiratory acidosis develops, and the patient ceases breathing entirely, culminating in fatal anoxic cardiac arrest.

stem: A patient receives an intravenous bolus of morphine for severe acute trauma. Within 2 minutes, he develops intense facial flushing, warm skin, pruritus, mild bronchospasm, and a drop in blood pressure from 125/80 to 95/60 mmHg. Which mechanism explains this reaction, and does it represent an IgE-mediated type I hypersensitivity allergy?

options.text: Non-immunologic direct mast cell degranulation with histamine release via MRGPRX2 receptor activation; not an IgE-mediated allergic reaction
Classical type I IgE-mediated anaphylaxis requiring immediate lifelong avoidance of all opioids
Type III immune complex deposition in dermal and pulmonary capillary beds
Direct stimulation of vascular alpha-1 adrenergic receptors causing peripheral pooling
Rapid inhibition of angiotensin-converting enzyme by morphine metabolites

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Non-immunologic direct mast cell degranulation with histamine release via MRGPRX2 receptor activation; not an IgE-mediated allergic reaction.

Morphine, codeine, and meperidine stimulate mast cells directly through non-IgE pathways (specifically via the Mas-related G-protein-coupled receptor X2 [MRGPRX2]):
• This triggers direct histamine exocytosis, causing localized or generalized flushing, pruritus, urticaria, bronchospasm, and mild hypotension.
• This is a pseudoallergy (anaphylactoid reaction), not an IgE-mediated allergy. It can be pretreated with antihistamines or managed by switching to synthetic opioids (such as fentanyl), which do not trigger mast cell degranulation.

stem: A 45-year-old man undergoing general anesthesia for coronary artery bypass graft surgery is administered an intravenous push of high-dose fentanyl. Moments later, the anesthesiologist finds that manual bag-valve-mask ventilation has become virtually impossible due to extreme, board-like chest wall and abdominal muscle rigidity. What is this phenomenon, and what is the immediate treatment of choice?

options.text: Fentanyl-induced wooden chest syndrome (chest wall rigidity); treated immediately with a neuromuscular blocking agent (succinylcholine or rocuronium) or naloxone
Malignant hyperthermia; treated immediately with intravenous dantrolene
Tension pneumothorax; treated immediately with needle thoracostomy
Acute bronchospasm; treated immediately with inhaled albuterol and epinephrine
Status epilepticus; treated immediately with intravenous lorazepam

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Fentanyl-induced wooden chest syndrome (chest wall rigidity); treated immediately with a neuromuscular blocking agent (succinylcholine or rocuronium) or naloxone.

Fentanyl wooden chest syndrome:
• Rapid intravenous administration of high-dose lipophilic synthetic opioids (fentanyl, sufentanil, remifentanil) can trigger acute chest wall and abdominal muscle rigidity mediated by central dopaminergic and GABAergic pathways in the striatum and locus coeruleus.
• The chest wall becomes board-like, preventing thoracic expansion and rendering bag-mask ventilation or mechanical ventilation impossible.
• Immediate management: Neuromuscular blocking agents (e.g., succinylcholine) to paralyze skeletal muscle, or intravenous naloxone to reverse opioid action, allowing prompt endotracheal intubation and ventilation.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is prescribed tramadol for moderate neuropathic pain after lumbar spine surgery. Which dual mechanism of action explains the analgesic efficacy of tramadol?

options.text: Weak mu-opioid receptor agonism combined with neuronal reuptake inhibition of norepinephrine (NET) and serotonin (SERT)
Potent kappa-opioid receptor agonism and selective COX-2 inhibition
Direct opening of GABA-A chloride channels and blockade of substance P receptors
Selective CB2 receptor agonism and inhibition of phosphodiesterase-5
Irreversible inhibition of voltage-gated calcium channels without any opioid receptor binding

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Weak mu-opioid receptor agonism combined with neuronal reuptake inhibition of norepinephrine (NET) and serotonin (SERT).

Tramadol mechanism:
1. Mu-opioid activity: Tramadol itself has very low affinity for mu receptors, but its hepatic CYP2D6 metabolite (O-desmethyltramadol / M1) is a significant mu-agonist with ~300x higher affinity.
2. Monoamine reuptake inhibition: The parent compound inhibits both norepinephrine transporter (NET) and serotonin transporter (SERT) reuptake, enhancing endogenous descending inhibitory pain pathways in the spinal dorsal horn.
• High-yield risks: Tramadol lowers the seizure threshold and carries a significant risk of Serotonin Syndrome when combined with other serotonergic medications.

stem: A 10-year-old boy undergoes adenotonsillectomy for obstructive sleep apnea. Postoperatively, he is prescribed liquid codeine for pain control. Within 12 hours of discharge, the child becomes unarousable and is found in cardiac arrest secondary to severe respiratory depression. Genetic testing reveals that the patient is a CYP2D6 'ultra-rapid metabolizer.' What pharmacokinetic explanation accounts for this tragedy?

options.text: Codeine is an inactive prodrug that requires CYP2D6 O-demethylation to become morphine; ultra-rapid metabolizers rapidly convert therapeutic doses of codeine into massive, lethal systemic levels of morphine
CYP2D6 ultra-rapid metabolizers fail to break down codeine, causing toxic accumulation of unchanged codeine
Codeine directly destroys pulmonary alveolar type II pneumocytes in patients with CYP2D6 duplications
CYP2D6 converts codeine directly into cyanide in pediatric hepatocytes
Codeine blocks the child's endogenous endorphin receptors irreversibly

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Codeine is an inactive prodrug that requires CYP2D6 O-demethylation to become morphine; ultra-rapid metabolizers rapidly convert therapeutic doses of codeine into massive, lethal systemic levels of morphine.

Codeine pharmacogenomics:
• Codeine has virtually no intrinsic analgesic activity (10-carbon methyl ether of morphine). It is a prodrug requiring hepatic CYP2D6 to undergo O-demethylation into active morphine (~10% of dose under normal conditions).
• Individuals with multiple functional gene copies of CYP2D6 (ultra-rapid metabolizers, ~1-10% of Caucasians and up to 29% of Ethiopians/Middle Easterners) convert codeine into dangerously high concentrations of morphine rapidly.
• In children following tonsillectomy, this produces fatal respiratory arrest. The FDA has issued a black box warning strictly contraindicating codeine and tramadol in children under 12.

stem: An over-the-counter antidiarrheal medication, loperamide, is a potent mu-opioid receptor agonist. Why does loperamide relieve diarrhea without producing central analgesia, euphoria, or respiratory depression at standard therapeutic doses?

options.text: Loperamide has poor oral bioavailability and is actively transported out of the brain back into the capillary lumen by P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters at the blood-brain barrier
Loperamide binds exclusively to kappa receptors and completely lacks mu receptor activity
Loperamide is completely degraded by gastric acid into inactive amino acids
Loperamide does not bind opioid receptors and works entirely as an osmotic laxative antagonist
Loperamide binds to albumin so tightly that it never dissociates in systemic tissues

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Loperamide has poor oral bioavailability and is actively transported out of the brain back into the capillary lumen by P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporters at the blood-brain barrier.

Loperamide pharmacology:
• Loperamide binds to mu-opioid receptors on the myenteric plexus of the gastrointestinal tract, decreasing circular and longitudinal muscle peristalsis and prolonging transit time.
• Although it is a potent mu-agonist, any small amount that crosses the blood-brain barrier is immediately recognized and extruded back into the bloodstream by the P-glycoprotein (MDR1 / ABCB1) efflux transporter on brain capillary endothelial cells.
• Note: Massive supra-therapeutic doses ('poor man's methadone') or co-administration with P-glycoprotein inhibitors (e.g., quinidine) can overwhelm the transporter, leading to central opioid toxicity and lethal cardiac arrhythmias (QT prolongation and QRS widening).

stem: Which of the following medications is a non-opioid, centrally acting antitussive (cough suppressant) that functions as an NMDA receptor antagonist and sigma-1 receptor agonist without producing significant mu-opioid analgesia?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Dextromethorphan.

Dextromethorphan is the D-isomer of the codeine analog levorphanol:
• Mechanism: Antagonizes NMDA glutamate receptors and acts as a sigma-1 receptor agonist in the medullary cough center, suppressing the cough reflex.
• Unlike the L-isomer (levorphanol), it has negligible affinity for mu or kappa opioid receptors and does not produce analgesia or physical dependence at therapeutic doses.
• At high recreational doses ('dexing', 'robo-tripping'), it acts as a dissociative hallucinogen similar to ketamine and PCP, and inhibits serotonin reuptake (risking serotonin syndrome).

stem: Which physiological mechanism is primarily responsible for the development of cellular and molecular tolerance to chronic opioid therapy at the level of the mu-opioid receptor?

options.text: G-protein coupled receptor kinase (GRK) phosphorylation of the receptor, leading to beta-arrestin binding, receptor uncoupling from G-proteins, and receptor endocytosis
Autoimmune antibody formation against mu-opioid receptors
Permanent covalent cross-linking of the receptor to presynaptic SNARE complexes
Exhaustion of vesicular calcium stores in the postsynaptic dendrite
Complete enzymatic destruction of spinal dynorphin by microglial proteases

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. G-protein coupled receptor kinase (GRK) phosphorylation of the receptor, leading to beta-arrestin binding, receptor uncoupling from G-proteins, and receptor endocytosis.

Molecular mechanism of opioid tolerance:
1. Agonist binding causes G-protein coupled receptor kinases (GRK2/GRK3) to phosphorylate serine and threonine residues on the C-terminal tail of the mu-opioid receptor.
2. Beta-arrestin is recruited to the phosphorylated receptor, physically blocking further interaction with Gi/o heterotrimeric G-proteins (receptor desensitization).
3. Beta-arrestin targets the receptor to clathrin-coated pits for internalization (endocytosis). Receptors are either degraded in lysosomes (downregulation) or dephosphorylated and recycled.
4. Concurrently, chronic Gi inhibition leads to compensatory upregulation of adenylyl cyclase (cAMP superactivation), requiring larger opioid doses to achieve the same inhibitory effect.

stem: A 32-year-old man who abruptly discontinued heroin 18 hours ago presents with severe dysphoria, diarrhea, rhinorrhea, lacrimation, piloerection ('goosebumps'), yawning, muscle spasms, and pupillary dilation. Which brainstem nucleus is the primary site of noradrenergic hyperactivity driving these autonomic manifestations of opioid withdrawal?
explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Locus coeruleus.

Pathophysiology of opioid withdrawal:
• The locus coeruleus (located in the dorsal rostral pons) is the primary noradrenergic center in the brain.
• Under normal conditions, chronic opioid use suppresses locus coeruleus firing via Gi-coupled mu receptors, prompting homeostatic upregulation of cAMP and PKA.
• When opioids are abruptly removed, the disinhibited locus coeruleus fires wildly, causing massive release of norepinephrine throughout the brain and spinal cord.
• This noradrenergic storm drives acute withdrawal symptoms: tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, piloerection (origin of 'cold turkey'), mydriasis, hyperreflexia, and anxiety.
• Clonidine (a central alpha-2 adrenergic agonist) dampens locus coeruleus outflow and is standard non-opioid treatment for withdrawal symptoms.

stem: A 21-year-old baseball player is struck directly in the right temple by a fastball. He loses consciousness for 30 seconds, awakens fully alert and conversant with a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15, and insists he is fine. Two hours later in the dugout, he develops an excruciating headache, vomits, and rapidly lapses into an unarousable coma with a blown, fixed right pupil. A non-contrast head CT will most likely demonstrate which characteristic finding?

options.text: Biconvex (lenticular), hyperdense extra-axial collection that does not cross cranial suture lines
Crescent-shaped (concave-convex), hyperdense extra-axial collection that crosses cranial suture lines
Hyperdensity filling the basal cisterns, sylvian fissures, and cerebral sulci
Punctate microhemorrhages at the gray-white matter junction and splenium of the corpus callosum
Hypodense wedge-shaped lesion confined to the middle cerebral artery territory

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Biconvex (lenticular), hyperdense extra-axial collection that does not cross cranial suture lines.

Epidural Hematoma (EDH):
• Classic presentation: Blow to the pterion (temporal bone) -> brief loss of consciousness -> 'lucid interval' (hours of normal neurological function) -> rapid secondary neurological deterioration as arterial bleeding expands.
• Mechanism: Laceration of the middle meningeal artery (a branch of the maxillary artery entering via foramen spinosum).
• Radiologic hallmark: Biconvex (lenticular or 'lemon-shaped') hyperdense extra-axial hematoma. Because the outer periosteal layer of the dura mater is tightly anchored to the skull at the cranial sutures, the expanding arterial blood cannot cross suture lines, causing it to push inward against the brain parenchyma.
• The fixed, dilated right pupil indicates ipsilateral uncal herniation with compression of CN III.

stem: An 82-year-old woman with mild cognitive impairment and chronic balance issues presents with 3 weeks of insidious, worsening morning headaches, progressive confusion, and unsteady gait. Her family recalls she had a minor fall from a chair a month ago without loss of consciousness. Non-contrast head CT reveals a crescent-shaped, hypodense extra-axial fluid collection along the left cerebral convexity that crosses cranial suture lines. What vascular structure is the source of this hemorrhage?

options.text: Bridging cortical veins draining into the superior sagittal sinus
Ruptured saccular aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery
Charcot-Bouchard microaneurysm in the lenticulostriate arteries
Cavernous portion of the internal carotid artery

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Bridging cortical veins draining into the superior sagittal sinus.

Chronic Subdural Hematoma (SDH):
• Mechanism: Tearing of the bridging cortical veins that traverse the subdural space from the cerebral cortex to drain into the superior sagittal sinus.
• Predisposing factors: Cerebral cortical atrophy (seen in the elderly and chronic alcoholism) increases the distance between the brain surface and the dural sinuses, stretching the fragile bridging veins so that even minor head trauma can shear them.
• Radiologic features: Crescent-shaped (concave-convex or 'banana-shaped') extra-axial collection. Because blood accumulates between the dura and arachnoid, it is not restricted by cranial sutures and can cross suture lines (limited only by dural reflections like the falx cerebri).
• Chronology on CT: Acute = hyperdense (bright); Subacute = isodense; Chronic (>2-3 weeks) = hypodense (dark) due to hemoglobin degradation.

stem: A 25-year-old unrestrained driver involved in a high-speed rollover motor vehicle collision arrives comatose with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 4. Emergency non-contrast head CT shows no skull fractures, no mass lesions, and no epidural or subdural hematomas, with only tiny punctate hyperdensities at the corticomedullary junction. However, susceptibility-weighted MRI (SWI) reveals extensive, widespread blooming artifact and microhemorrhages throughout the gray-white matter junction, corpus callosum (splenium), and dorsolateral midbrain. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Global cerebral ischemia secondary to cardiac arrest

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Diffuse axonal injury (DAI).

Diffuse Axonal Injury (DAI):
• Mechanism: High-velocity angular or rotational acceleration-deceleration forces that cause rapid deformation, stretching, and shearing of long axonal tracts at boundaries between tissues of differing densities (gray-white matter junction, splenium of corpus callosum, rostral brainstem).
• Clinical picture: Severe, immediate coma without a lucid interval and without a focal surgical mass lesion on initial CT. It is the most common cause of persistent coma and vegetative state following closed head trauma.
• Imaging: Routine non-contrast CT is frequently normal or shows only subtle petechiae. MRI (especially GRE or Susceptibility-Weighted Imaging [SWI]) is vastly superior, demonstrating widespread hypointense punctate foci with 'blooming artifact' from microscopic hemosiderin deposition.
• Histology: Axonal retraction balls (spheroids) and positive immunohistochemical staining for beta-amyloid precursor protein (beta-APP), which accumulates due to disrupted anterograde axonal transport.

stem: A 35-year-old construction worker falls 15 feet from scaffolding, landing on his head. On examination, he has ecchymosis behind his left ear over the mastoid process ('Battle sign'), bilateral periorbital ecchymosis ('raccoon eyes'), clear, watery fluid draining from his left ear, and hemotympanum. Which type of skull fracture does this patient have?

options.text: Basilar skull fracture involving the petrous temporal bone
Isolated orbital blowout fracture of the maxillary sinus floor

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Basilar skull fracture involving the petrous temporal bone.

Basilar Skull Fracture:
• Fractures involving the floor of the cranial vault (most commonly the petrous portion of the temporal bone, followed by orbital plate of frontal bone and cribriform plate of ethmoid).
• Classical signs:
  1. Battle sign: Postauricular ecchymosis over the mastoid process (indicates temporal bone fracture).
  2. Raccoon eyes: Periorbital ecchymosis without direct facial eye trauma (indicates anterior cranial fossa fracture).
  3. CSF rhinorrhea or CSF otorrhea: Clear drainage due to dural laceration (confirmed by testing for beta-2 transferrin, a protein unique to CSF).
  4. Hemotympanum: Blood behind the tympanic membrane.
  5. Cranial nerve palsies: Particularly CN VII (facial palsy) and CN VIII (sensorineural hearing loss/vertigo), which traverse the internal acoustic meatus of the petrous temporal bone.

stem: A 19-year-old snowboarder strikes a tree, sustaining severe cranial trauma. On arrival at the trauma center, his vital signs are blood pressure 195/105 mmHg, heart rate 44/min, and irregular, slow, gasping respirations (6/min). Pupils are unequal. This clinical constellation (hypertension with widened pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular respirations) is known as Cushing's triad. What pathophysiological crisis does Cushing's triad signify?

options.text: Life-threatening intracranial hypertension with imminent brainstem herniation
Hypovolemic hemorrhagic shock secondary to internal bleeding
Neurogenic shock secondary to complete high cervical spinal cord transection
Cardiac tamponade secondary to blunt thoracic trauma
Thyroid storm triggered by physical trauma

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Life-threatening intracranial hypertension with imminent brainstem herniation.

Cushing Triad (Cushing Reflex):
• Physiologic response to dangerously elevated intracranial pressure (ICP) that compromises cerebral perfusion pressure (CPP = MAP - ICP):
  1. Hypertension (with widened pulse pressure): Severe brainstem ischemia triggers a massive central sympathetic discharge, constricting peripheral arterioles to raise MAP in a desperate attempt to restore cerebral blood flow.
  2. Bradycardia: The severe hypertension stimulates carotid sinus and aortic arch baroreceptors, triggering compensatory parasympathetic vagal output that slows the heart rate.
  3. Irregular respirations (Cheyne-Stokes or ataxic breathing): Increased ICP causes mechanical compression and ischemia of the medullary respiratory centers.
• Cushing's triad is a late, ominous sign of impending brainstem herniation requiring emergency neurosurgical intervention and hyperosmolar therapy.

stem: An unconscious patient with an expanding right-sided epidural hematoma exhibits an uncal herniation. The medial temporal lobe uncus herniates inferiorly past the tentorium cerebelli. Which cranial nerve and which cerebral arterial territory are typically compressed first by this herniating mass?

options.text: Ipsilateral Oculomotor nerve (CN III) and Posterior cerebral artery (PCA)
Contralateral Abducens nerve (CN VI) and Middle cerebral artery (MCA)
Bilateral Optic nerves (CN II) and Anterior cerebral artery (ACA)
Ipsilateral Trochlear nerve (CN IV) and Basilar artery
Contralateral Trigeminal nerve (CN V) and Superior cerebellar artery (SCA)

explanation:
Correct Answer: A. Ipsilateral Oculomotor nerve (CN III) and Posterior cerebral artery (PCA).

Uncal (Transtentorial) Herniation:
• The uncus of the medial temporal lobe is displaced medially and inferiorly through the tentorial notch (incisura):
  1. Compression of ipsilateral CN III: Parasympathetic pupillomotor fibers run superficially on the outer dorsomedial surface of CN III.
